content: 茉莉花深度报道 文 / 孙亦然 中国政情撰稿人 中共二十届五中全会10月29日闭幕，公报第一次证实前中联部部长刘建超出了事：中纪委认定他严重违纪违法，中央政治局此前已开除他的党籍。他做了什么，公报没有说。 原始文件 网页 中国共产党第二十届中央委员会第五次全体会议公报 news.cn 打开 网页 中国共产党章程 news.cn 打开 网页 中华人民共和国公职人员政务处分法 npc.gov.cn 打开 要点 查明 刘建超去年7月30日在阿尔及利亚公开露面以后，再没有出现；9月底，中联部官网显示刘海星已接任部长。 查明 按中共党内的规定，开除中央委员的党籍要由全会三分之二以上多数决定；刘建超的党籍是政治局先开除、五中全会再追认，政治局作出时没有宣布。 查明 五中全会追认开除33人，比四中全会多19人；出席的中央委员和候补中央委员只有279人，是二十大选出人数的74%。 还不知道 刘建超到底做了什么，有没有被降为处级——公报只写了严重违纪违法，没有说是泄密、转移资产、贪腐还是别的问题。 我们的判断 到2027年6月30日，官方不会公布刘建超的具体违纪违法事实。这是因为，政治局开除他时没有宣布，全会追认时也只列了名字。 2024年7月，中共二十届三中全会「接受秦刚同志辞职申请」，免去这位前外长的中央委员职务，公报里他仍是「同志」。两年多以后，五中全会公报写到前中联部部长刘建超，用的词换成了「严重违纪违法问题」和「开除党籍处分」：中纪委关于他的审查报告获得通过，中央政治局此前开除他党籍的决定得到确认。从去年7月底他不再公开露面算起，官方沉默了一年多，这一次究竟交代了多少？ 只交代了结论。开除党籍是党内的最高处分，按官方记录，刘建超受到的处理比秦刚重得多；可是政治局哪一天作出这个决定、他做了什么、会不会被追究刑事责任，公报一个字也没写。外界知道的他被查的原因，全部来自未经证实的说法。 从外交部、中纪委到中联部 1964年2月出生的刘建超是吉林德惠人，资深外交官出身。2008年北京奥运期间，他以外交部发言人的身份开始受到注意；2009年3月中菲关系高度紧张之际，他由外交部新闻司司长调任驻菲律宾大使，之后改任驻印度尼西亚大使，2013年11月升任外交部部长助理。 2015年8月，他离开外交部进入纪检系统，任国家预防腐败局副局长（专职，副部长级）和中央纪委国际合作局局长，并担任中央反腐败协调小组国际追逃追赃工作办公室负责人，中央社形容这次任命「出人意料」。2017年4月，他出任浙江省委常委、省纪委书记，同年7月兼任浙江省监察委员会主任。2018年3月，他回到外事系统，任中央外事工作委员会办公室副主任；2022年5月接替宋涛出任中联部部长，同年10月进入二十届中央委员会。中央社、美国之音和香港01都报道过，他是下任外长的热门人选；美国之音还说，他也有望接替杨洁篪出任中央外办主任。 刘建超最后一次出访是在7月下旬：7月23日至24日在新加坡，25日至27日在约翰内斯堡出席解放运动峰会，28日至30日在阿尔及利亚。据中央社报道，他最后一次公开露面是7月30日在阿尔及利亚会见该国国家总体战略研究院院长穆贾希德。9月30日，中联部官网「部领导」一栏更新，显示原中央国家安全委员会办公室副主任、1963年4月出生的刘海星已经接任部长。 时间线：刘建超：从外交部发言人到被开除党籍——2008年，北京奥运期间任外交部发言人，开始受到注意；2009年3月，由外交部新闻司司长调任驻菲律宾大使，之后改任驻印尼大使；2013年11月，任外交部部长助理；2015年8月，调入纪检系统，任中央纪委国际合作局局长、国际追逃追赃工作办公室负责人；2017年4月，任浙江省委常委、省纪委书记，7月兼任省监察委员会主任；2018年3月，任中央外事工作委员会办公室副主任；2022年5月，接替宋涛任中联部部长，10月进入二十届中央委员会；2025年7月30日，在阿尔及利亚会见该国国家总体战略研究院院长，此后没有再公开露面；2025年9月30日，中联部官网显示刘海星已接任部长；2026年10月29日，五中全会公报确认中央政治局此前开除他党籍的处分。 政治局先开除，全会再追认 按中共党内的规定，给中央委员、候补中央委员撤销党内职务、留党察看或开除党籍的处分，必须由中央委员会全体会议三分之二以上的多数决定；全会闭会期间，可以先由中央政治局作出决定，等召开全会时追认。刘建超的党籍就是这样先由政治局开除、再由五中全会追认的。 公报确认开除党籍的共33人，刘建超是其中之一，名单上还有前中央军委副主席张又侠、前政治局委员马兴瑞。美国之音和香港01都指出，这个人数创下改革开放以来历届中央全会的最高纪录。党员的纪律处分有五种：警告、严重警告、撤销党内职务、留党察看、开除党籍；同一份公报给金监总局原局长李云泽的是撤销党内职务。一年前的四中全会确认开除何卫东、苗华等14人，这次多了19人，两次全会合计47人；再往前，2024年7月的三中全会确认开除的是李尚福、李玉超、孙金明3人。 出席全会的人也在减少。二十大选出中央委员205人、候补中央委员171人，共376人；这次出席的只有中央委员162人、候补中央委员117人，合计279人，比四中全会少了36人。香港01按官方公开资料计算，74%的出席比例是1978年改革开放以来最低的。全会同时按党章把卢东亮、包钢等10名候补中央委员递补为中央委员，四中全会递补的是11名。全会还决定，中共二十一大于2027年下半年在北京召开。 表：二十大选出的人数和一中、三中、四中、五中全会：出席的少了，开除的多了——二十大选出（2022年）：中央委员 205人，候补中央委员 171人，追认开除党籍 —；一中全会出席（2022年）：中央委员 203人，候补中央委员 168人，追认开除党籍 —；三中全会出席（2024年7月）：中央委员 199人，候补中央委员 165人，追认开除党籍 3人；四中全会出席（2025年10月）：中央委员 168人，候补中央委员 147人，追认开除党籍 14人；五中全会出席（2026年10月）：中央委员 162人，候补中央委员 117人，追认开除党籍 33人。 由正部级降为处级：只有明报这样说 香港《明报》引述消息说，刘建超被认定严重违纪违法，由正部级贬为处级；消息还说，他的问题比在三中全会「辞去」中央委员的前国务委员、外交部长秦刚严重很多，秦刚据悉被降为副部级（中央社在全会开幕第二天转述，未经证实）。中央社转述的报道还说，中纪委大约在今年初已经完成对他的审查报告（未经证实）。两天后的公报对他的职级没有任何说法。 从正部级降到处级，降了多少？按官方规定，公务员的领导职务从国家级正职、国家级副职、省部级正职一直排到乡科级副职，共10个层次。部长属于省部级正职，处级属于县处级，两者之间隔着省部级副职、厅局级正职、厅局级副职三个层次。按香港01的解释，县处级正职包括各县四套班子的正职领导。被撤职的人要按规定降低职务、职级和级别，同时降低工资和待遇。有中国媒体把这种连降多级的处理称为「断崖式降级」。2018年底，甘肃省人大常委会原副主任李建华、河南省人大常委会原副主任王铁被政务撤职，降为副处级非领导职务。 最接近的先例是前工信部长肖亚庆。2022年12月，他被开除党籍，由国家监委给予政务撤职处分，降为一级主任科员，办理退休手续。香港01的解释是，肖亚庆犯了错，但没有严重到要开除公职，所以按规定降低职级。如果刘建超被降为处级，他受到的就是和肖亚庆一样的处理：开除党籍，保留公职，按降低后的职级领工资和待遇。 为什么是他：几种说法 公报给中纪委和中央军委两份审查报告点到的每一个人，用的都是同一句「严重违纪违法问题」，从这几个字看不出刘建超的问题和名单上的其他人有什么不同。 《华尔街日报》去年8月引述知情人士报道，刘建超7月底结束海外工作返回北京后被带走，被拘留的原因尚未明朗（中央社转述，未经证实）。据中央社当时报道，中国网络上从8月8日起盛传他被带走，说法不一，有的说他可能涉及泄密，有的传他居间协助中国富豪把资产搬到海外（未经证实）；到去年10月，中央社又提到他传出涉贪腐被查，下落不明（未经证实）。 另一种说法与他访美有关。据中央社报道，刘建超2024年1月选在台湾总统大选的同时访美5天，见了美国国务卿布林肯，「国际能见度宛如中国外长」。据香港01转述的一篇报道，有消息指，他那年访美时，在官方正式宣布之前就以候任外长的姿态示人，这种不合政治规矩的举动引起了北京注意（未经证实）。 学者谈的是这一轮开除高层党籍的范围和代价。据中央社报道，淡江大学两岸关系研究中心的张五岳在一场解读二十届四中全会的座谈会上说，那时有中共高层、军方「反习」的传言，有的话应该只是习一派独大之下的成员彼此竞争、甚至相互举报，习基于零容忍不分亲疏一并处理，这在军事和外交上造成人才断层；以二十大时的外事系统看，属于外事系统的中央委员只有5个，到那时只剩下3个。10月29日，张五岳又对中央社说，五中全会强调「全面从严治党关键在从严治吏」，查有没有贪腐只是「基本款」，更重要的是政治忠诚与政治纪律，「21大前还会继续再反（贪腐），会继续从严治党」。三立新闻网去年8月综合外电报道，新加坡南洋理工大学助理教授骆明辉说，若刘建超真的被免职，可能影响中国外交部的士气，并进一步削弱北京高层外交政策的专业。 能和官方记录对上的，只有明报说的他的问题比秦刚严重很多。我们认为，其余几种说法里，访美时以候任外长的姿态示人这一说依据最多，泄密、帮富豪转移资产和涉贪腐几种说法依据最少。这是因为，前者出自一篇报道引述的消息，后者到现在都只是中央社报道的传言。不过，这条消息也只说那次访美引起了北京注意，没有说他是因为访美被查。张五岳说比查贪腐更要紧的是政治忠诚与政治纪律，这一点访美和泄密两种说法都对得上，分不出哪一种依据更多。本文的判断不取决于哪一种说法属实，因为不管是哪一种，官方都没有说。 不同意本文的人会说，公报本来就不是交代案情的地方，案情要等审判：2024年6月27日，中共中央政治局会议决定开除李尚福的党籍，把他的涉嫌犯罪问题移送军事检察机关；将近两年后的2026年5月7日，军事法院一审以受贿罪、行贿罪判处他死刑，缓期二年执行，期满减为无期徒刑后终身监禁。他们还会指出：据中央社报道，长期行踪不明的中央军委办公厅原主任方永祥，也是到这份公报才第一次被官方证实涉及严重违纪违法。我们同意这两点，刘建超的案情以后也可能写进起诉书或判决书。但上面李尚福那一次，开除的日期和移送都有记录；四中全会开幕前三天，国防部发言人张晓刚就宣布何卫东、苗华等9名将领被开除党籍。刘建超的处分，政治局作出时没有宣布。 接下来看什么 如果官方接下来公布刘建超的具体违纪违法事实，北京就只是把交代放在了全会之后，本文说的只公布处分、不公布理由就站不住。 第一，检察机关会不会对刘建超提起公诉，会不会有中央纪委国家监委的通报写明他的职级：若提起公诉，说明他涉嫌犯罪，要像李尚福那样被追究刑事责任；若通报写明职级，明报说的降为处级就有了答案；若到明年年中两样都没有，说明官方对他的交代就停在五中全会公报上。我们判断，到2027年6月30日，官方不会公布刘建超的具体违纪违法事实。这是因为，政治局开除他时没有宣布，全会追认时也只把他的名字列进名单，两次可以交代的时候官方都没有交代。 第二，二十一大召开前的全会还会追认开除多少人：若仍在两位数，说明到换届前中共还在大批开除中央委员会成员的党籍；若只有个位数，说明这类开除在换届前已经基本停下。我们判断，从现在到二十一大开幕，二十届中央委员会的全会还会再追认开除至少10人的党籍。这是因为，全会追认开除的人数从三中全会到五中全会一次比一次多；五中全会强调从严治吏，张五岳也认为二十一大前还会继续从严治党。 2022年，同样被开除党籍的前部长肖亚庆有一份通报，写明他能在较短时间内如实说明违纪违法事实、认错悔错、全额退缴违纪违法所得，所以「可予从宽处理」；刘建超的案子，官方至今只给了33人名单中的一个名字，和「严重违纪违法」这几个字。 茉莉花深度报道独立调研、撰写。 参考报道：世界新闻网（10月27日） · 德国之声中文网（10月28日） · 中央通讯社（台湾）（10月28日） · 新华社（10月29日） · BBC中文网（10月29日） · 纽约时报中文网（10月29日） · 法国国际广播电台 RFI 中文（10月29日）

title: PRC Escalates Political Warfare Against Philippines
zh_title: 中国升级针对菲律宾的政治战争
summary: 内容摘要：北京正在加紧针对菲律宾的政治战争。自2022年小费迪南德·马科斯政府上台以来，北京方面的紧张局势升级可能是因为它认为马尼拉在海上的自信和围绕台湾海峡的言论有所增强。中国政府于六月制裁了菲律宾国防部长吉尔伯托·“吉博”·特奥多罗，这是针对与其保持外交关系的国家的内阁官员采取的前所未有的举措。制裁阻止了任何降级的可能性，至少在特奥多罗离开他的职位之前是这样。是
content:
内容摘要：北京正在加紧针对菲律宾的政治战争。自2022年小费迪南德·马科斯政府上台以来，北京方面的紧张局势升级可能是因为它认为马尼拉在海上的自信和围绕台湾海峡的言论有所增强。中国政府于六月制裁了菲律宾国防部长吉尔伯托·“吉博”·特奥多罗，这是针对与其保持外交关系的国家的内阁官员采取的前所未有的举措。制裁阻止了任何降级的可能性，至少在特奥多罗离开他的职位之前是这样。北京的政治战也瞄准了菲律宾国内政治。菲律宾当局指责中华人民共和国（PRC）干涉选举，并与菲律宾副总统萨拉·杜特尔特（Sara Duterte）存在不当的财务联系。北京的回应是在菲律宾参议员弗朗西斯·托伦蒂诺提出中国干预选举的证据后对其进行制裁。中国行动的效果似乎有限。相反，这种影响力运动可能会煽动菲律宾民族主义，并推动该国与美国、日本和台湾走得更近。中华人民共和国正在升级针对菲律宾的政治战运动，以抹黑亲美派的名誉。总统小费迪南德·马科斯 (Ferdinand Marcos Jr.) 的政府，并促使一位更加包容主义的领导人在马尼拉 2028 年 5 月的总统选举中获胜。
马科斯于 2022 年当选，受到本国宪法的限制，任期为六年（《菲律宾共和国宪法》，1987 年 2 月 2 日）。近几个月来，中华人民共和国口头攻击菲律宾高级官员，制裁菲律宾国防部长，声称菲律宾巴丹群岛属于中国主权，并放大了支持马科斯政治对手之一的宣传言论。北京出于对马尼拉海上自信的愤怒而采取的策略可能会适得其反。它的行动将加剧该国已经面临的高度不信任，同时促使马尼拉与美国、日本和台湾走得更近。打制裁牌 长期以来，中国和菲律宾在南海主权争议问题上存在分歧。值得注意的是，中华人民共和国拒绝遵守 2016 年南海国际法庭做出的有利于马尼拉的裁决（中华人民共和国外交部 [MFA]，2016 年 7 月 12 日）。然而，两国历来都试图防止这些紧张局势破坏更广泛的双边关系。然而，近几个月来，中国对菲律宾采取了更强硬的态度，因为菲律宾采取了更加积极主动的防御姿态。马尼拉拒绝在南海问题上让步，深化与美国和日本的安全合作，并更加直言不讳地表达其对两岸和平的利害关系。
北京对国防部长吉尔伯托·“吉博”·特奥多罗保留了最严厉的待遇，认为他是马尼拉挑战其所谓“核心利益”的策划者。 6 月，特奥多罗在新加坡年度安全论坛香格里拉对话会上批评北京在其领海的侵略行为后，北京禁止他和他的家人进入中国领土并与中国实体开展业务（外交部，6 月 11 日）。 10 月，网易的一篇文章嘲笑特奥多罗是一位“可怜的支持率”的“代总统”，试图通过“创造一个低劣的支持率”来破坏总统府。

【原文 English Original】
Executive Summary: Beijing is ramping up its political warfare targeting the Philippines. Beijing’s escalation since the Ferdinand Marcos Jr. administration came to power in 2022 is likely due to what it perceives as Manila’s increased maritime assertiveness and comments surrounding the Taiwan Strait. The Chinese government sanctioned Philippine defense minister Gilberto “Gibo” Teodoro Jr. in June, an unprecedented step against a cabinet official of a country with whom it maintains diplomatic relations. The sanctioning forecloses any deescalation, at least until Teodoro leaves his position. Beijing’s political warfare is also targeting domestic Philippine politics. Philippine authorities have accused the People’s Republic of China (PRC) of election interference and of improper financial links with Philippine vice president Sara Duterte. Beijing’s response has been to sanction Philippine senator Francis Tolentino after he presented evidence of PRC electoral interference. The efficacy of the PRC’s actions appears limited. Instead, the influence campaign is likely stoking Philippine nationalism and pushing the country closer to the United States, Japan, and Taiwan. The People’s Republic of China (PRC) is escalating its political warfare campaign against the Philippines in a bid to discredit the pro-U.S. government of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and enable the victory of a more accommodationist leader in Manila’s May 2028 presidential election. Elected in 2022, Marcos is limited by his country’s constitution to a single six-year term ( Constitution of the Republic of the Philippines , February 2, 1987). In recent months, the PRC has verbally attacked senior Philippine officials, sanctioned the Philippine defense minister, claimed that the Philippines’ Batanes archipelago is under Chinese sovereignty, and amplified propaganda narratives that support one of Marcos’s political rivals. Beijing’s gambit, driven by anger with Manila’s maritime assertiveness, is likely to backfire. Its actions will aggravate the high levels of distrust it already faces in the country while pushing Manila closer to the United States, Japan, and Taiwan.   Playing the Sanctions Card The PRC and the Philippines have long been at odds over conflicting South China Sea claims. Notably, the PRC has refused to abide by a 2016 South China Sea international tribunal ruling in favor of Manila ( PRC Ministry of Foreign Affairs [MFA] , July 12, 2016). Yet both countries have historically sought to prevent those tensions from undermining the broader bilateral relationship. In recent months, however, the PRC has taken a hard line against the Philippines for its more proactive defense posture. Manila has refused to yield in the South China Sea, deepened security cooperation with the U.S. and Japan, and become more outspoken about its stake in cross-Strait peace. Beijing has reserved the harshest treatment for Defense Secretary Gilberto “Gibo” Teodoro Jr., whom it sees as the architect of Manila’s challenges to its so-called “core interests.” In June, after Teodoro criticized Beijing’s aggressiveness in its territorial waters at the Shangri-La Dialogue, an annual security forum in Singapore, Beijing banned him and his family from entering PRC territory and doing business with PRC entities ( MFA , June 11). In October, a NetEase article mocked Teodoro as an “acting president” (代总统) with “pitiful approval ratings” (可怜的支持率) trying to undermine the Presidential Palace by “creating a separate policy towards China” (制定另一套对华政策) ( NetEase News , October 15). While largely symbolic, the sanctions are still significant. They marked the first time Beijing has targeted a sitting cabinet official of a country whom it diplomatically recognizes. By defining the Philippine defense secretary as a direct geopolitical adversary, Beijing has closed off a key de-escalation ramp with Manila until he leaves his position.  [1] The PRC, meanwhile, may double down on the sanctions tool. In October, Chinese-language Philippine media, citing “well-informed sources,” warned that Beijing is “running out of patience” (失去耐心) with Manila. Among measures to punish the Philippines being considered is sanctioning a group of Filipino politicians considered “anti-China.” The article further stated that if the Philippines allows Taiwan to open a representative office in Cebu, Beijing could demand that Manila close some of its consulates in the PRC, including the one in Hong Kong ( Chinese Commercial News , October 21).  Claiming the Batanes In some cases, the PRC aims to pressure the Philippines through lower-level unofficial channels. For instance, at a June 30 academic symposium in Guangzhou, academics from Jinan University, Nanjing University, and the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences argued that the northernmost Philippine island province of Batanes, which is about 88 miles from Taiwan, belongs to the PRC. To support this argument, they claimed that the archipelago is a natural geographic extension of Taiwan that was governed by the Ming and Qing dynasties. The academics said that the symposium was convened in direct response to the launch of maritime delimitation negotiations between the Philippines and Japan ( South , July 2).   The National Historical Commission of the Philippines swiftly refuted the Chinese scholars’ claims about the Batanes, noting that Spanish records from 1687 show no Chinese governance, that Spain claimed the archipelago in 1783, and that the islands have long been considered part of the Philippines ( Philippine Daily Inquirer , July 10). PRC media commentaries suggest the Batanes claim is not just a response to maritime delimitation discussions Beijing opposes, but also reflects more deeply-seated security anxieties. Highlighting recent U.S.-Philippines military cooperation in the Batanes, a July commentary published by the Jiangxi provincial government said, “Holding a knife to China’s doorstep and calling it ‘defense’—that’s Manila’s real intention” (把刀子架在中国家门口，还说是“防御”。这就是马尼拉的真实算盘) It further accused the Philippines of using the Batanes as “a springboard for intervening in the Taiwan Strait” (干预台海的跳板) ( Sohu , July 15). Political Interference Arguably Beijing’s most aggressive political warfare moves against the Philippines are its direct interference in Manila’s domestic politics. In April 2025, Senator Francis Tolentino presented evidence during a Senate hearing linking the Chinese embassy in Manila to online disinformation campaigns against the Philippine government ahead of midterm elections the following month ( Philippine Daily Inquirer , April 24, 2025). That prompted President Marcos to order an investigation into the alleged election interference. The PRC’s foreign ministry spokesperson rejected these claims, insisting that it “adheres to the principle of non-interference in the internal affairs of other countries” (一贯奉行不干涉内政原则) ( PRC MFA , April 24, 2025). It subsequently sanctioned Tolentino, barring him and his family from entering the PRC and any business dealings with Chinese entities ( PRC MFA , July 1, 2025). New allegations have emerged that suggest deepening PRC meddling in Philippine politics. In October 2026, Manila’s National Security Council said that it would investigate reports of remittances totaling Philippine Peso (PHP) 319 million ($4.8 million) sent from the PRC to a company linked to the husband of Vice President Sara Duterte ( Daily Tribune , October 8). Duterte, the daughter of former president Rodrigo Duterte, is a political rival of Marcos, despite serving as vice president in his administration (In the Philippines, the offices of president and vice president are elected separately.) After the allegations surfaced, Sara Duterte was accused of improperly amassing wealth and impeached. Her trial is expected to run through December ( Philippine News Agency , October 27). Duterte denies the allegations, claiming the Marcos administration is using them to sideline a political rival ( Davao Today , October 7). Duterte’s public comments suggest, at a minimum, that she favors a more accommodating PRC policy than Marcos. She has consistently advocated for a less assertive stance on maritime sovereignty issues. At a recent press conference, she said that the Philippines is “becoming a troublemaker in Southeast Asia,” echoing PRC propaganda ( ABS-CBN , October 14). When Marcos warned that the allegations against her could constitute a grave national security threat, she said that the president’s statement “is a bold and dangerous challenge to China” ( OneNews , October 13). Chinese media has been supportive of Duterte. A Chinese scholar quoted by Global Times said “she holds relatively pragmatic stances,” in contrast to the Marcos administration’s “increasingly radical China policy” ( Global Times , October 13). Conclusion The PRC has intensified its political warfare campaign against the Philippines in recent months to undermine the Marcos administration, underscore its sweeping maritime territorial claims, and lend support to Filipino politicians it sees as friendlier to its interests. Yet thus far, Beijing’s strategy has failed to bear fruit.  Instead, the PRC’s heavy-handed tactics have stoked Philippine nationalism, allowed Manila to strengthen its alliance network, and exposed the vulnerability of Marcos’s Beijing-friendly political rivals. Even if Sara Duterte is found not guilty in her impeachment trial, her alleged close ties to the PRC and accommodationist approach to Beijing will be heavily scrutinized if she runs for president in 2028. Notes [1] The PRC has sanctioned other politicians, such as Tom Tugendhat in the United Kingdom and Marco Rubio in the United States, but only before they were promoted to cabinet-level positions. And since sanctioning Teodoro Jr., Beijing has also sanctioned two more cabinet-level politicians: Francis Fonseca, Belize’s foreign minister, and Gustavo Villate, Paraguay’s minister of information and communication technologies. However, the PRC lacks official diplomatic relations with Belize and Paraguay due to their official recognition of Taiwan. title: AI Lessons From Russia’s War in Ukraine
zh_title: 俄罗斯乌克兰战争中的人工智能教训
summary: 摘要：研究人工智能（AI）在俄罗斯乌克兰战争中的应用的中国军事作家得出的结论是，其决定性价值在于缩短杀伤链，而不是完全自主的武器。在他们的解读中，人工智能扮演着四个角色：将传感器数据转化为目标，加速规划和指挥，在干扰切断链路时使无人机保持在目标上，以及大规模生产宣传和深度伪造。这些角色都依赖于中国希望在国内控制的战斗数据、计算能力、芯片和人工智能模型。星链的战时限制
content:
摘要：研究人工智能（AI）在俄罗斯乌克兰战争中的应用的中国军事作家得出的结论是，其决定性价值在于缩短杀伤链，而不是完全自主的武器。在他们的解读中，人工智能扮演着四个角色：将传感器数据转化为目标，加速规划和指挥，在干扰切断链路时使无人机保持在目标上，以及大规模生产宣传和深度伪造。这些角色都依赖于中国希望在国内控制的战斗数据、计算能力、芯片和人工智能模型。星链的战时限制和俄罗斯对美国芯片的依赖都是警告。中国人民解放军 (PLA) 正在将这些经验教训转化为人工智能规划系统、无人部队以及国产大语言模型 (LLM) 的采购。一些人承认解放军的人工智能仍然主要用于辅助任务，这些作者承认这种学说落后于技术进步。编者注：本文是詹姆斯敦中国研究研究员 Sunny Cheung 撰写的关于俄罗斯乌克兰战争中中国教训的系列文章中的最新一篇。 8月2日，中央电视台播出了建军节系列纪录片《制胜》一集，展示了中国人民解放军空军的“智能打击计划系统”，使100多个战术单位能够进行同步打击（环球时报，8月3日）。
10月初，解放军中部战区部队开始从俄罗斯多国中心2026演习返回，无人机群向地面作战群提供精确的目标信息（环球时报，10月3日）。10月12日，国防大学联合作战学院的作者在《解放军报》上撰文称，人工智能（AI）已经“从作战辅助工具跃升为指挥保障系统的核心赋能引擎” （从作战保障辅助工具跃升为指挥系统的核心赋能引擎），以乌克兰的Delta和俄罗斯的Svod战斗管理系统为证（《解放军报》，10月12日）。这些事态发展表明，中国军事专家一直从俄罗斯乌克兰战争中汲取教训，他们认为这是对“智能化”战争（解放军的术语，即人工智能渗透到指挥和武器系统的战争）的首次重大考验。过去两年在军事期刊上发表的中国研究论文明确指出，人工智能对军事胜利的主要贡献是压缩杀伤链中从最初命令到执行打击的时间滞后。它通过协助完成四项主要任务来实现这一目标：寻找目标、做出决策、在干扰下进行打击以及发动认知战。
将数据转化为打击 中国研究人员对乌克兰作家所说的“滴滴打车”模式印象深刻，该模式以中国的 Uber 同类产品命名，在该模式中，小型部队通过战术应用程序接受零碎的打击命令，并报告执行情况。 2024 年 9 月，乌克兰国防部报告称，其“复仇者人工智能”平台通过分析无人机视频和固定目标，每周自动检测到约 12,000 个俄罗斯装备目标。相机，这给国防科技大学的研究人员留下了深刻的印象（乌克兰国防部，2024年9月23日；Zhang和Liang，2025年）。 [1] 华中科技大学教授、启元拉原首席战略研究科学家房超主导论文

【原文 English Original】
Executive Summary: Chinese military writers studying the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in Russia’s war in Ukraine have concluded that its decisive value lies in shortening the kill chain rather than in fully autonomous weapons. In their reading, AI plays four roles: turning sensor data into targets, accelerating planning and command, keeping drones on target when jamming cuts the link, and mass-produced propaganda and deep-fakes. Each of these roles rests on the combat data, computing power, chips, and AI models that the PRC wishes to control domestically. Starlink’s wartime restrictions and Russia’s reliance on U.S. chips serve as warnings. The People’s Liberation Army (PLA) is turning these lessons into AI planning systems, unmanned units, and procurement of domestic large language models (LLMs). Some concede that PLA’s AI is still used mainly for auxiliary tasks, with these authors acknowledging that doctrine lags technological advancements. Editor’s note: This article is the latest in an occasional series by Jamestown China Studies Fellow Sunny Cheung on Chinese lessons from Russia’s war in Ukraine. On August 2, China Central Television (CCTV) aired an episode of Zhisheng (制胜; “Victory”), an Army Day documentary series, showing a People’s Liberation Army (PLA) Air Force “intelligent strike-planning system” that enabled more than 100 tactical units to conduct synchronized strikes ( Global Times , August 3). In early October, troops from the PLA Central Theater Command began returning from Russia’s multinational Center 2026 exercise, where drone swarms fed precise target information to ground combat groups ( Global Times , October 3). And on October 12, authors from the National Defense University’s Joint Operations College wrote in the PLA Daily that artificial intelligence (AI) has “leapt from a combat auxiliary tool to the core enabling engine of the command-support system” (从作战辅助工具跃升为指挥保障体系的核心赋能引擎), citing Ukraine’s Delta and Russia’s Svod battle-management systems as proof ( PLA Daily , October 12). These developments show that Chinese military experts have consistently learned from Russia’s war in Ukraine, which they see as the first major test of “intelligentized” (智能化) warfare—the PLA’s term for war in which AI pervades command and weapons systems. Chinese research papers published in military journals over the last two years make clear that AI’s principal contribution to military victory is in compressing the time lag in a kill chain from the initial order to executing a strike. It does this by assisting with four primary tasks: finding targets, making decisions, striking under jamming, and waging cognitive warfare. Turning Data into Strikes Chinese researchers are impressed by what Ukrainian writers call the “Didi ride-hailing” (滴滴打车) model, named after the PRC’s Uber equivalent, in which small units accept piecemeal strike orders via tactical apps and report back when they have been carried out. In September 2024, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry reported that its “Avengers AI” platform automatically detected roughly 12,000 Russian equipment targets per week via analysis of video from drones and fixed cameras, something that impressed researchers at the National University of Defense Technology ( Ministry of Defense of Ukraine , September 23, 2024; Zhang and Liang, 2025).  [1] A paper led by Fang Chao (房超), a professor at Huazhong University of Science and Technology and former chief strategy research scientist at Qiyuan Laboratory (启元实验室), contends that the GIS Arta artillery app, a Ukrainian targeting app that matches artillery units with targets reported by drones and spotters, has slashed the time between receiving a fire order and striking a target from 20 minutes to just 30 seconds (Fang Chao et al., 2025).  [2] Researchers point to the whole process—from sifting through enormous volumes of drone and satellite feeds, to decoding intelligence gathered from intercepted communications and civilian tips, to the speed of target acquisition—as a model to emulate. Experts from the National University of Defense Technology believe that the PLA should treat private sector AI and big data capabilities as part of its arsenal, cataloguing them as “potential resources” (潜力资源) for conversion into military uses (Zhang and Liang, 2025).  [3] Li Chen (李晨) of Renmin University is more measured in his assessment, noting that although information-network operations and electronic warfare have figured heavily in the Ukraine conflict, they have not “paralyzed either side’s operational system” (未导致任何一方作战体系瘫痪) (Li Chen, 2025).  [4] Ultimately, he argues, the advantage from faster target identification has not been decisive. AI Making Decisions in the Command Post Several experts believe that AI will be instrumental in improving decision-making processes in future wars. An article in the journal Military Digest (军事文摘), for example, argues for the creation of “joint operations intelligent computing centers” (联合作战智算中心) and specialized large models trained on joint operations scenarios to deliver “dimension reduction strikes” (降维打击). This refers to attacks from a level of capability so far above the opponent’s that it cannot respond in kind, which could be used against “the U.S.-allied intelligentized combat system” (美盟智能化作战体系). In a future high-end conflict, the author writes, “what is fought over is information, what is fought with is algorithms, and what is contested is intelligence” (斗的是信息，打的是算法，争的是智能) (Li Zhongqiang, 2025).  [5] The PLA has made progress in using gathered intelligence in the decision-making process. The Global Times reported that the Air Force strike-planning system seen on CCTV can coordinate targets, formations, and successive waves of attack far more quickly than conventional planning ( Global Times , August 3). An aerospace editor at state-affiliated China Aerospace Daily reported the next day that intelligence gathered from PLA Air Force drones can be fed into an open-architecture system that relies on AI to evaluate it and “generate optimal operational plans in seconds or tens of seconds” ( Global Times , August 4). According to procurement records, PLA entities have issued tenders that explicitly call for tools based on DeepSeek and other domestically developed AI models, while university researchers use DeepSeek to examine battlefield scenarios and to improve drone-swarm targeting decisions ( Reuters , October 27, 2025; China Brief , October 27, 2025). However, members of the People’s Armed Police (PAP), the paramilitary police force under the command of the Central Military Commission, have acknowledged that PLA AI applications remain limited to auxiliary support functions such as answering queries and generating content, and lag foreign models in performance considerably. The application of AI in offensive combat remains at an exploratory stage (Li, Wu, and Wang, 2026).  [6] Experts at the PRC’s National Defense University see militaries moving toward a hybrid approach in which AI assists with various functions but humans make the final call (AI辅助推演、人类最终定夺)—something also referred to as “humans in the loop, machines speeding up” (人在回路、机在提速) ( PLA Daily , October 12). Ukraine’s new decision-support system Marichka is an early version of this kind of system. The same PLA Daily article voices fears, however, that if AI is integrated too deeply into decision mechanisms, “human-machine authority will be eroded in the pursuit of efficiency in war” (人机权责在战争中被效率侵蚀) ( PLA Daily , October 12). Mixed Views on Autonomy’s Decisiveness Autonomy addresses the problem of communications jamming. As Yang Zhen (杨震) of the China Electronics Standardization Institute wrote for the defense industry publication China Defense Conversion (中国军转民), “the core lesson of the Russia–Ukraine battlefield is that the electronic warfare environment determines the technology route” (俄乌战场的核心教训是电子战环境决定了技术路线), but fully autonomous use of lethal force is still far from being mainstream (Yang Zhen, accessed October 30, 2026).  [7] Autonomy is nevertheless widely understood to be potent, and Chinese defense-industry researchers have been quick to take note of the use of autonomy in Ukraine. An engineer at the 54th Research Institute of the China Electronics Technology Group Corporation (CETC) mentioned that Ukrainian forces now routinely use “last-mile” autonomy, in which a drone can identify a target, hone in on it, and make impact after communications with the operator are jammed. “Last-mile” autonomy boosts hit rates in a strike mission from 10–20 percent to 70–80 percent, and troops can learn to use the technology in under 24 hours (Hao Yunfeng, April 2025).  [8] Some PLA writers see autonomy as fully decisive. One author in the Military Digest urged the PLA to build forces around algorithms, stating that “algorithms are king, the system wins” (算法为王、体系制胜), and using Ukraine’s June 2025 Operation Spiderweb as evidence that “human-out-of-the-loop” (人在回路外) operations are increasingly common. Despite the piece’s enthusiasm, however, it makes unsupported claims about AI swarm coordination, and PLA doctrine lags behind its proposals (Liu Zhenggang, 2026).  [9] As authors from PLA Unit 63893 wrote in 2025, drone attack-and-defense theory in general “has not yet formed valuable combat guidance manuals or regulations” (尚未形成有价值作战指导手册、作战条例等) and called deeper research “a real and urgent task for us” (对我们来说是一项现实而紧迫的工作) (Liu Zhengtang et al., 2025).  [10] The PLA is instead focusing on building unmanned ground units and counter-drone capabilities. At the September 2025 military parade in Beijing, unmanned ground formations were described as capable of “remote control, autonomous action, and flexible grouping” (远程操控、自主行动、灵活编组) (Xinhua, September 5, 2025). In an exercise the following month, a PLA brigade trained counter-drone tactics, using equipment that could detect drones’ radio frequencies and match them to a catalog of more than 800 commercial drone models ( CSIS , October 7). Cognitive Warfare Offers Cheap Offensive Measures The fourth PLA use case for AI is deception. Military researchers have worked on deepfake technologies with the aim of deceiving, persuading, and shaping the cognitive battlefield. Deepfake technology is cheap—researchers at a Chinese military academy note that they can create a voice clone by using just a ten-second audio sample and that the cost of creating deepfakes has collapsed to the point that “the side defending against deepfakes always pays more than the side using them” (防御深度伪造技术的一方付出的代价总是要多于应用它的一方) (Gu Junwei et al., 2025).  [11] Rather than curbing deepfakes through detection, the paper recommends “offense as defense” (以攻代守), or the pre-emptive creation of deepfakes by the defensive side. By creating a flood of its own deepfakes, an army can seize the “cognitive high ground” (抢占认知域的高地). Doing so, the authors argue, will save money and prove effective. Another paper cites an example of Russian attempts to create low-quality websites that, when scraped for data to train large language models, pollute the dataset (Wang Ling et al., 2026).  [12] In this way, the authors argue, AI can be used to deceive the enemy, just as it is already used to deceive consumers. There is some debate about how effective these techniques can be. Writing in the PLA Daily earlier this year, an academic from the Academy of Military Sciences argued that AI enables more granular targeting of propaganda, turning propaganda wars from “flood irrigation” (漫灌) into more precise “drip irrigation” (滴灌) ( PLA Daily , April 13). By contrast, civilian scholars note that AI propaganda may not pay off. In Ukraine, they say, the sheer volume of AI-generated material led to massive fatigue and mistrust, and ultimately limited its influence (Shi and Huang, 2025).  [13] Fears of Hardware Dependencies The AI technologies empowering modern military capabilities rely on an array of software and hardware supply chains that are vulnerable. Chinese experts treat control of these resources as an essential military requirement. First, AI needs combat data for training. According to a Military Digest assessment of Russian military AI, Moscow started collecting combat data from unmanned combat systems in mid-2025 to train its AI models, which cannot be substituted by laboratories. Li Zhongqiang (李忠强), a PLA researcher, has called for “an all-army mechanism for reporting military training data samples” (全军军事训练数据样本上报机制) (Li, 2025).  [14] Second, AI needs hardware. The same Military Digest assessment notes that Nvidia’s Jetson Orin Nano, an edge AI computer, is used in Russia’s long-range Shahed drone, the MS001, while more than half of the key AI components in Russia’s unmanned systems are supplied by U.S. firms (Yuan Li et al., 2026).  [15] Third, AI needs networking. As Peking University researcher Pang Xun (庞珣) points out, SpaceX can unilaterally control the coverage area and functional scope of a sovereign state’s critical wartime infrastructure by deciding where its Starlink system is available (Pang and Qu, 2026).  [16] Gao Jixiang (高际香), a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, draws the conclusion from Russia’s experience of Western sanctions that only self-controlled AI can ensure the continuation and iteration of a nation’s AI system in the face of a blockade (Gao and Liu, 2026).  [17] Moscow has thus turned to its Chinese partners for assistance, with Sberbank cooperating on the “joint improvement and adaptation of open-source large language models” (开源大语言模型的共同改进和适配) ( S&T Daily , September 25, 2025). This assistance would be in conflict with Russia’s draft AI law, however, which excludes foreign software or components from its definition of “sovereign” models (Gao and Liu, 2026).  [18] Clearly, sovereignty is easier to claim than to achieve. Conclusion Chinese military writers interpret Russia’s war in Ukraine as one in which AI matters most as an accelerator—of targeting, planning, and strikes under jamming—and as a cheap amplifier of propaganda. They also observe that all of these innovations rest on data, chips, and networks that must be brought under national control. They are divided, however, on some of the other takeaways from the conflict. Some argue that the PLA should develop AI planning systems, unmanned formations, and domestically-produced large language models, while others argue that the PLA should focus instead on developing “upstream capabilities” (上游能力建设) such as intelligence, navigation, communications, and command-and-control, as well as operator training, arguing that these are better investments than drones (Huang and Yan, 2026).  [19] The establishment of a system-wide method for collecting training data, formation of special units to employ unmanned systems, and exercises designed to test unmanned systems in heavily-jammed environments are all worth watching out for in the coming months. After all, PLA officers are aware of the shortcomings of PLA doctrine, performance of AI models, and lack of combat experience, and Beijing wants to understand the war in Ukraine before having to fight its own. title: U.S.–PRC Competition Enters New Phase in Central Asia
zh_title: 中美竞争在中亚进入新阶段
summary: 执行摘要 美国国务卿马可·卢比奥最近对乌兹别克斯坦的访问标志着华盛顿为与北京在中亚竞争而采取的最具体的行动，特别是在关键矿产和互联互通方面。卢比奥强调，华盛顿不会强迫塔什干在美国和中华人民共和国之间做出选择，这与第一届特朗普政府更具对抗性的做法不同。美国对乌兹别克斯坦的接触仍然落后于中国的接触。就在卢比奥访问之前，中国宣布对乌兹别克斯坦投资 600 亿美元，而可能的投资额为 16 美元
content:
执行摘要 美国国务卿马可·卢比奥最近对乌兹别克斯坦的访问标志着华盛顿为与北京在中亚竞争而采取的最具体的行动，特别是在关键矿产和互联互通方面。卢比奥强调，华盛顿不会强迫塔什干在美国和中华人民共和国之间做出选择，这与第一届特朗普政府更具对抗性的做法不同。美国对乌兹别克斯坦的接触仍然落后于中国的接触。就在卢比奥访问之前，中国宣布对乌兹别克斯坦投资 600 亿美元，而美乌会议期间可能签署的交易额为 160 亿美元。同样的滞后现象也出现在美国的关键矿产优先领域。美国进口该地区约 2% 的关键矿产，而中国则进口近 50%。远离波斯湾和乌克兰的地缘政治热点，双重内陆的乌兹别克斯坦已成为美国和中华人民共和国之间竞争的新竞技场。 10月20日，美国国务卿卢比奥率200余人的美国企业代表团抵达撒马尔罕（达里奥10月14日电）。在该市历史悠久的中心广场上，卢比奥在讲话中表示，“我们现在就在这里”推进美国与乌兹别克斯坦的互联互通，就像历史上的丝绸之路通过该地区带来全球贸易一样（美国驻华大使馆，10 月 20 日）。
中国花了几十年的时间投资重振卢比奥提到的贸易路线。他在回应当地记者时承认“这是一场竞争”，但美国企业应该“有公平的机会参与竞争”（美国驻华大使馆，10 月 20 日）。北京预料到了华盛顿的示好，在卢比奥发表演讲三天前派遣总理李强前往塔什干。对于中国来说，乌兹别克斯坦是其连接欧亚大陆的重要合作伙伴。对于美国来说，该地区潜在的巨大关键矿藏提供了实现供应链多元化并减少其前沿技术行业对中国零部件依赖的机会（RFE/RL，10 月 21 日）。竞争掩盖了其他利益卢比奥的访问标志着自唐纳德·特朗普总统第一任期以来地区战略的变化。 2020 年，时任国务卿迈克·蓬佩奥 (Mike Pompeo) 提请人们注意中国虐待维吾尔人和哈萨克人的行为，认为这是中亚和中国之间潜在的隔阂（当前时间，2020 年 2 月 2 日）。最近夏天，当国务院试图迫使哈萨克斯坦在美国的 Pax Silica 计划和中国的世界人工智能合作组织之间做出选择时，对这种二元方法的担忧再次浮出水面（RFE/RL，9 月 17 日）。十月份的访问采取了一种不那么对抗性的方式。
卢比奥承认，“乌兹别克斯坦已经明确表示他们希望与所有人成为朋友”，但他表示，美国不希望强迫乌兹别克斯坦停止与其他国家对话或停止与其他国家合作（美国驻华大使馆，10 月 20 日）。这表明美国认识到中亚各国政府本身已成为更有能力的地缘战略参与者。他们现在可以有效地利用影响力，与比苏联解体以来任何时候都更广泛的参与者建立有利关系，包括他们之间的关系（《中亚时报》，9 月 23 日）。华盛顿正在寻求挑战

【原文 English Original】
Executive Summary U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s recent visit to Uzbekistan marked Washington’s most concrete push yet to compete with Beijing in Central Asia, especially on critical minerals and connectivity. Rubio emphasized that Washington would not force Tashkent to choose between the United States and the People’s Republic of China (PRC), unlike the more confrontational approach of the first Trump administration. U.S. outreach to Uzbekistan still trails PRC engagement. The PRC announced $60 billion in investment in Uzbekistan just before Rubio’s visit, as compared to a possible $16 billion in deals signed during the U.S.–Uzbekistan meetings. The same lag appears in the U.S. priority sector of critical minerals. The United States imports around 2 percent of the region’s critical minerals, while the PRC imports nearly 50 percent. Far from the geopolitical flashpoints of the Persian Gulf and Ukraine, double-landlocked Uzbekistan has become a new arena for competition between the United States and the People’s Republic of China (PRC). On October 20, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in Samarkand, accompanied by an American business delegation totaling over 200 people ( Daryo , October 14). On the city’s historic central square, Rubio said in his speech that “we’re here now” to advance U.S.–Uzbekistan connectivity, just as the historic Silk Road brought global trade through the region ( U.S. Embassy in the PRC , October 20). The PRC has spent decades investing in reinvigorating the very trade routes Rubio invoked. He recognized in a response to a local journalist that “it’s a competition,” but that American businesses should “have a fair shot to compete” ( U.S. Embassy in the PRC , October 20). Anticipating Washington’s overtures, Beijing dispatched Premier Li Qiang (李强) to Tashkent three days before Rubio’s speech. For the PRC, Uzbekistan is a critical partner in its efforts to connect Eurasia. For the United States, the region’s potentially vast critical mineral deposits offer an opportunity to diversify supply chains and reduce its frontier technology sector’s dependence on Chinese components ( RFE/RL , October 21). Competition Overshadows Other Interests Rubio’s visit marked a change in regional strategy since President Donald Trump’s first term. In 2020, then-Secretary of State Mike Pompeo drew attention to the PRC’s mistreatment of Uyghurs and Kazakhs as a potential wedge between Central Asia and the PRC ( Current Time , February 2, 2020). Fears of this binary approach recently resurfaced in the summer when the State Department sought to force Kazakhstan to choose between the United States’s Pax Silica initiative and PRC’s World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization ( RFE/RL , September 17). The October visit presented a less confrontational approach. Rubio acknowledged that “Uzbekistan has been clear that they want to be friends with everybody,” but said that the United States does not wish to force Uzbekistan to stop talking to somebody else or stop working with some other country ( U.S. Embassy in the PRC , October 20). This suggests a U.S. recognition that Central Asian governments have become more capable geostrategic players in their own right. They can now effectively wield leverage to gain favorable relations with a wider range of actors than at any point since the collapse of the Soviet Union, including among themselves ( Times of Central Asia, September 23). Washington is seeking to challenge Beijing’s dominance in Central Asia in critical minerals. After a regional minerals dialogue in 2024 and a White House summit in 2025, the United States signed a new investment framework with Uzbekistan in February 2026, targeting mineral exploration, extraction, and processing, along with plans for a joint investment company ( Reuters , February 18). Rubio’s visit was the next test of whether Washington could turn those ambitions into tangible investment. Nearly 300 representatives of American businesses accompanied him and announced potential deals worth around $12 billion ( Kun , October 25). Local media reports that almost 54 agreements were signed, including plans involving GE Aerospace, railway equipment manufacturer Wabtec, financial institutions such as Citigroup and BlackRock, and companies active in mineral development ( Gazeta , October 19). Surprisingly, the joint statement issued after the visit failed to mention critical minerals specifically. The statement emphasized supporting the development of Central Asian economies. It singled out the U.S. goal of helping Central Asia achieve its “export potential” by “developing innovative ways to increase value-added products within the region and [create] pathways to introduce these products to the international market” ( Department of State , October 19). It also added that the United States seeks to “foster a region where e-commerce flourishes, innovative solutions abound, and talented entrepreneurs thrive” by leveraging “secure and trusted technology, American technological excellence, and the growing technology sectors of Central Asia.” PRC–Central Asia Relations Exceed U.S. Outreach Even if realized, U.S. investments trail significantly behind the $60 billion that the PRC promised three days before the highly anticipated U.S. visit ( President of Uzbekistan , October 17). This disparity also shows up in the critical minerals sector. The United States imports just 2.1 percent of the region’s critical minerals, according to the Oxus Society’s Central Asia Resource Tracker, while the PRC imports almost 50 percent ( Oxus Society , accessed October 26). The pattern extends to broader trends in PRC–Central Asian trade, which topped $100 billion for the first time in 2025, of which Uzbekistan accounted for $16 billion ( Xinhua , January 18). In the broader region, the PRC is also the largest trade partner for isolated Iran and Afghanistan ( Ministry of Foreign Affairs , October 23, 2023). Model of the BYD Car Factory in Jizzakh Free Economic Zone displayed in the Tashkent Islamic Civilization Center (Source: Author’s photograph) Tashkent sees the PRC as being essential to its modernization. Beijing is investing in renewable energy and advanced manufacturing, and is spearheading major infrastructure projects such as the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway ( Xinhua , October 18). During a recent visit to Tashkent, the authors saw how prominently these investments feature in the country’s vision for the future. Inside the lavish, marble-clad, $150 million Center for Islamic Civilization, exhibits showcase Chinese-backed projects across Uzbekistan, including a scale model of BYD’s auto factory in the southern Jizzakh region. The exhibits illustrated how much the Uzbek government is promoting the PRC’s investments as part of its broader development ambitions. During his meeting with Li Qiang on October 17, President Mirziyoyev described Uzbekistan–PRC relations as enjoying a “golden age,” a phrase he had previously used in conversations with General Secretary Xi Jinping. He also reaffirmed Tashkent’s support for the PRC’s One-China policy and Beijing’s efforts to combat what Chinese officials call the “three evil forces” of terrorism, separatism, and extremism ( South China Morning Post [SCMP] , October 18). In an interview with the South China Morning Post , Zhu Yongbiao (朱永彪), a regional specialist at Lanzhou University, emphasized the breadth of the PRC’s commercial offerings, ranging from electric vehicles and renewable energy to ordinary manufactures. He argued that Chinese firms could provide products and solutions suited to individual Central Asian markets, which is “an advantage the U.S. simply lacks” ( SCMP , October 18). Model of New Tashkent Displayed at the Center of Islamic Civilization in Tashkent (Source: Author’s photograph) Conclusion Chinese commentary on Rubio’s visit has so far combined recognition of Washington’s growing ambitions in Central Asia with skepticism about its capacity to act on them. In the lead-up to the trip, Zhang Jiadong (张家栋), a professor at Fudan University’s Center for American Studies, argued that the U.S. was merely a “distant friend” (远方朋友) to the region ( Global Times , October 19). Central Asian governments welcome Washington’s engagement because it gives them greater leverage with the PRC. Unless U.S. investment follows, though, Washington will remain a “distant friend,” lagging the PRC in influence and access. The post U.S.–PRC Competition Enters New Phase in Central Asia appeared first on Jamestown .

title: China Claims GJ-21 Naval UCAV has Flown from Type 076 Sichuan LHD
zh_title: 中国声称GJ-21海军无人战斗机已从076型四川两栖攻击舰起飞
source: 航空报 The Aviationist（战机/无人机/防空）
summary: 中国海军表示，GJ-21已在配备电磁弹射器和拦阻系统的076型两栖攻击舰上完成首次起降。据中国军方于 2026 年 10 月 30 日宣布，中国 GJ-21 海军无人作战飞机 (UCAV) 在 076 型四川两栖攻击舰上进行了首次起飞和降落。这一进展首先由官方通讯社新华社和环球时报报道，随后由国防部和官方的中国军号社交媒体公布。
content:
中国海军表示，GJ-21已在配备电磁弹射器和拦阻系统的076型两栖攻击舰上完成首次起降。据中国军方于 2026 年 10 月 30 日宣布，中国 GJ-21 海军无人作战飞机 (UCAV) 在 076 型四川两栖攻击舰上进行了首次起飞和降落。官方通讯社新华社和环球时报首先报道了这一进展，随后国防部和中国军号官方社交媒体账号进行了宣传。军方将GJ-21描述为该国“首款舰载隐身侦察攻击无人机”，并称其“最近在076两栖攻击舰‘四川’号上首次成功起降”。然而，官方媒体和军方都没有发布任何实际飞行操作的官方图像或视频。这一进展正值美国海军推进自己的 MQ-25 Stingray 无人空中加油机计划之际。 MQ-25 主要设计为舰载加油机，还将提供辅助海上情报、监视和侦察 (ISR) 能力。黄貂鱼预计将有助于成熟无人舰载航空所需的技术和操作概念，为海军未来的协同作战飞机（CCA）机队奠定基础。
空中捕获的 GJ-21 飞行中，制动钩已放下。资料来源：中国互联网，来自 Andreas Rupprecht 迄今为止，GJ-21 一直与 076 型航母联系在一起，但也有人建议未来在传统航空母舰上进行操作，有人猜测这款无人机最终会在中国最新的航母福建舰上操作。在我们之前的报告中，我们评估过GJ-21可以为两栖任务群提供无人舰载情监侦和打击能力，有可能将侦察和精确攻击选项扩展到舰艇周围范围之外。中国首架舰载隐形侦察攻击无人机“GJ-21”最近在076两栖攻击舰“四川”号上首次成功起降。 51）。这是中国两栖攻击舰发展的又一重大突破，标志着中国海军现已具备在大型海上作战平台上操作固定翼隐形无人机的能力。四川舰（舷号51）于2024年12月27日下水，是我国自主设计研发的076型两栖攻击舰首艘。它采用自动着舰引导系统、新型综合动力系统、电磁弹射助降降落技术，可搭载固定翼无人机、直升机、两栖装备等。
自2025年11月首次海试以来，四川舰按照计划稳步开展各项海上试验，顺利完成各项设备调试和整体运行稳定性试验。#GJ21 #StealthDrone #UCAV #Sichuan #Type076 #LHA #AmphibiousAssaultShip #DroneCarrier #CatapultLaunchSystem #EMALS #PLA #Navy #ChinaMilitary #ChinaMilBugle — 中国军号(@ChinaMilBugle) 2026 年 10 月 30 日第一艘配备电磁弹射系统和战斗无人机的两栖攻击舰中国军号官方帐号强调了解放军海军“操作固定翼飞机的能力”

【原文 English Original】
The PLA Navy says the GJ-21 has completed its first takeoff and landing aboard the Type 076 amphibious assault ship, which is fitted with an electromagnetic catapult and arresting system. China’s GJ-21 naval Unmanned Combat Aerial Vehicle (UCAV) has reportedly conducted its first takeoff and landing aboard the Type 076 Sichuan amphibious assault ship, the Chinese military announced on Oct. 30, 2026 . The development was first reported by state news agencies Xinhua and Global Times , and subsequently publicized by the Ministry of National Defense and the official China Military Bugle social media account. The military described the GJ-21 as the country’s “first ship-borne stealth reconnaissance and attack drone,” saying that it “recently made its first successful take-off and landing on 076 amphibious assault ship, the ‘Sichuan’.” However, neither the state press nor the military released any official image or video of the actual flight operations.   The development comes as the U.S. Navy advances its own MQ-25 Stingray unmanned aerial refueler program. Primarily designed as a carrier-based tanker, the MQ-25 will also provide a secondary maritime intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) capability. The Stingray is expected to help mature the technologies and operational concepts needed for unmanned carrier aviation, laying the groundwork for the Navy’s future Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) fleet. Unofficial overhead capture of the GJ-21 in flight with the arrestor hook lowered. | Source: Chinese internet via Andreas Rupprecht The GJ-21 has so far been associated with the Type 076, but future operations from conventional aircraft carriers have also been suggested, with speculation about the drone eventually operating from Fujian, China’s newest carrier. In our previous reports, we have assessed that the GJ-21 could provide an amphibious task group with an embarked unmanned ISR-and-strike capability, potentially extending reconnaissance and precision-attack options beyond the ship’s immediate surroundings China’s first ship-borne stealth reconnaissance and attack drone “GJ-21” recently made its first successful take-off and landing on 076 amphibious assault ship, the “Sichuan” (Hull 51). This is another significant breakthrough in the development of China’s amphibious assault ship, indicating that the Chinese Navy now has the capability to operate fixed-wing stealth drones from large maritime combat platforms.  Launched on December 27, 2024, the Sichuan (Hull 51) is the first vessel of Type 076 amphibious assault ships designed and developed independently by China. It incorporates the automatic carrier landing guidance system, new integrated power system, and electromagnetic catapult-assisted takeoff and arrested landing technology, and is capable of carrying fixed-wing unmanned aircraft, helicopters, and amphibious equipment, etc. Since its first sea trial in November 2025, the Sichuan warship has been steadily conducting various maritime tests as planned, successfully completing the debugging of various equipment and overall operational stability tests. #GJ21 #StealthDrone #UCAV #Sichuan #Type076 #LHA #AmphibiousAssaultShip #DroneCarrier #CatapultLaunchSystem #EMALS #PLA #Navy #ChinaMilitary #ChinaMilBugle — China Military Bugle (@ChinaMilBugle) October 30, 2026 First amphibious assault ship with EMALS and combat drone The official China Military Bugle account emphasized the PLA Navy’s “capability to operate fixed wing stealth drones from maritime combat platforms.” The statement added: “[The Sichuan] incorporates the automatic carrier landing guidance system, new integrated power system, and electromagnetic catapult-assisted takeoff and arrested landing technology, and is capable of carrying fixed-wing unmanned aircraft, helicopters, and amphibious equipment, etc. Since its first sea trial in November 2025, the Sichuan warship has been steadily conducting various maritime tests as planned, successfully completing the debugging of various equipment and overall operational stability tests.” Type 076 + GJ-21 Stealth Drone Swarm China’s Type 076 amphibious assault ship is being fitted with the GJ-21 stealth carrier-based UAV. Flying-wing design, fluidic thrust vectoring for autonomous carrier landings, electromagnetic catapult launch. Estimated 30 drones per ship, over 2-ton internal payload, ~2,000 km combat radius and 12+ hours endurance. Extremely low RCS allows deep stealth penetration to clear air defenses, airfields and anti-ship sites before troops even hit the beach. It can also act as loyal wingman with the J-35. Unlike the US “Lightning Carrier” concept of F-35B on amphibious ships, limited by vertical takeoff payload and range, plus the risk and cost of every manned jet; the Type 076 uses electromagnetic catapults and stealth UAV swarms for higher launch rate, longer reach, better endurance and zero pilot risk. This upgrades amphibious warfare from bloody beach assaults into non-contact, industrial-scale stealth suppression. China knows its priority building advanced defense capabilities for the people! Not war! #Type076 #GJ21 #StealthUAV #ChinaMilitary #PLANA #AmphibiousAssault #ElectromagneticCatapult #LoyalWingman #F35B #AmazingChina #PeopleFirst #NavalPower #DroneSwarm — GeoPaul626 (@Paull626) August 10, 2026 Global Times additionally quoted Chinese military analyst Song Zongping, who described the GJ-21’s flight operations from the Sichuan as a “global first” and compared it to the U.S. Navy’s X-47B program. “[The] US X-47B carrier-based drone program was designed for aircraft carriers, yet multiple technical constraints led to its cancellation. By contrast, the GJ-21 program has advanced steadily with an efficient development timeline,” Song told GT . However, the comparison requires some qualification: the X-47B was an experimental demonstrator that successfully completed a series of carrier-aviation milestones before the UCAS-D (Unmanned Combat Air System – Demonstrator) program concluded in 2015. The Navy subsequently redirected its follow-on unmanned-aircraft effort toward the CBARS (Carrier-Based Aerial-Refueling System) aerial-refueling role, which evolved into the MQ-25 Stingray. Song further added that the GJ-21 may also operate from China’s other EMALS carrier, the Fujian. He argued that this would help “building the technical know-how for China’s third aircraft carrier to host manned-unmanned teaming, expanding the operational modes of carrier strike groups.”   Pre-Commissioning Unit: China’s first Type 076 amphibious assault ship, PLANS Sichuan (Hull 51), has completed the deck marking, and its electromagnetic catapult system and arresting gear have been installed in place. #PLA #Navy #AmphibiousAssaultShip #Sichuan #EMALS #DroneCarrier #ChinaMilitary #ChinaMilBugle — China Military Bugle (@ChinaMilBugle) July 5, 2026 GJ-21 and Sichuan evolution The announcement provides official confirmation of a capability that had been the subject of considerable open-source speculation. Initial indications of an Electromagnetic Launch System (EMALS) aboard the Sichuan Landing Helicopter Dock (LHD) emerged from photographs taken during the ship’s construction and launch. Official images of the Sichuan’s introduction in the People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) confirmed the catapult’s presence, but it was still not clear at the time whether it was meant for a drone. Open-source imagery and reporting provided further indications of progress, suggesting the Sichuan’s EMALS was tested with a sled load . Other imagery published between late 2025 and 2026 showed what appeared to be the GJ-21 flying with its arresting hook lowered , as well as a mockup of the tailless flying wing aircraft on the vessel and an image which appeared to show extended landing gear and a catapult launch bar .  Test de catapultage à charge morte du système EMALS à bord du navire d’assaut amphibie Type 076 Sichuan (51) https://t.co/lrfp5lwEDQ — East Pendulum (@HenriKenhmann) August 2, 2026 Subsequent official imagery confirmed that the Sichuan was fitted with a catapult and arresting system, with images showing the catapult being tested with trial loads . The Oct. 30 announcement now provides China’s first official confirmation that the ship has conducted takeoff and landing operations with the GJ-21. Leading Chinese military aviation researcher Andreas Rupprecht said on LinkedIn : “By late 2025, several GJ-21 aircraft were reportedly undergoing simulated EMALS launches and arrested landings at the PLAN’s land-based facility at Huangdicun. In early 2026, loading and deck-handling trials were conducted aboard the Sichuan using a mock-up.”  Type-076’nın EMALS testi https://t.co/AzCA7EuUkH — Enis Şenol (@senolenis) July 29, 2026 The GJ-21’s land-based variant, the GJ-11, had been officially unveiled in the 2019 parade. However, a section of China military watchers were still skeptical about whether the country will actually field a flying example of the GJ-11. Then, in November 2025, the GJ-11 suddenly appeared in an official video flying with a PLA Air Force J-20 and a J-16 , providing the first official visual confirmation of the drone in flight.

title: Party Pitches Global Governance in Xi’s Potemkin City
zh_title: 党在习近平的波将金城宣传全球治理

内容摘要：2026 年全球治理论坛由统战系统一部分的中国人民外交学会精心策划，旨在向世界其他国家展示中华人民共和国（PRC）作为技术乌托邦解决方案的仁慈提供者的形象。北京善于利用论坛等活动来增强其合法性并扩大其在国际体系中的影响力，该论坛结束了一年来令人印象深刻的共识建立，特别是在联合国，特别是在全球南方国家之间。成果包括关于制定新领域（深海、极地和外层空间）和新兴领域（人工智能和网络空间）国际规则的立场文件。各国还共同努力塑造国际人权制度，并得到了联合国难民事务高级专员的支持。该论坛的目标明显对西方怀有敌意。外交部长王毅的讲话指责美国奉行“垄断权力、实行双重标准”的模式，而中共智库《全球治理倡议》的一份报告则将北京的做法描述为“脱离了传统上西方主导的叙事框架”。十月底的四天内，中国共产党举办了一场雄心勃勃的活动，向外界宣示其全球领导地位。
This was the 2026 Global Governance Forum, which brought together members of the “strategic, political, academic, and business communities of 97 countries and international organizations” (来自97个国家和国际组织的战略界、政界、学界、工商界等代表) to provide a sheen of legitimacy to Beijing’s attempts to refashion the international system in a way that better reflects its interests.The forum’s theme was “Rebuilding Confidence and Cooperation: Changes Unseen in A Century and Reforming and Improving Global Governance” (重建信心与合作：百年变局与改革完善全球治理) ( Xinhua , October 26). United Front Fingerprints The primary host for the event was the Chinese People’s Institute of Foreign Affairs (CPIFA; 中国人民外交学会), a “mass organization” (群团组织) that operates under the direction of the Office of the Central Institutional Organization Commission. [1] Although it does not have direct ties to the Party’s United Front Work Department, the institute functions as part of the Party’s wider united front system—as do other mass organizations, such as the All-China Federation of Returned Overseas Chinese and the Chinese People’s Association for Friendship with Foreign Countries (China Brief, May 9, 2019 , June 21, 2024 ). The involvement of CPIFA, through which the Party works to shape foreign perceptions of the People’s Republic of China (PRC), is key to understanding the forum’s messaging function.
尽管习近平总书记在论坛期间通过歌颂党的“长征”英雄并加倍强调党内普遍存在的腐败问题来煽动民族主义，但论坛试图通过投射高科技未来的愿景来消除对国家持续存在的经济问题的担忧。论坛举办地雄安新区凸显了这次活动的宣传价值。雄安是习近平的标志性项目之一，是一座位于北京郊外的规划城市。政府声称其职能是通过搬迁非必要的政府办公场所来缓解首都的拥堵，但实际上远不止于此。雄阿

【原文 English Original】
Executive Summary: The 2026 Global Governance Forum was carefully stage-managed by the Chinese People’s Institute of Foreign Affairs—part of the united front system—to present an image of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) as a benevolent provider of techno-utopian solutions for the rest of the world. Beijing is adept at using events like the forum, which capped a year of impressive consensus-building, particularly at the United Nations, and particularly among Global South countries, to enhance its legitimacy and expand its influence within the international system. Outcomes included position papers on shaping international rules for new frontiers (the deep sea, polar regions, and outer space) and for emerging domains (artificial intelligence and cyberspace). Concerted efforts were also made to shape the international human rights regime, which received support from the UN High Commissioner for Refugees. The forum’s aims are explicitly hostile to the West. Foreign Minister Wang Yi’s speech accused the United States of pursuing a model that “monopolizes power and practices double standards,” while a Party think tank report on the Global Governance Initiative described Beijing’s approach as “breaking away from the traditionally Western-dominated narrative framework.” Over four days in late October, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) staged an ambitious event to stake its claim to global leadership to the outside world. This was the 2026 Global Governance Forum, which brought together members of the “strategic, political, academic, and business communities of 97 countries and international organizations” (来自97个国家和国际组织的战略界、政界、学界、工商界等代表) to provide a sheen of legitimacy to Beijing’s attempts to refashion the international system in a way that better reflects its interests. The forum’s theme was “Rebuilding Confidence and Cooperation: Changes Unseen in A Century and Reforming and Improving Global Governance” (重建信心与合作：百年变局与改革完善全球治理) ( Xinhua , October 26). United Front Fingerprints The primary host for the event was the Chinese People’s Institute of Foreign Affairs (CPIFA; 中国人民外交学会), a “mass organization” (群团组织) that operates under the direction of the Office of the Central Institutional Organization Commission.  [1] Although it does not have direct ties to the Party’s United Front Work Department, the institute functions as part of the Party’s wider united front system—as do other mass organizations, such as the All-China Federation of Returned Overseas Chinese and the Chinese People’s Association for Friendship with Foreign Countries (China Brief, May 9, 2019 , June 21, 2024 ). The involvement of CPIFA, through which the Party works to shape foreign perceptions of the People’s Republic of China (PRC), is key to understanding the forum’s messaging function. While General Secretary Xi Jinping spent the weeks surrounding the forum stoking nationalism by exalting the heroes of the Party’s “Long March” and doubling down on the Party’s endemic corruption issues, the forum sought to dispel fears of the country’s persistent economic problems by projecting a vision of a high-tech future. The venue for the forum, Xiong’an New Area, underscored the propaganda value of the occasion. One of Xi’s signature projects, Xiong’an is a planned city located just outside Beijing. The government argues that its functional role is to relieve congestion in the capital by relocating non-essential government offices, but in practice it is much more than this. Xiong’an is a hubristic project that, in under a decade, has sought to create a new type of digitally integrated city, incorporating the various emerging technologies that Beijing has championed in recent years. Foreign Minister Wang Yi (王毅), in his keynote speech at the forum, hit all of the propaganda points used in the Party’s messaging to describe the city. He called it “a project of millennial significance” (千年大计), “a city of the future” (未来之城), “a brand-new endeavor in exploring modernized governance” (探索现代化治理的崭新实践), and “an exemplar of high-quality development” (高质量发展样板) ( PRC Ministry of Foreign Affairs [MFA] , October 23). External observers have been more skeptical. Around the time that Wang Yi announced the Global Governance Forum earlier this year, the urban studies scholar Andrew Stokols wrote that Xiong’an “has been largely seen as a failure so far” ( Substack/Sinocities , May 20).  [2] The critique is largely based on concerns about the decision to build the city on a floodplain, the lack of demand from people wishing to relocate into the city, and the enormous investments made that are yet to realize returns. Xiong’an nevertheless has significant propaganda value. As Stokols notes, the city is a “showcase for a new ideology of the urban under Xi Jinping” (Stokols, 2025). [3] Its conceptual structure of three cities in one—the built environment above ground, an underground network of over 100 kilometers of utility tunnels below ground, and a digital twin in the cloud—is supposed to show the benefits of Chinese-style modernization and provide a model to the world. During the forum, a video pushed by a number of state media and PRC embassy accounts on Western social media platforms tried to dispel doubts about Xiong’an. But as of October 30, the short video, which is hosted by the Western, PRC-based influencer Tom Shanahan and funded by the Hebei International Communication Center, had accrued fewer than 200 views ( YouTube/iHebei , October 26). Participants literally signed on to the official narrative about Xiong’an at the forum, which the People’s Daily framed as “both a grand gathering of ideas on global governance and an important window for the world to observe China’s governance” (既是一场全球治理的思想盛会，也是世界观察中国之治的重要窗口) ( People’s Daily , October 25). After tours around the city, including to its “smart city innovation center,” all participants affirmed in the “Forum Vision Document” (论坛愿景文件) released at the event that “we … believe that the principles upheld in [Xiong’an’s] planning and construction have important reference value for reforming and improving global governance” (我们 … 认为雄安新区规划建设中秉持的理念对于改革完善全球治理具有重要借鉴意义) ( Xinhua , October 26). Xiong’an’s importance for international messaging is evident in the sensitivity about the topic within the PRC. Stokols recounts an attempt to interview officials involved in the city’s planning, but was rebuffed, with one professor declining to write a letter of introduction for fear of reprisals ( Substack/Sinocities , May 20). Blunter commentators have described Xiong’an as a “Potemkin metropolis” ( Hudson Institute , May 13). Human Rights Hypocrisy Among Forum Outcomes Beijing is adept at using events like the Global Governance Forum to enhance its legitimacy and expand its influence within the international system. Despite the fragile foundations of the event itself—echoed ironically in the choice of venue—the forum capped a year of impressive consensus-building, particularly at the United Nations, and particularly among Global South countries. Chinese experts have praised these efforts as helping the PRC “acquire the institutional capacity to coordinate positions and form a collective voice within the UN framework” (具备了在联合国框架内协调立场、形成集体声音的制度能力) ( Guangming Daily , October 26). Following Xi’s proposal of the Global Governance Initiative (GGI)—his fourth global initiative—at the Tianjin Summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization in September 2025, Beijing first set up a “Friends of Global Governance Group” at the UN in New York. This group has branches in Geneva and Vienna, and in May released a joint communiqué with signatories from over 60 countries ( PRC Mission to the UN , December 9, 2025; MFA , May 29; People’s Daily , May 30). In June, the State Council released a detailed white paper on “Building a More Just and Reasonable Global Governance System” (构建更加公正合理的全球治理体系), providing more detail on the specifics of Beijing’s plans to reform global governance ( SCIO , June 6; China Brief , June 26). Beijing already claims tangible results of the GGI, presenting the Hong Kong-based International Court of Mediation, the Shanghai-based World AI Cooperation Organization, and the Beijing-based World Data Organization as “vivid implementations” (生动实践) of the initiative ( Guangming Daily , October 26). Beijing’s sought to use the forum to advance its agenda in several key directions. Amid the expected advocacy for expanding the discourse power of Global South countries within the UN system, including through reforms to the UN Security Council, and reforming the global financial and trade systems, two areas of intent stood out. The first is Beijing’s desire to shape international rules in both new frontiers—such as the deep sea, polar regions, and outer space—and emerging domains—AI, cyberspace, and outer space. The clearest evidence for this was the release of a “Progress Report on the AI Capacity-Building Action Plan for Good and for All” (人工智能能力建设普惠计划〉进展报告) and a paper titled “China’s Position on Strengthening Outer Space Governance” (关于加强外空治理的中国立场) (MFA, October 23 ; October 26 ). As these and other documents released at the summit make clear, Beijing’s institutional and normative innovations are explicitly anti-Western. Wang Yi presented his audience with a “stark” (对比鲜明) choice between a model that “exalts strength, favors self-interest, monopolizes power, and practices double standards” (迷信实力地位，推行本国优先、少数垄断、双重标准) and one that “champions multilateralism, and upholds sovereign equality, mutual respect and international law” (践行多边主义，坚持主权平等、相互尊重、国际法治) ( MFA , October 23). A report released at the event by the Xi Jinping Thought on Diplomacy Studies Centre, meanwhile, lambasts the United States explicitly for “relying on self-defined legal standards such as the “effects doctrine” and “minimum contacts”, extends the reach of its domestic law infinitely across the globe, exercising jurisdiction without the consent of other states, even carrying out arrests on the territory of third countries, completely disregarding the legal sovereignty and judicial jurisdiction of the states where the conduct occurs.” It describes the GGI as “breaking away from the traditionally Western-dominated narrative framework of global governance, and avoiding the outdated discourse traps of ‘a strong country is bound to seek hegemony’ and ‘bloc confrontation,’” while criticizing the “rules-based international order” for serving as “an ideological tool for a small number of states to pursue hegemonism and construct a hierarchical order” ( Xi Jinping Thought on Diplomacy Studies Centre , October 2026). The outer space position paper, meanwhile, “opposes any country abusing its domestic laws to obstruct or impose unilateral sanctions on other countries’ external airspace activities” (反对一国滥用其国内法对他国外空活动设置障碍或进行单边制裁). Another area in which Beijing used the forum to press for material changes to the international system was in human rights. It was well placed to do so, as the event was co-organized by the United Nations Association of China, and its partners included the China Society for Human Rights Studies (中国人权研究会) and the China Foundation for Human Rights Development (中国人权发展基金会). Also in attendance were UN Under-Secretary-General for Policy Guy Bernard Ryder, the UN Human Rights Council’s Independent Expert on the Promotion of a Democratic and Equitable International Order George Katrougalos, and, most pertinently, the UN High Commissioner for Refugees Barham Salih. Remarkably, Salih praised Xi’s signature initiative, stating that the Human Rights Council “looks forward to building a close partnership with China … jointly addressing the refugee challenge within the framework of the GGI ” (期待同中方构建紧密伙伴关系，开展“以人为本”的合作，在全球治理倡议框架下共同应对难民挑战) ( People’s Daily , October 24). Such statements help fuel Beijing’s revisionist approach to the international human rights regime. As Wang Yi declared in his speech, the PRC “promotes the recalibration of global human rights governance” (推动校正全球人权治理), aiming to “place the right to development high on the multilateral human rights agenda” (将发展权置于多边人权议程突出位置)—in other words, to undermine individual human rights and censor critics of its own practices ( MFA , October 23). The report from the Xi Jinping Thought on Diplomacy Studies Centre made this unambiguous, arguing that “we must reject the misguided notion of ‘human rights above sovereignty,’ and make it clear that it is up to the people of each country to assess and improve their own human rights situation” ( Xi Jinping Thought on Diplomacy Studies Centre , October 2026). Holding the forum in Xiong’an only underscored the reality of Beijing’s approach to human rights. Not only were the homes of tens of thousands of villagers demolished to make way for the city, but the entire edifice is an exemplar of a technologically empowered surveillance state ( Substack/Sinocities , May 20). As an article in the People’s Daily lays out, the “Eye of Xiong’an” (雄安之眼)—which in English sounds unfortunately like the “Eye of Sauron”—integrates data feeds to allow for live monitoring of the entire city. And in the neighborhood of Nanwenying (南文营), which Xi inspected in 2023, “each of the more than 3,700 households has its own file” (3700多户居民‘一户一档’) that is “dynamically updated” (动态更新) every two months ( Xinhua , June 23, 2023; People’s Daily , October 24). Conclusion The success of the 2026 Global Governance Forum in Xiong’an is hard to assess. On the one hand, it was able to attract a diverse and influential international crowd: beyond the UN representatives listed above, World Economic Forum founder Klaus Schwab, former Chancellor of Germany Gerhard Schröder, the Asia Society’s John L. Thornton, and even New York Times columnist Thomas Friedman were in attendance; and prominent Western scholars, such as the political scientist David Shambaugh, sat on panels to opine on topics such as “Multilateral Solutions for Global Governance.” On the other hand, no world leaders made appearances, and Xi himself only sent a letter, which Wang Yi duly read out. The active politicians that did attend were largely those already clearly aligned with the Party (or with the Party in opposition to the West). The event itself nevertheless does appear to have advanced Beijing’s international standing. It helped show that the PRC is serious about changing the rules of the game and is building support to shape how the world approaches emerging frontiers and domains; and through its efforts to build new governance institutions and enlist other countries to endorse its initiatives and adopt its standards, it will continue capitalize on a lack of a positive vision from the rest of the world. Notes [1] Co-organizers of the event included Hebei’s provincial government, the Administrative Committee of Xiong’an New Area, United Nations Association of China, China Institute of International Studies, China Foreign Affairs University. The event’s partners included University of International Business and Economics, Renmin University of China, Red Cross Society of China, China International Communications Group, China Society for Human Rights Studies, and the China Foundation for Human Rights Development. [2] Andrew Stokols has previously written for China Brief : https://jamestown.org/analyst/andrew-stokols-100993/ . [3] Andrew Stokols, “A new city for a new era: Xiong’an as showcase of China’s evolving urban ideology,” Cambridge Journal of Regions, Economy and Society , Volume 18, Issue 2, July 2025, Pages 293–307, https://doi.org/10.1093/cjres/rsaf003 . The post Party Pitches Global Governance in Xi’s Potemkin City appeared first on Jamestown .

封面图：国民党蒋万安（左）、民进党沈伯洋（右）。 （资料来源：英联邦杂志） 台湾即将于 2026 年 11 月 28 日星期六举行“九合一”地方选举。虽然总统赖清德没有参加投票，但这次选举将成为台湾选民对国民党和民进党评价的首次重大选举考验。自2025年“大罢免”以来，“民主进步党”在不同城市进行选举，台北市长竞选可以说是两大政党之间最突出、最关键的战场。本分析旨在于 10 月 31 日两位候选人之间的正式政策辩论之前，提供 2026 年台北市长竞选的两大竞选背景。 台北市长选举的历史意义 台北市长选举一直备受关注，不仅因为台北作为台湾省会城市的地位，还因为这场竞选在国家层面的政治影响。历史上，台北市长竞选的候选人经常成为台湾总统选举的候选人。因此，今年的台北市长竞选被预计为“2028总统大选的开场小战”（2028总统大选的前哨战）。
表：选定的台北市长候选人和随后的政治角色。政治人物 党派 竞选台北市长年份 竞选总统年份 其他重要职务 陈水扁 民进党 1994 年（当选） 1998 年（落选） 2000 年（当选） 2004 年（当选） 民进党主席（2002-2004 年； 2007-2008) 马英九 国民党 1998 (当选) 2002 (当选) 2008 (当选) 2012 (当选) 国民党主席 (2005-2007; 2009-2014) 郝龙斌 国民党 2006 (当选) 2010 (当选) N/A 国民党副主席 (2014-2020) 谢长廷 民进党 2006 (落选) 2008 (落选) 民进党主席 (2000-2002) 驻日本大使 (2016-2024) 苏贞昌 民进党 2010 (落选) 2008 (落选) 民进党主席 (2005-2008; 2012-2014) 行政院院长 (2006-2007; 2019-2023) 柯文哲 (TPP, 台湾民众党) 2014 (当选) 2018 (当选) 2024 (落选) TPP 主席 (2019-2025) Sean Lien (连胜文) 国民党 2014 (遗失) N/A 国民党副主席 (2021-2025) (资料来源：作者编译)。左图：1994年竞选台北市长的民进党陈水扁（资料来源：BBC中文）。 /右图：时任国民党台北市市长马英九在 2006 年台北马拉松赛上发表讲话（来源：Wikimedia Commons）。随后，两人都利用台北市长的任期成功竞选总统。 “蓝北绿南”台北几十年来一直被广泛认为是国民党的据点，几乎没有例外。
自1994年台湾首次地方直选以来，台北市只选出了两位非国民党市长：1994年民进党的陈水扁；1994年当选的民进党陈水扁；以及2014年和2018年独立的柯文哲。就陈的情况而言，民主运动的势头很可能促成了他的胜利。 （1994年竞选中的另外两名候选人也平分了泛蓝选票。）然而，尽管陈水扁的市长职位满意度高达70%，但他在1998年的连任竞选中输给了马英九。这表明国民党在国内仍然拥有坚实的支持基础。
