summary: 内容提要 中华人民共和国（PRC）已成为俄罗斯无人机的主要外国供应商，提供发动机、导航部件和技术支持，一家中国国有公司现在也运输用于制造无人机碳纤维的前体。俄罗斯国营公司 Rosatom 于 2021 年开设了一家工厂，以结束俄罗斯对中国前体的依赖。然而，进口量持续激增，2026 年批准的新生产线再次寻求进口替代。俄罗斯向中国支付其无法大规模生产的商品的溢价不断上涨。与此同时，乌克兰不断扩大的长期需求
content:
内容提要 中华人民共和国（PRC）已成为俄罗斯无人机的主要外国供应商，提供发动机、导航部件和技术支持，一家中国国有公司现在也运输用于制造无人机碳纤维的前体。俄罗斯国营公司 Rosatom 于 2021 年开设了一家工厂，以结束俄罗斯对中国前体的依赖。然而，进口量持续激增，2026 年批准的新生产线再次寻求进口替代。俄罗斯向中国支付其无法大规模生产的商品的溢价不断上涨。与此同时，乌克兰不断扩大的远程打击威胁着关键的工业基地，这些工业基地的损失将加深俄罗斯对中国零部件的依赖。乌克PAN 前体是用于制造碳纤维的丙烯酸纤维，Alabuga-Volokno 在鞑靼斯坦的 Alabuga 经济特区开展业务，该经济区还拥有俄罗斯最大的 Geran 无人机工厂。这批货物被申报为民用纺织品，文件显示自 2022 年以来至少有八次类似招标。
这批货物是最新的证据，表明中华人民共和国 (PRC) 已成为俄罗斯无人机战争的主要外国供应商，其援助现已涵盖制造无人机的基本材料。它还暴露了俄罗斯国家原子能公司 (Rosatom) 在 2021 年做出的承诺的失败，当时该公司开设了一家旨在使俄罗斯摆脱中国前体的工厂（Rosatom，2021 年 11 月 22 日）。这种动态揭示了俄罗斯在制裁下实现自给自足的局限性，以及中国如何维持俄罗斯无人机行业。远程攻击无人机已成为俄罗斯打击乌克兰城市和基础设施的主要工具。据乌克兰情报总局 (HUR) 称，俄罗斯国家对 Shahed 型无人机的订单从 2024 年的约 12,000 架增加到 2026 年的超过 100,000 架，新型喷气动力 Geran-4 和 Geran-5 的产量已达到每月约 3,000 架（Ukrinform，6 月 1 日）。俄罗斯政府将无人机行业的发展视为技术独立的问题，目标是到 2030 年将该行业的自给率从 2024 年的 37.8% 提高到 81.1%（塔斯社，2025 年 1 月 9 日）。然而，实际上，扩张几乎在每个阶段都依赖中国供应商，从单个部件到完整的发动机和技术支持。
俄罗斯 Gerans 使用源自伊朗原始设计的德国发动机的中国仿制品，以及中国导航模块和调制解调器（基辅邮报，2023 年 12 月 10 日；The Insider，3 月 24 日）。第二架俄罗斯攻击无人机 Garpiya 使用来自厦门林巴赫的发动机，美国于 2024 年 10 月制裁了这家中国公司，作为美国首次指定与俄罗斯联合开发完整武器系统的中国公司的一部分（美国财政部，10 月） 2024 年 17 日）。尽管如此，随后发动机仍不断抵达，并被宣称为工业制冷机组，中国专家多次访问库波尔测试无人机并培训工作人员（路透社，2025年7月23日；RBC-乌克兰，2025年9月25日）。跨越更广泛的战场货品

【原文 English Original】
Executive summary The People’s Republic of China (PRC) has become Russia’s main foreign supplier of drones, providing engines, navigation components, and technical support, and a Chinese state-owned company now also ships the precursor used to make the drones’ carbon fiber. Russia’s state corporation, Rosatom, opened a plant in 2021 to end Russia’s reliance on Chinese precursors. Imports kept surging, however, and a new line approved in 2026 again pursues import substitution. Russia pays the PRC a rising premium for goods it cannot produce at scale. At the same time, Ukraine’s expanding long-range strikes threaten critical industrial sites, whose loss would deepen Russia’s dependence on Chinese components. Documents obtained by Ukraine’s Security and Cooperation Center (USCC) and shared with Politico in September revealed that Jilin Chemical Fiber Group, a Chinese state-owned company, had shipped 46 metric tons of polyacrylonitrile (PAN) precursor to Alabuga-Volokno, a subsidiary of Russia’s state corporation Rosatom ( Politico , September 4). PAN precursor is the acrylic fiber used to make carbon fiber, and Alabuga-Volokno operates in Tatarstan’s Alabuga Special Economic Zone, which also hosts Russia’s largest factory for Geran drones. The cargo was declared as civilian textile, and the documents point to at least eight similar tenders since 2022. The shipment is the latest evidence that the People’s Republic of China (PRC) has become the main foreign supplier of Russia’s drone warfare, and that its assistance now reaches the basic materials from which the drones are built. It also exposes the failure of a pledge that Rosatom made in 2021, when it opened a plant meant to free Russia from Chinese precursors ( Rosatom , November 22, 2021). This dynamic reveals both the limits of Russia’s drive for self-sufficiency under sanctions and how the PRC sustains the Russian drone industry. Long-range attack drones have become Russia’s main instrument for striking Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. According to Ukraine’s Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR), the Russian state order for Shahed-type drones grew from about 12,000 units in 2024 to more than 100,000 in 2026, and output of the newer jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 has reached about 3,000 units a month ( Ukrinform , June 1). The Russian government has framed the growth of its drone industry as a matter of technological independence, aiming to raise the industry’s self-sufficiency from 37.8 percent in 2024 to 81.1 percent by 2030 ( TASS , January 9, 2025). In practice, however, the expansion has relied on Chinese suppliers at almost every stage, ranging from single components to complete engines and technical support. Russian Gerans use Chinese copies of the German engine from the original Iranian design, along with Chinese navigation modules and modems ( Kyiv Post , December 10, 2023; The Insider , March 24). A second Russian attack drone, the Garpiya, uses engines from Xiamen Limbach, a Chinese firm the United States sanctioned in October 2024 as part of its first designation of Chinese companies for jointly developing a complete weapons system with Russia ( U.S. Treasury Department , October 17, 2024). Nevertheless, the engines kept arriving afterward, declared as industrial refrigeration units, and Chinese specialists visited Kupol repeatedly to test drones and train staff ( Reuters , July 23, 2025; RBC-Ukraine , September 25, 2025). Across the wider range of battlefield goods that Western governments have placed under export controls, the PRC accounts for about 75 percent of Russia’s imports ( Kyiv School of Economics , July 3). The precursor trade extends this pattern to the material from which the drones themselves are built. Carbon fiber keeps Russia’s drones light enough to carry fuel and explosives over more than 1,000 kilometers (621 miles) and increases stealthiness. The Geran-2 fuselage and wings are built on a carbon fiber structural frame, and the newer jet-powered Geran-5 has a carbon fiber skin, wings, and tail mounted on the internal airframe ( Ukrainska Pravda , November 25, 2023; New Voice of Ukraine , January 19). Without this material, drones would be heavier, sacrificing either range or payload.  Carbon fiber is only as good as its precursor. Research on carbon fiber production shows that the fiber’s mechanical properties depend heavily on precursor quality ( Progress in Materials Science , 2020). The precursor accounts for about half the cost of standard carbon fiber and more than three-quarters of the cost of fine grades used in aerospace ( Heliyon , October 2019). Producing it requires specialized expertise in polymer chemistry and fiber spinning, which Russia has long lacked. Until 2021, the PRC supplied about 80 percent of Russia’s precursor supply ( Economic Security Council of Ukraine , 2025). The war has further narrowed Russia’s options. Sanctions and export controls imposed since 2022 have cut Russia off from Western and Japanese high-grade fiber producers. In the first nine months of 2024, Chinese companies supplied 72 percent of Russia’s carbon fiber imports by weight ( Economic Security Council of Ukraine , 2025). The PRC has since become the world’s leading producer, holding more than half of global carbon fiber capacity in 2025, with Jilin Chemical Fiber as the world’s largest producer ( ATA Carbon Fiber Technology , 2025).  Rosatom’s precursor plant was meant to end this dependence. Opened at Alabuga in November 2021, it was designed to produce 5,000 tons of precursor a year and to replace the material previously imported from the PRC ( Rosatom , November 22, 2021). Trade data, however, show that Chinese precursors continued to arrive after the plant opened. Between March 2022 and January 2025, Alabuga-Volokno imported about 3,000 tons of Chinese synthetic yarn worth $21.4 million from two companies of the Jilin group ( Frontelligence Insight , August 21, 2025). Because each ton of carbon fiber requires 2 to 2.5 tons of precursor, these imports, at roughly 1,000 tons a year, would have produced about 400–500 tons of fiber, close to the 407 tons Alabuga-Volokno produced in 2022 ( Economic Security Council of Ukraine , 2025). Chinese precursors alone could have supplied almost the entire output of Rosatom’s fiber line, suggesting the domestic plant has not replaced Chinese supply. Since 2022, demand has risen sharply. By early 2024, Umatex, the Rosatom division that owns Alabuga-Volokno, reported that its carbon fiber plant was fully loaded and that customers were waiting in line for its output, a change it attributed to the growth of Russia’s civilian composites market ( Atomvestnik , April 1, 2024). The timing coincides with the expansion of drone production at Alabuga, however, where the plant has become an important source of carbon fiber for Shahed-type drones. In May, Russian officials approved a new Alabuga-Volokno line with its own precursor unit, due in 2027, and justified it as import substitution ( Politico , September 20; Ukrainska Pravda , September 21). Five years after the first plant opened, Rosatom is building a second to solve the same problem, implicitly admitting the 2021 plant did not end Russia’s reliance on Chinese precursors. Chinese assistance comes at a growing price for Russia. Moscow paid roughly 300 percent more for Chinese battlefield goods in 2025 than Beijing’s other customers did, and this premium has risen in step with Russia’s reliance on Chinese supply ( Kyiv School of Economics , July 3). The relationship is asymmetric. Russia depends on the PRC for materials it cannot produce at the required scale, while the PRC can set the price and terms. The optical fiber case shows what this dependence looks like when domestic production disappears altogether. Russia’s only optical fiber plant, located in Saransk, stopped working after Ukrainian drone strikes in the spring of 2025, which left Moscow completely dependent on Chinese optical fiber ( Militarnyi , February 26). For Ukraine, the case points to targets that are harder for Russia to replace than other defense-industrial infrastructures. A carbon fiber plant takes years to build and relies on highly specialized equipment; losing it would affect every drone that depends on its output, inflicting significant damage on the entire industry. It would raise the cost of war for Russia, as it would be forced to deepen its dependence on Chinese components to keep delivering drones to the frontline. Russia treats Alabuga-Volokno as a site worth protecting, as satellite imagery shows lattice towers built around the plant to carry nets against Kyiv’s long-range drones ( Institute for Science and International Security , August 27; New Voice of Ukraine , August 29). For Russia, the drone program is absorbing capacity once meant for civilian industry. Carbon fiber from the Alabuga plant was intended for civilian aviation and Rosatom’s nuclear fuel centrifuges, yet by 2030 up to 89 percent of the plant’s output is expected to go to defense enterprises ( Militarnyi , September 7). For Europe, sanctioning the Chinese side of this chain could be politically coherent and costly at the same time. When the European Union listed Chinese entities in its sanctions package in July, Beijing responded the following day by placing 14 European companies and institutions under its own export controls ( European Commission , July 22; South China Morning Post , July 24). Consequently, sanctioning Chinese suppliers such as Jilin would come at a cost, including for European defense companies that depend on Chinese components. The Jilin shipment is small in isolation. It confirms, however, that the PRC’s assistance to Russia’s drone industry now extends from engines and electronics to the materials used to build the drones. Rosatom promised in 2021 to end Russia’s reliance on Chinese precursors, and five years later it is building a second plant to reach the same goal, most plausibly because the first cannot produce the fine grades required by the drone program at scale. The rapid scaling of Ukraine’s long-range drone attacks poses a new threat to Russia’s carbon fiber supply chain, since plants such as Alabuga-Volokno now lie within reach of Ukrainian strikes. The post Russia’s Drone Surge Depends on Chinese Supplies appeared first on Jamestown .

content: 中美对标   @new_voa  ·  Oct 22 (上) 文章说：今天的中国，正在出现类似明朝的政治和社会特征。明朝初期曾经探索外部世界，但随后逐渐转向闭关锁国。统治者对外国的影响越来越警惕，强调恢复所谓正统的中华文明。习总近年来推动的意识形态政策，与明朝存在明显的相似之处。 例如，明朝压制某些外来宗教信仰；今天，北京推动基督教和伊斯兰教中国化。明朝强调儒r家伦2理和传统家庭秩序；习总则不断强调要求妇女发挥贤x妻良母、建设家庭文明的作用。这些政策不仅不能解决人口危机，反而可能让问题更加严重。 2013年至2024年，中国新登记结婚人数下降了约55%。越来越多女性希望接受教育、发展事业，拥有自主决定婚姻和生育的权利。但中共最高领导层全部由男性组成；他们仍然试图通过生育补贴、宣传多孩家庭，以及收紧离婚等措施，鼓励年轻人结婚生育。 这种政策忽视了年轻人的真实处境，也进一步加剧了男女之间的矛盾。中国人口在2021年达到约14亿的顶峰，此后每年减少300万到400万人，相当于每年少掉一座洛杉矶。按照作者引用的人口趋势，到2040年代，中国每年可能减少约1000万人。 另一个可能的解决生育率持续下降的办法，就是引进外国移民。韩国也曾经是一个相对封闭的社会，但为了应对劳动力短缺，已经开始接纳更多的外国劳工。如今外国居民约占韩国人口的5%。相比之下，外国居民只占中国人口的约0.1%。中共不断宣传外国文化渗透、间谍威胁和民族主义，可能让中国未来更难吸引外国劳工。 随着经济增长放缓、人口持续老化，中国面临的问题可能逐渐演变成更严重的社会不满。 但北京的应对方式，很可能不是进行制度改革，而是加强监控和维稳。文章预测，未来几十年，中共可能越来越倾向于把人口、经济，和社会问题，当成国家安全问题来处理；通过网格化管理、全面监控和政治压制，维持表面上的社会稳定。但是，压制不等于解决问题。(未完) (中) 明朝已经给我们提供了一个历史教训。到了16世纪末期，明朝已经出现严重的财政问题。长期战争和政府开支耗尽了国库。当时的改革家 张居正 试图扩大税基，让地主和权贵承担更多的财政负担。但这遭到了这些阶层的强烈反对。 1582年 张居正 去世之后，他推动的改革遭到推翻，甚至他本人也被追究。结果，国家财政负担最终落到了普通农民的身上。今天的中国也出现了类似的局面。 首先，中国的财政压力也已经开始显现。 一些地方政府出现赤字，甚至难以及时支付教师和公务员的工资和福利。与此同时，农村居民和农民工参加医保的个人缴费，在过去20年里平均每年上涨约20%。由于无力承担费用，近年来约8300万人退出了相关医保。最近，中共还开始大数据找人交社保。这些情况与明朝晚期的财政危机中，国家将负担不断转嫁给社会弱势群体的做法，非常相似。 明朝晚期的政治体系也逐渐陷入瘫痪。万历皇帝因为接班人问题，与朝廷官员长期对立。他在位后期，朝廷的大量奏z章无人批阅，重要官职长期空缺，官僚集团陷入严重的派系斗争。整个国家虽然仍然维持着庞大的行政体系，但最高层的政治僵局，已经严重削弱了政府的治理能力。 习总上台以后，政治权力重新向个人集中，官员们也越来越不敢纠正最高领导人的错误。疫情期间，上海官员发现，原本尝试采取相对精准的防疫措施与习总坚持的清零政策不一致之后，最终选择服从中央。 结果是，上海经历了长达两个月的严厉封锁，许多居民甚至无法稳定获得食物和药品。但上海市委书记李强没有因此失去政治前途，反而在2022年进入政治局常委，2023年成为国务院总理。这种政治环境向官员传递的信号是：执行最高领导人的意志，比解决实际问题更加重要。 这种政治瘫痪，也反映在中国的人口和社会保障政策上。中国长期实行较低的退休年龄。研究人员早已预测，覆盖约5亿城镇职工和退休人员的主要养老金基金，可能在2030年代中期耗尽。提高退休年龄的改革讨论了十多年，直到2024年才正式启动，而且要到2040年才能全部落实。(未完) (下) 习总长期掌权，官僚体系越来越缺乏自主决策能力，而接班人问题迟迟没有解决。到了2030年代或者2040年代，中国可能同时面临政治停滞、官僚体系衰弱，以及最高领导层的继承危机。 更值得注意的是，明朝最终并不是被某一个单独的问题击垮的。而是财政困难、政治瘫痪、社会不平等和自然灾害不断叠加，最终引爆的危机。 1620年代，明朝政府削减开支，导致原本担任驿站职员的 李自成 失去工作。后来他加入反叛势力，发动了起义；到了1630年代，严重的旱灾和饥荒，让大批走投无路的农民投靠李自成。1644年，明朝灭亡。 问题是，未来，中国如果为了应对财政危机，削减体制内人员的养老金和福利，会不会激起类似的不满？当政治制度长期无法解决社会矛盾时，看似不相关的问题，可能在某个时刻相互叠加，形成危机。 一些美国学者也担心，当中国领导层意识到国家实力可能已经接近顶峰、未来将面临更严重的人口和经济压力时，可能选择在形势进一步恶化之前，对台湾采取军事冒险。 很难想象，今天的中国可能面临类似明朝晚期的历史危机。但大国衰落往往不是因为某一天突然出现一个无法解决的问题。而是原本可以解决的问题，被统治者一再拖延；原本可以改革的制度，因为既得利益而无法改变；原本可以缓和的社会矛盾，在政治压制下不断累积。等到这些矛盾最终爆发时，往往已经太晚。 400多年前的明朝，曾经拥有庞大的疆域、人口和财富，却最终被财政崩溃、政治瘫痪与社会动荡拖入深渊。今天的中国当然不是明朝，历史也不会简单重复。但如果一个国家只能不断强化统治，却越来越无法解决自己的问题，那么再强大的国家机器，也不能够阻止它走向自己的黄昏。(完) https:// youtu.be/xrzgEVZXLNA?si =tuMtbmkcmC2mh41w 来自 @YouTube

title: Hong Kong police arrest man allegedly caught lacing cat food with rat poison
zh_title: 香港警方逮捕一名涉嫌在猫粮中掺入老鼠药的男子
summary: 一名 34 岁男子在给流浪猫准备的食物碗中掺入老鼠药，被动物福利志愿者发现，警方以涉嫌虐待动物罪逮捕了他。何的监控录像发布在Threads上。照片：截图来自@sum_nicholas。警方在周六的一份声明中表示，当天凌晨 3.37 分左右接到举报，称这名何姓男子在猫粮碗中下了毒药。志愿者设置的摄像头录制的监控录像拍下了他的行为，并在社交媒体上疯传，还有志愿者后来对峙的视频。
content:
一名 34 岁男子在给流浪猫准备的食物碗中掺入老鼠药，被动物福利志愿者发现，警方以涉嫌虐待动物罪逮捕了他。何的监控录像发布在Threads上。照片：截图来自@sum_nicholas。警方在周六的一份声明中表示，当天凌晨 3.37 分左右接到举报，称这名何姓男子在猫粮碗中下了毒药。志愿者设置的摄像头录制的监控录像捕捉到了他的行为，并在社交媒体上疯传，还有志愿者后来与他对峙的视频。警方简报称，到达现场的警员在嫌疑人身上发现了一包老鼠诱饵和一把14厘米水果刀，并以涉嫌虐待动物和持有攻击性武器的罪名逮捕了他。受污染的猫粮的图像。照片：@hksaar.io，来自 Threads。何先生被扣留作进一步调查，案件由深水埗警区重案组接手。警方声明称，此案中没有猫受到伤害。 “请不要伤害它们” 在志愿者与何先生对峙的视频中，何先生否认试图伤害这些猫，并表示他只是想阻止流浪猫吃这些食物，以保持该地区的清洁。志愿者回应称，中毒的猫只会死在公共场所，造成更多卫生问题。
视频中可以看到何鸿燊穿着一件跑步背心，上面贴有“狼天使”或“狼钩”徽章——这一符号起源于中世纪德国纹章，后来在纳粹象征主义中广泛采用。截获34岁的香港涉嫌虐待动物报告（HKSAAR）的动物福利组织之一在Threads上表示，它已经监视何鸿燊一个多月了。 Ho 的跑步装备上有 Wolfsangel 补丁。照片：线程。香港特别行政区早在六月份就发布了有毒猫粮的照片，当时它是由与之合作的另一个志愿者组织首次发现的。照片显示，干粗粮上覆盖着一层厚厚的黑色糊状物，水碗里还有疑似老鼠诱饵的蓝色颗粒。根据香港法律，虐待动物的最高刑罚为罚款20万港元和监禁三年。其中一名志愿者尼古拉斯·萨姆(Nicholas Sum)周日在一篇帖子中表示：“你不必爱他们，但请不要伤害他们。” “我们埋伏了整整一个月，终于抓住了他。”萨姆说。 “非常感谢所有猫类救援志愿者、当地邻居和香港特别行政区管理局连续多个通宵追捕（嫌疑人）。”

【原文 English Original】
Police have arrested a 34-year-old man on suspicion of animal cruelty after animal welfare volunteers caught him lacing bowls of food left out for stray cats with rat poison. Surveillance footage of Ho posted on Threads. Photo: Screenshot via @sum_nicholas. In a Saturday statement, police said that a report was received at around 3.37am that day alleging that the man, surnamed Ho, had spiked bowls of cat food with poison. Surveillance footage recorded using cameras set up by the volunteers caught him in the act and went viral on social media, along with videos of the volunteers later confronting him. The police brief stated that officers who arrived on the scene found a packet of rat bait and a 14 cm fruit knife on the suspect and arrested him on suspicion of animal cruelty and possession of an offensive weapon. Images of the contaminated cat food. Photo: @hksaar.io via Threads. Ho was detained for further investigation, with his case taken over by the Sham Shui Po police district’s crime unit. No cats were harmed in the case, the police statement said. ‘Please do not harm them’ In the viral video of volunteers confronting Ho, he denied trying to harm the cats and said that he only wanted to deter the strays from eating the food to keep the area clean. The volunteers responded that the poisoned cats would only die in public areas, causing more hygiene issues. Ho can be seen in the video wearing a running vest with a patch bearing the Wolfsangel or “wolf’s hook” insignia – a symbol that originated in medieval German heraldry and was later adopted widely in Nazi symbolism. One of the animal welfare groups that intercepted the 34-year-old, Hong Kong Suspected Animal Abuse Report (HKSAAR), said on Threads that it had been monitoring Ho for more than a month. A Wolfsangel patch on Ho’s running gear. Photo: Threads. HKSAAR released photos of the poisoned cat food as far back as June, when it was first uncovered by another volunteer group it had been working with. The photos showed a thick black paste covering pieces of dry kibble, as well as blue granules of suspected rat bait in bowls of water. Under Hong Kong law, the maximum penalty for animal cruelty is a HK$200,000 fine and three years’ imprisonment. One of the volunteers, Nicholas Sum, said in a post on Sunday: “You don’t have to love them, but please do not harm them.” “After lying in wait for an entire month, we finally caught him,” Sum said. “Huge thanks to all the cat rescue volunteers, local neighbours, and HKSAAR for pulling multiple all-nighters in a row to track [the suspect] down.”

summary: 香港 香港赛马会捐赠 3,200 万港元，与香港高尔夫球会慈善基金合作推出为期两年的社区高尔夫计划。该倡议旨在每年向超过 25,000 名学童、青少年和贫困居民介绍这项运动。 [![图片 1: Adam](https://clb.org.hk/en/static/img/editors/clb-adam-192.png)](https://clb.org.hk/en/desks/clb-desk) 作者：[Adam](https://clb.org.hk/en/desks/clb-desk)，主编 2026 年 10 月 25 日 23:16 HKT · 2 分钟阅读《香港报》公开赛于 10 月 25 日在粉岭高尔夫球场结束，抽签十名
content:
香港
香港赛马会捐款3,200万港元，与香港高尔夫球会慈善基金合作推出为期两年的社区高尔夫计划。该倡议旨在每年向超过 25,000 名学童、青少年和贫困居民介绍这项运动。

[![图片1：Adam](https://clb.org.hk/en/static/img/editors/clb-adam-192.png)](https://clb.org.hk/en/desks/clb-desk)

作者：[Adam](https://clb.org.hk/en/desks/clb-desk)，主编

2026 年 10 月 25 日 23:16 香港时间 · 阅读 2 分钟

香港公开赛于10月25日在粉岭高尔夫球场落幕，吸引了数万名来自香港、中国内地及海外的观众。香港赛马会（HKJC）首次作为赛事官方社区合作伙伴参与其中，以新的社区举措支持M-Mark锦标赛。

在颁奖典礼上，香港赛马会企业事务执行董事谭志源颁发马会杯予赛事的低位香港业余选手林马强。财政司司长陈茂波、文化体育及旅游局局长罗淑佩也出席。
香港赛马会捐赠 3,200 万港元，与香港高尔夫球会慈善基金合作推出为期两年的赛马会社区高尔夫计划。该计划旨在向更广泛的受众介绍高尔夫运动，支持当地年轻的人才，并将锦标赛的好处扩展到球场之外。预计每年将有超过 25,000 名学童、青少年和贫困社区成员受益。

香港赛马会与香港高尔夫球会合作开展多项参与活动，包括校本活动、中学间比赛以及为各种水平的青少年举办的高尔夫球训练营。比赛之前，国际高尔夫球手参观了当地的一所小学，以激励学生，而俱乐部教练则通过实践高尔夫诊所来促进包容性。向贫困社区分发免费门票，以鼓励更广泛的参与。

赛事期间，赛马会球迷村的游客可享受推杆挑战等互动活动，而香港赛马会的义工团队则以气球人偶及其他景点招待大众。来访的高尔夫球手还可以参观香港的标志性景点，包括在跑马地赛马场观看欢乐星期三赛马之夜，这有助于向国际观众推广香港的赛马旅游业。

[![图片3：Adam](https://clb.org.hk/en/static/img/editors/clb-adam-192.png)](https://clb.org.hk/en/desks/clb-desk)

主编
负责 CLB.org.hk 报道和编辑标准的主编。

【原文 English Original】
Hong Kong
The Hong Kong Jockey Club has donated HK$32 million to launch a two-year community golf programme in partnership with the Hong Kong Golf Club Charitable Foundation. The initiative aims to introduce the sport to over 25,000 schoolchildren, teenagers and underprivileged residents annually.

[![Image 1: Adam](https://clb.org.hk/en/static/img/editors/clb-adam-192.png)](https://clb.org.hk/en/desks/clb-desk)

By [Adam](https://clb.org.hk/en/desks/clb-desk), Editor in Chief

25 Oct 2026 at 23:16 HKT · 2 min read

The Hong Kong Open concluded on 25 October at the Fanling Golf Course, drawing tens of thousands of spectators from Hong Kong, mainland China and overseas. For the first time, the Hong Kong Jockey Club (HKJC) participated as the event's official community partner, supporting the M-Mark tournament with new community initiatives.

At the awards ceremony, Raymond Tam Chi-yuen, HKJC's executive director for Corporate Affairs, presented the Club Cup to Markus Lam, the tournament's Low Hong Kong Amateur Player. Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po and Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism Rosanna Law Shuk-pui also attended.

HKJC has donated HK$32 million to launch the Jockey Club Community Golf Programme, a two-year initiative in partnership with the Hong Kong Golf Club Charitable Foundation. The programme is designed to introduce golf to a broader audience, support young local talent, and extend the tournament's benefits beyond the course. It is expected that more than 25,000 schoolchildren, teenagers and underprivileged community members will benefit each year.

HKJC and the Hong Kong Golf Club collaborated on engagement activities, including school-based events, inter-secondary school competitions and golf clinics for young people of all abilities. Ahead of the tournament, international golfers visited a local primary school to inspire students, while club coaches promoted inclusion through hands-on golf clinics. Complimentary tickets were distributed to underprivileged communities to encourage wider participation.

During the tournament, visitors to the Jockey Club Fan Village enjoyed interactive activities such as a putting challenge, while a volunteer team from HKJC entertained crowds with balloon figures and other attractions. Visiting golfers were also treated to signature Hong Kong attractions, including a night at the Happy Wednesday races at Happy Valley Racecourse, helping to promote the city's horse racing tourism to an international audience.

（中央社記者王朝鈺基隆2日電）尋求連任的國民黨基隆市長謝國樑今天說，目前民調領先不多，但他對連任有信心，因為有做事，也推出「謝國樑12建設」讓市民了解。
謝國樑上午接受「POP撞新聞」主持人黃暐瀚專訪，被問及近期有2份民調，國民黨內部參考民調顯示謝國樑領先，另1份稍微落後，現在是否可說選情穩定領先。
謝國樑說，領先不多，內參民調是供內部了解選情，目的是呈現真實，通常在他覺得民調受到不公平對待時才會公開。
針對民進黨台北市長參選人沈伯洋引起的「洋流」是否影響基隆的選舉，謝國樑說，沈伯洋會不會影響基隆，就像台北市長蔣萬安的選情會不會影響基隆一樣。
謝國樑說，蔣萬安是區域的母雞，蔣萬安好，大家就會好，蔣萬安在電視辯論會表現不錯，蔣萬安的妻子石舫亘掃街拜票時，也受到民眾熱烈歡迎，她昨天也說以蔣萬安的辯論內容為榮，希望自己的辯論內容同樣精彩優秀。
謝國樑表示，他認為藍軍被壓抑很久，因為許多人被偵辦，媒體報導的時間大多對蔣萬安及國民黨較不利，國民黨支持者會比較悶、憋在心裡。選舉現象中有「沉默螺旋」理論，他無法肯定有或沒有，因為民調測不出來，要等開票才知道，現在不用講太多。
謝國樑表示，基本上，北北基桃還是藍大於綠，基隆又比台北更藍一點，新北市長侯友宜在2024年總統大選，基隆開出的票數，是北北基桃唯一贏過總統賴清德的縣市，而他提出「謝國樑12建設」，大家就會知道他有做事，選起來會比較容易些。（編輯：李亨山）1151102

2026年10月29日，中国驻菲律宾武官杨雷出席在宿务举行的第十三届东盟防长扩大会。
埃洛伊萨·洛佩兹（Eloisa Lopez），台球（法新社）
菲律宾马尼拉——中国指责国防部长吉尔伯托·特奥多罗阻止中国参加上周在宿务举行的东盟防务会谈，并声称菲律宾是在其他东南亚国家的压力下才邀请中国参加会谈的。
11月1日星期日晚间，中国驻马尼拉大使馆在Facebook上发布声明，声称特奥多罗“出于个人利益”行事，无视10月28日至29日菲律宾在宿雾主办的东盟防长扩大会（ADMM-Plus）的开放性和包容性原则。
“在其他东盟国家对此类行为表示强烈反对后，菲律宾国防部才于10月22日才勉强向中国发出了邀请函，”大使馆表示，并补充说，这封信是由一位副部长签署的，“他甚至不愿意在信上注明日期”。
Philstar.com 已联系特奥多罗征求意见。本报告将根据他的回应进行更新。
在此指控之前，中国国防部发言人10月29日发表讲话，暗示一名“菲律宾政客”据称阻碍中国参加会谈。
张晓刚在北京举行的新闻发布会上对记者表示，菲律宾纵容“某个自私的政客肆意妄为”，并利用其主席身份阻止中国参与，但他没有点名特奥多罗。
大使馆表示，所有其他 ADMM-Plus 成员均在 9 月底或 10 月初收到了邀请。
“10月23日，特奥多罗在新闻发布会上表示，前一天才向中方发出通知，”大使馆表示。 “留给中国的准备时间不到五个工作日。中国还被要求在短短两天内完成注册。”
“在这种情况下，几乎不可能完成必要的准备，”它补充道。
特奥多罗在 10 月 23 日的新闻发布会上表示，菲律宾已通过国防部副部长伊格纳西奥·马德里加签署的一封信向北京发出邀请。
四天后，DND 发言人阿森尼奥·安多隆证实已发出邀请，但中国尚未确认其代表。
北京最终派出驻马尼拉武官杨雷高级上尉代替国防部长，这是自 2010 年论坛启动以来中国在论坛上的代表级别最低。
特奥多罗亲自到会场迎接其他代表团团长，但没有向杨致意，而是由马德里加接见。
特奥多罗表示，级别应该平等，副部长欢迎武官“非常有礼貌”。
大使馆没有具体说明哪些东盟国家反对菲律宾处理邀请的方式。
张上周也提出了类似的主张，但特奥多罗认为这是北京的观点，而不是东盟的观点。

China says Gibo gave Beijing less than five working days’ notice for ASEAN defense talks
Cristina Chi - Philstar.com
November 2, 2026 | 12:19pm
China's Defence Attache to the Philippines Yang Lei attends the 13th ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) in Cebu on October 29, 2026.
Eloisa Lopez, pool via AFP
MANILA, Philippines — China has accused Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. of blocking its participation in last week’s ASEAN defense talks in Cebu, claiming that the Philippines invited China to join the talks only after pressure from other Southeast Asian states.
In a statement posted on Facebook late Sunday, November 1, the Chinese Embassy in Manila claimed Teodoro “acted out of personal self-interest” and disregarded the principle of openness and inclusivity of the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus), which the Philippines hosted in Cebu on October 28 and 29.
“Only after other ASEAN countries expressed strong opposition to such acts that the Philippines Department of National Defense (DND) reluctantly sent an invitation letter to China on October 22,” the embassy said, adding that the letter was signed by an undersecretary “who was unwilling to even put a date on the letter.”
Philstar.com has reached out to Teodoro for comment. This report will be updated with his response.
The allegation follows remarks by China's defense ministry spokesperson on October 29, who alluded to a "Philippine politician" who allegedly obstructed China's participation in the talks.
During a press conference in Beijing, Zhang Xiaogang told reporters that the Philippines had allowed “a certain self-serving politician to act recklessly” and use its chairmanship to block China’s participation, but he did not name Teodoro.
The embassy said all other ADMM-Plus members received their invitations in late September or early October.
"On October 23, Teodoro said in a press conference that China had been sent notice only the previous day," the embassy said. "It left China fewer than five working days for preparation. China was also required to complete its registration within just two days."
"Under such circumstances, it was virtually impossible to complete the necessary preparation," it added.
At his October 23 briefing, Teodoro said the Philippines had sent an invitation to Beijing through a letter signed by Defense Undersecretary Ignacio Madriaga.
Four days later, DND spokesperson Arsenio Andolong confirmed that an invitation had been sent but China had yet to confirm its representative.
Beijing eventually sent Senior Capt. Yang Lei, its defense attaché in Manila, instead of its defense minister, marking China's lowest level of representation at the forum since its launch in 2010.
Teodoro personally welcomed the other delegation heads at the venue but did not greet Yang, who was instead received by Madriaga.
Teodoro said there should be parity in rank, and that an undersecretary welcoming an attaché was “more than courteous.”
The embassy did not identify which ASEAN countries that had supposedly objected to the Philippines’ handling of the invitation.
Zhang made a similar claim last week, but Teodoro dismissed it as Beijing’s view rather than that of ASEAN.
“So it is China’s position, it is not ASEAN’s position,” Teodoro said at the close of the meetings.

title: Australia unveils secretive Ghost Shark underwater drone payloads
zh_title: 澳大利亚推出神秘的“幽灵鲨”水下无人机有效载荷
summary: 新西兰基督城——澳大利亚军方官员一直对如何使用 Anduril 开发的 Ghost Shark 超大型自主水下航行器（XLAUV）守口如瓶。然而，他们最近揭开了澳大利亚皇家海军正在部署的一些有效载荷的神秘面纱。 10 月 19 日，在澳大利亚悉尼 Anduril 制造中心举行的正式揭幕仪式上，展示了三枚“幽灵鲨”有效载荷。其中一个是水雷，另一个是一群 Altius-600 徘徊弹药，第三个是后勤补给库。换句话说：三个有效载荷中的两个包含动力学效应
content:
新西兰基督城——澳大利亚军方官员一直对如何使用 Anduril 开发的 Ghost Shark 超大型自主水下航行器（XLAUV）守口如瓶。然而，他们最近揭开了澳大利亚皇家海军正在部署的一些有效载荷的神秘面纱。 10 月 19 日，在澳大利亚悉尼 Anduril 制造中心举行的正式揭幕仪式上，展示了三枚“幽灵鲨”有效载荷。其中一个是水雷，另一个是一群 Altius-600 徘徊弹药，第三个是后勤补给库。换句话说：三个有效载荷中的两个包含动能效应器，可以为幽灵鲨提供更大的咬合力。这意味着一艘 XLAUV 可以秘密部署十几个水雷，也许是在冲突期间的海上咽喉要道。与此同时，安杜里尔的 Altius 武器可以执行监视和打击任务。关于补给储备，一位官员表示，“这么说吧，人们可以发挥自己的想象力，想象哪些部队会在部署时使用这些补给储备。”国防部在一份新闻稿中表示：“这些平台的模块化设计使它们能够操作一系列不同的有效载荷，并根据所需的任务进行定制。”幽灵鲨正在开发其他有效载荷，可能涉及轻型和重型鱼雷以及电子战。国防工业部长帕特·康罗伊解释说，“幽灵鲨”可以从集装箱、相对较小的船只的船尾或码头部署。
他说：“这给对手留下了问号。”由于澳大利亚必须等待数年才能获得核动力潜艇，像“幽灵鲨鱼”这样的自主水下系统可以填补六艘老化的柯林斯级柴电潜艇继续缓慢前进的能力差距。安杜里尔澳大利亚工厂不到一年前开业，“能够在远离我们海岸执行一系列复杂任务的‘幽灵鲨鱼’现在正以越来越快的速度下线，落入澳大利亚海军手中，”康罗伊说。堪培拉为其幽灵鲨舰队花费了 17 亿澳元（12 亿美元）。这相当于“数十艘”XLAUV，但澳大利亚并未透露具体数量。澳大利亚皇家海军还部署了澳大利亚 C2 Robotics 公司生产的小型 Speartooth XLAUV。海军中将
马特·巴克利说：“就我们的平台本身而言，它们当然必须继续发展，而我们可以安装到像“幽灵鲨鱼”这样的无人船上的模块化有效载荷的发展……为我们创造了巨大的灵活性，并使我们能够使这些系统适应未来的任务和未来的要求。”他补充道：“我们的目标很明确——我们需要以相关的速度提供能力，加强我们进行水下作战和海底行动的能力，为海上拒止做出贡献，并帮助保护我们关键的海底基础设施。” “幽灵鲨鱼”号及其有效载荷参加了过去几届太平洋海上大型活动，包括 10 月份在圣地亚哥举行的活动。第一艘“幽灵鲨鱼”号于 2026 年初移交给澳大利亚海军进行测试和验收。

【原文 English Original】
CHRISTCHURCH, New Zealand — Australian military officials have been furtive about how they will use Anduril-developed Ghost Shark extra-large autonomous underwater vehicles – or XLAUVs. However, they recently lifted the lid on some payloads the Royal Australian Navy is fielding. In an official unveiling at Anduril Australia’s manufacturing center in Sydney on Oct. 19, three Ghost Shark payloads were revealed. One entailed sea mines, another was a swarm of Altius-600 loitering munitions, and the third was logistics supply caches. In other words: Two of the three payloads comprise kinetic effectors to give the Ghost Shark greater bite. This means a single XLAUV can clandestinely deploy a dozen sea mines, perhaps in maritime chokepoints during a conflict. Meanwhile, Anduril’s Altius weapons can perform both surveillance and strike. Regarding the supply caches, an official said, “Let’s just say, people can use their imagination about the sort of forces that would use these on deployment.” The Department of Defence said in a press release: “The modular design of these platforms allows them to operate a range of different payloads, customized to the required mission.” Other payloads are being developed for the Ghost Shark, likely  involving lightweight and heavyweight torpedoes, as well as electronic warfare. Ghost Sharks can deploy from shipping containers, off the stern of relatively small ships or from wharves, Minister for Defence Industry Pat Conroy explained. “It places question marks in adversaries’ minds,” he said. With Australia having to wait years for nuclear-powered submarines to arrive, autonomous underwater systems like the Ghost Shark can fill capability gaps as six aging Collins-class diesel-electric submarines continue to plod along. Anduril Australia opened its factory less than a year ago, and “Ghost Sharks capable of a range of complex missions operating far from our shores are now rolling off the line at an increasing rate into the hands of the Australian navy,” Conroy said. Canberra is spending A$1.7 billion (US$1.2 billion) on its fleet of Ghost Sharks. This amounts to “dozens and dozens” of XLAUVs, but Australia is not saying how many exactly. The Royal Australian Navy is also fielding the smaller Speartooth XLAUV from Australian firm C2 Robotics. Navy Chief Vice Adm. Matt Buckley said: “In terms of our platforms themselves, of course they must continue to evolve, and the evolution of modular payloads that we can fit to uncrewed vessels like the Ghost Shark … creates enormous flexibility for us and allows us to adapt these systems to future missions and future requirements.” He added: “Our purpose is clear – we need to deliver capability at the speed of relevance, strengthen our ability to conduct undersea warfare and seabed operations, contribute to sea denial and help protect our critical undersea infrastructure.” The Ghost Shark and its payloads have participated in the past few Maritime Big Play Pacific events, including one in San Diego in October. The first Ghost Shark was handed over to the Australian Navy for testing and acceptance in early 2026.

美国国防部长皮特·赫格斯于 2026 年 10 月 28 日出席在宿务举行的东南亚国家联盟 (ASEAN) 国防部长会议后离开。
亚伦·法维拉（Aaron Favila），泳池（法新社）
菲律宾马尼拉——美国大使李·利普顿 (Lee Lipton) 11 月 2 日星期一表示，美国对菲律宾安全的承诺是“铁定的”，华盛顿对此“是长期的”。几周后，预计美国总统唐纳德·特朗普将在马尼拉与中国领导人习近平举行会谈。
利普顿发表声明的几天前，他称美国国防部长皮特·赫格斯对宿务进行了“非常成功的访问”，参加了东盟高级别防务会议，该会议此后成为马尼拉和北京之间公开争议的主题。
利普顿表示，赫格斯与东南亚伙伴的“频繁接触”表明了政府“加强联盟的决心”并确保“和平以实力为后盾”。
在东盟国防部长扩大会议（ADMM-Plus）上，赫格斯提出了美国-东盟防务合作框架，并将华盛顿在该地区的做法描述为“强有力、安静和明确”。
利普顿在声明中表示：“我们对菲律宾安全的承诺是铁定的。美国和菲律宾与小费迪南德·马科斯总统建立了强大的伙伴关系，其基础是共同原则、相互尊重和对地区稳定的坚定承诺。”
利普顿提到美国继续向菲律宾提供安全援助等，他说：“我们是为了长期利益而这样做的。”
中国只派出了驻马尼拉的防务武官参加在宿务举行的 ADMM-Plus，这是该论坛自 2010 年创办以来的最低级别代表，并指责一位“自私”的菲律宾政客阻止其参与。
中国驻马尼拉大使馆更进一步指责国防部长吉博·特奥多罗故意在防务峰会之前向北京发出迟到的邀请。
特朗普出席东盟峰会。特朗普预计将与其他世界领导人一起出席11月16日至18日在马尼拉举行的东盟峰会。随后，他将飞往深圳出席亚太经合组织领导人会议，并将在那里与习近平举行今年的第三次会晤。
赫格斯六月表示，美国与北京的关系“比多年来任何时候都要好”。
捍卫主权。在纪念《共同防御条约》签署 45 周年之际，利普顿表示，华盛顿“坚定地与菲律宾人民站在一起，捍卫主权、保护领土完整和维护航行自由”。
利普顿表示：“我们还认为，我们的安全伙伴关系必须与同样强大的经济伙伴关系相匹配。”他称“互惠互利的贸易”至关重要。
自 7 月 24 日以来，菲律宾出口产品面临美国 12.5% 的关税，此前美国发现马尼拉未能实施和执行强迫劳动进口禁令。
菲律宾官员还表示，两国计划于 11 月签署 Pax Silica 框架协议，这是一项由美国主导的倡议，旨在建立全球科技供应链，旨在减轻对中国的依赖。

US ambassador affirms 'ironclad' PH ties after controversial ASEAN defense talks
Cristina Chi - Philstar.com
November 2, 2026 | 5:29pm
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth leaves after attending the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Defence Ministers' Meeting in Cebu on Oct. 28, 2026.
Aaron Favila, pool via AFP
MANILA, Philippines — The United States' commitment to Philippine security is "ironclad" and Washington is "in this for the long-term," US Ambassador Lee Lipton said on Monday, November 2, weeks before US President Donald Trump is expected to stop in Manila on his way to talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
Lipton's statement came days after what he described as US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's "very successful visit" to Cebu for a high-level ASEAN defense meeting, which has since become the subject of a public dispute between Manila and Beijing.
Lipton said Hegseth's "frequent engagements" with Southeast Asian partners showed the administration's "determination to strengthen alliances" and ensure "peace is backed by strength."
At the ASEAN Defense Ministers' Meeting Plus (ADMM-Plus), Hegseth proposed a US-ASEAN framework for defense cooperation and described Washington's approach in the region as "strong, quiet, and clear."
"Our commitment to Philippine security is ironclad. With President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr., the United States and the Philippines have built a powerful partnership grounded in shared principles, mutual respect, and an unwavering commitment to regional stability," Lipton's statement read.
Citing the US' continued provision of security assistance to the Philippines, among others, Lipton said: "We're in this for the long-term."
China sent only its Manila-based defense attaché to the ADMM-Plus in Cebu, its lowest-level representation since the forum began in 2010, and blamed a "self-serving" Philippine politician for blocking its participation.
The Chinese Embassy in Manila has gone a step further and accused Defense Secretary Gibo Teodoro of deliberately sending a late invitation to Beijing ahead of the defense summit.
Trump to join ASEAN summit. Trump, along with other world leaders, is expected to attend the ASEAN summit in Manila from November 16 to 18. Afterward, he will fly to Shenzhen for the APEC leaders' meeting, where he is set to hold his third meeting with Xi this year.
Hegseth said in June that the US' relations with Beijing were "better than they have been in many years."
Defense of sovereignty. Marking 45 years since the signing of the Mutual Defense Treaty, Lipton said Washington stands "firmly with the Filipino people in defending sovereignty, protecting territorial integrity, and upholding the freedom of navigation."
"We also believe our security partnership must be matched by an equally strong economic partnership," Lipton said, calling "reciprocal, mutually beneficial trade" essential.
Philippine exports have faced a 12.5% US tariff since July 24, after the US found that Manila had failed to impose and enforce a ban on imports made with forced labor.
Philippine officials have also said the two countries aim to sign a framework agreement in November under Pax Silica, a US-led initiative to build a global tech supply chain that aims to ease dependence on China.
Malacañang has declined to say whether it will be signed during Trump's visit.

content:
台湾将流感和 COVID-19 疫苗接种范围扩大到 50-64 岁的成年人 - 焦点台湾
台湾将流感和 COVID-19 疫苗接种范围扩大到 50-64 岁的成年人
要激活文字转语音服务，请首先同意以下隐私政策。
周一，一名公众接种了疫苗。中央通讯社照片2026年11月2日
中新社台北11月2日电 台湾公共资助的流感和COVID-19疫苗接种计划的第二阶段于周一开始，年龄在50-64岁的健康人群现在有资格接种疫苗。
卫生部副部长庄人祥在台北市南港区的疫苗接种站卷起袖子接受了两针注射，疾病预防控制中心在此举行新闻发布会，标志着第二阶段计划的启动。
Chang 说，流感和 COVID-19 疫苗不仅可以预防感染，还可以降低严重疾病和并发症的风险，包括影响心脏和肺部的并发症。他敦促 50 岁及以上的健康成年人尽快接种疫苗。
CDC发言人林明诚在新闻发布会后对记者表示，预计本周台湾流感活动将降至11%以下的流行阈值。
根据疾病预防控制中心的监测标准，疫情必须连续两周保持在阈值以下才能宣布结束，这意味着最早可能会在下周宣布结束。
然而，林警告说，即使疫情平息后，严重疾病和死亡的风险仍然存在。他说，超过 99% 的重症病例和死亡病例涉及未接种本季流感疫苗或 COVID-19 疫苗的人。
庄和林都敦促老年人、孕妇、慢性病患者和 50 岁及以上的健康成年人尽快接种流感和 COVID-19 疫苗，以保护自己并降低患严重疾病和并发症的风险。
第一阶段疫苗接种计划于10月1日开始，但仅限于医疗专业人员； 65 岁及以上的人； 55岁及以上的原住民；住在长期护理机构的人们及其工作人员； 6 个月至学龄前儿童；孕妇；以及患有既往疾病（包括慢性疾病）的人。
CDC 数据显示，10 月份总共注射了 585 万剂流感和 COVID-19 疫苗。
与此同时，疾病预防控制中心主任罗一钧周一在新北举行的另一场新闻发布会上表示，最新的 COVID-19 疫苗比以前的版本副作用更少。
罗说，这种更新后的疫苗用量为之前剂量的五分之一，副作用较少，局部红肿和疼痛也明显减轻，鼓励公众放心接种。
疾病预防控制中心主任罗宜群周一接受疫苗接种。中央通讯社照片2026年11月2日
Lo说，尽管人们普遍认为50-64岁的人患有较少的慢性疾病和健康风险，但统计数据显示，该年龄段的流感和COVID-19重症病例均排名第二。
Lo补充说，尽管第二阶段将疫苗接种资格扩大到50-64岁的健康成年人，但其他高危人群，包括患有慢性疾病的人、65岁及以上的老年人和儿童，仍然有资格接种疫苗。
（陈杰玲、曹亚燕、柯林撰）

Taiwan expands flu, COVID-19 shots to adults aged 50-64
To activate the text-to-speech service, please first agree to the privacy policy below.
A member of the general public is inoculated with a vaccine on Monday. CNA photo Nov. 2, 2026
Taipei, Nov. 2 (CNA) The second phase of Taiwan's publicly funded influenza and COVID-19 vaccination program began Monday, with healthy people aged 50-64 now eligible to receive the shots.
Deputy Health Minister Chuang Jen-hsiang (莊人祥) rolled up his sleeve and received both shots at a vaccination station in Taipei's Nangang District, where the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) held a news conference to mark the launch of the program's second phase.
Chuang said flu and COVID-19 vaccinations can not only prevent infections but also reduce the risk of severe illness and complications, including those affecting the heart and lungs. He urged healthy adults aged 50 and older to get vaccinated as soon as possible.
Speaking to reporters after the press event, CDC spokesperson Lin Min-cheng (林明誠) said flu activity in Taiwan is expected to fall below the 11 percent epidemic threshold this week.
Under the CDC's monitoring criteria, the outbreak must remain below the threshold for two consecutive weeks before it can be declared over, meaning the announcement could come as early as next week.
However, Lin warned that the risk of severe illness and death remains even after the outbreak subsides. More than 99 percent of severe cases and deaths have involved people who had not received this season's flu vaccine or a COVID-19 vaccine, he said.
Both Chuang and Lin urged seniors, pregnant women, people with chronic illnesses and healthy adults aged 50 and older, to get vaccinated against flu and COVID-19 as soon as possible to protect themselves and reduce the risk of severe illness and complications.
The first phase of the vaccination program began on Oct. 1 but was limited to medical professionals; people aged 65 and older; Indigenous people aged 55 and older; people living in long-term care facilities and their staff; children aged 6 months through preschool age; pregnant women; and people with preexisting conditions, including chronic illnesses.
CDC data showed that a total of 5.85 million doses of flu and COVID-19 vaccines were administered in October.
Meanwhile, CDC Director-General Lo Yi-chun (羅一鈞) said at a separate news conference in New Taipei on Monday that the latest COVID-19 vaccine has fewer side effects than previous versions.
This updated vaccine uses one-fifth of the previous dose and causes fewer side effects, with localized redness and pain also significantly reduced, Lo said, encouraging members of the public to get vaccinated without concern.
CDC Director-General Lo Yi-chun receives a vaccination on Monday. CNA photo Nov. 2, 2026
Although people aged 50-64 are generally perceived as having fewer chronic illnesses and health risks, Lo said, statistics show that this age group ranks second in terms of severe cases of both flu and COVID-19.
Lo added that although the second phase expands eligibility to healthy adults aged 50-64, other high-risk groups, including people with chronic illnesses, seniors aged 65 and older, and children, remain eligible for vaccination.
(By Chen Chieh-ling, Tsao Ya-yen and Ko Lin)

content:
HKGAI、科大讯飞、杜小满推出自我进化金融AI模型轩辕4.5 |中国劳工公告栏
星期二, 3 十一月 2026 · 香港 香港和中国劳工新闻（英文）
HKGAI、科大讯飞、杜小满推出自主进化金融AI模型轩辕4.5
HKGAI、科大讯飞、杜小满在香港金融科技周上推出首个自进化金融大语言模型轩辕4.5。该模型采用递归自我改进技术，核心财务任务的性能提升了30%，而成本仅为一般财务任务的10%
香港生成人工智能研究发展中心（HKGAI）、香港科技大学（HKUST）和金融科技公司度小满于2026年11月2日在香港金融科技周上推出了首个自进化金融大语言模型轩辕4.5。该倡议旨在支持人工智能（AI）在金融技术领域的全球扩张。
据HKGAI介绍，轩辕4.5利用尖端的递归自我改进（RSI）技术，在核心金融应用场景（包括获客、风险管理和客户关系管理）方面的性能提升了30%。该中心表示，其计算成本仅为通用模型的 10%。
杜小满集团行政总裁朱光表示：“三方共同推动人工智能在金融领域的深度应用，助力香港金融业智能化升级。香港作为杜小满集团的国际总部，我们将继续深化与科大的科研合作，携手HKGAI开拓国际市场。”
在杜小满的实际业务运营中，大模型已构建了千余个AI代理和5000多个技能，每日代币消耗超过1000亿。该公司报告称，短期逾期风险下降了约50%，总体年化信贷逾期风险下降了12%。在信贷审批流程中，人工智能审批人员的性能超过了80%的人类审批人员，客户等待时间从10分钟缩短到2分钟。
杜小曼表示，企业微信AI坐席可以为客户经理提供精准的沟通策略和应对建议，将单个客户经理的服务能力提升一倍，达到2万人，相当于传统模式下10名经理的工作量。
HKGAI表示，通过未来的战略合作，将与杜小满共同将这项金融AI技术推向国际市场，继续展示香港在生成人工智能领域的研发实力。

Tuesday, 3 Nov 2026 · Hong Kong Hong Kong and China labour news in English
HKGAI, HKUST and Du Xiaoman launch self-evolving financial AI model XuanYuan 4.5
HKGAI, HKUST and Du Xiaoman launched XuanYuan 4.5, the first self-evolving financial large language model, at Hong Kong FinTech Week. The model uses recursive self-improvement technology, showing a 30 per cent performance improvement in core financial tasks while costing only 10 per cent of general
The Hong Kong Generative AI Research and Development Center (HKGAI), Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) and financial technology firm Du Xiaoman on 2 November 2026 launched the first self-evolving financial large language model, named XuanYuan 4.5, at Hong Kong FinTech Week. The initiative aims to support the global expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) in financial technology.
According to HKGAI, XuanYuan 4.5 leverages cutting-edge Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) technology and has demonstrated a 30 per cent improvement in performance across core financial application scenarios, including customer acquisition, risk management and customer relationship management. Its computing cost is only 10 per cent of that of general-purpose models, the centre said.
Guang Zhu, chief executive of Du Xiaoman, said: “The three parties are jointly promoting the deep application of AI in the financial sector, assisting the intelligent upgrade of Hong Kong's financial industry. Hong Kong serves as the international headquarters of Du Xiaoman Group, and we will continue to deepen our scientific research collaboration with HKUST, joining hands with HKGAI to explore international markets.”
In Du Xiaoman's actual business operations, the large model has built over a thousand AI agents and more than 5,000 skills, with daily token consumption exceeding 100 billion. The company reported that short-term overdue risks have dropped by around 50 per cent, and the overall annualised credit overdue risk has decreased by 12 per cent. In the credit approval process, the performance of AI approvers surpasses that of 80 per cent of human approvers, and customer waiting times have been reduced from 10 minutes to 2 minutes.
Enterprise WeChat AI agents can provide relationship managers with precise communication strategies and response suggestions, doubling the service capacity of a single relationship manager to 20,000 people, a workload equivalent to ten managers under the traditional model, Du Xiaoman said.
HKGAI said that through future strategic cooperation, it and Du Xiaoman will jointly promote this financial AI technology to the international market, continuing to showcase Hong Kong's research and development strength in the field of generative artificial intelligence.

title: Anthropic's IPO prospectus is big on promises, short on answers to tough questions
zh_title: Anthropic 的 IPO 招股说明书充满了承诺，但对棘手问题缺乏答案
summary: 官方消息：Anthropic 即将上市，天哪，我们的眉毛已经厌倦了仔细研究数百页的可疑声明吗？您可以在此页面以及 Spotify、Apple Music 或 YouTube 上收听《The Kettle》的最新一集。这些平台还允许您订阅《The Kettle》，因此当最新剧集上线时，您始终会收到通知。正如系统编辑 Tobias Man n 和高级记者 Tom Claburn 在本周节目中告诉主持人 Brandon Vigliarolo 的那样，Anthropic 需要做很多事情才能使其大规模 IPO 不仅仅是昙花一现
content:
官方消息：Anthropic 即将上市，天哪，我们的眉毛已经厌倦了仔细研究数百页的可疑声明吗？您可以在此页面以及 Spotify、Apple Music 或 YouTube 上收听《The Kettle》的最新一集。这些平台还允许您订阅《The Kettle》，因此当最新剧集上线时，您始终会收到通知。正如系统编辑 Tobias Man n 和高级记者 Tom Claburn 在本周的节目中告诉主持人 Brandon Vigliarolo 的那样，Anthropic 需要做很多事情才能使其大规模 IPO 不仅仅是昙花一现。首先，该公司需要支付近一万亿美元的计算费用，这意味着它将比数据中心燃气轮机消耗的现金还要多。除了在可预见的未来的巨额支出之外，还有一个事实是，它的大部分计算能力依赖于同时也是竞争对手的客户。简而言之，我们对此表示怀疑，但您可能已经知道了。毕竟，这是 El Reg，我们不会只相信人工智能行业所声称的表面价值——如果它看起来像纸牌屋，那么它很可能就是这样。经过轻微编辑的文字记录如下： Brandon (00:03) 大家好，欢迎收看 The Register 的 Kettle 播客的最新一集。
我是主持人，Reg 记者 Brandon Vigliarolo，本周我们的重点是我认为我们的撰稿人 Carly Page 恰当地描述了过去几年我们所处的人工智能炒作周期的顶峰，这就是 Anthropic 首次公开募股文件的公开发布。与我一起谈论这个问题的是我们的系统编辑 Tobias Mann 和高级记者 Tom Claburn，我相信他们对此事都有很多话要说。欢迎大家。托比亚斯·曼 (00:34) 很高兴来到这里。汤姆·克拉伯恩 (00:34) 很高兴来到这里。 Brandon (00:36) 所以，我确信我们有很多内容需要讨论。 614 页的内容实在是太多了。托拜厄斯，我知道你正在用细齿梳子梳理这件事。在我们讨论本次 IPO 中一些更不稳定的部分之前，请先告诉我们具体的数据。托比亚斯·曼 (00:56) 当然。从表面上看，进入任何 S-1 文件，这都是一种风险缓解的混乱，有点掩盖你的屁股。它们读起来几乎就像是世界末日预言。布兰登 (01:18) 对。 Tobias Mann (01:18) S-1 确实做到了这一点。但在数字方面，市场的收获有点有趣，因为有些人看着这些数字，然后说：“好吧，这实际上看起来很合理。”他们的营业亏损仅约7亿美元。 Brandon (01:40) 我认为净 [收入] 为 163 亿，对吧？这就是他们的报告。托拜厄斯·曼 (01:46) 对。
Brandon (01:47) 现在他们还提到，我想，我本来想问你这个问题，807 亿美元的总损失，但我知道这是某种会计调整。他们在 IPO 中提到了这具体意味着什么吗？托比亚斯·曼 (Tobias Mann) (02:01) 没有具体的。有点模糊，而且总是这样。布兰登 (02:07) 当然是，对吧？ Tobias Mann (02:09) Anthropic 的业务需要大量现金，因此他们必须向合作伙伴说：“嘿，我们需要资金来支付训练这些模型的计算费用。我们可以借债，也可以通过估值（我们的股权）获得回报。”所以我相信损失的很大一部分是他们试图冲销他们必须偿还的大量股本

【原文 English Original】
It's official: Anthropic is going public, and boy, are our eyebrows tired from poring over hundreds and hundreds of pages of questionable claims. You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle right here on this page, as well as on Spotify , Apple Music , or YouTube . Those platforms also let you subscribe to The Kettle, so you are always notified when the latest episode goes live. Anthropic is going to need to do a lot to make its massive IPO more than just a flash in the pan, as systems editor Tobias Man n and senior reporter Tom Claburn tell host Brandon Vigliarolo on this week's episode. For one, the company has nearly a trillion dollars in compute commitments to pay for, which is going to mean it'll be burning through more cash than a datacenter gas turbine turned up to 11. In addition to its massive spending for the foreseeable future, there's also the fact that much of its computing power relies on customers who are also competitors. In short, we're skeptical, but you probably already knew that. It's El Reg, after all, and we're not just taking what the AI industry claims at face value - if it looks like a house of cards, it probably is. A lightly edited transcript is below: Brandon (00:03) Hey everyone, and welcome to the latest episode of The Register 's Kettle podcast. I'm your host, Reg reporter Brandon Vigliarolo, and this week we're focusing on what I think our contributor Carly Page aptly described as the peak of the AI hype cycle we've been in for the past few years, and that's the public release of Anthropic's initial public offering filing. With me to talk this over is our systems editor Tobias Mann and senior reporter Tom Claburn, both of whom I'm sure have plenty to say about this matter. Welcome guys. Tobias Mann (00:34) Good to be here. Tom Claburn (00:34) Good to be here. Brandon (00:36) So, I'm sure we've got a lot to cover. 614 pages is a lot to go through. Tobias, I understand you were combing through this thing with a fine-toothed comb . Talk us through the hard numbers before we get into some of the more wobbly parts of this IPO. Tobias Mann (00:56) Sure. At face value, going into any S-1 filing, it is a kind of mess of risk mitigation, kind of covering your butt. They all pretty much read like a doomsday prophecy. Brandon (01:18) Right. Tobias Mann (01:18) The S-1 definitely did that. But on the numbers side of things, the takeaway for the market was kind of interesting because there were some people looking at the numbers and going, "OK, this actually seems reasonable." Their operating losses were only about 700 million dollars. Brandon (01:40) I think on 16.3 billion net [revenues], right? That was what they reported. Tobias Mann (01:46) Right. Brandon (01:47) Now they also mentioned, I think, and I was going to ask you about this, $80.7 billion total losses, but I understand that was an accounting adjustment of some kind. Did they mention in the IPO what that meant specifically? Tobias Mann (02:01) Not specifically. It's a little fuzzy, and it's always kind of like this. Brandon (02:07) Of course it is, right? Tobias Mann (02:09) Anthropic's business is extremely cash heavy, and so they had to go to partners and say, "Hey, we need capital in order to pay for compute to train these models. We can either take it in debt or you could also get repaid in valuation, our equity." And so I believe a large part of that loss is they're trying to write off a lot of the equity that they're going to have to pay off when they do go public. And so I do believe that's the lion's share of that loss. Because it does look huge, but when you think about how companies go public and how they raise capital as startups, it's not really that surprising. It's just a huge number because Anthropic is arguably the largest IPO in US history at this point. Brandon (03:02) Right. But bottom line is their actual day-to-day business losses were $693 million....It was $1.2 billion, I think, for the first half of the year or same time last year or something like that. So it's gone down. Tobias Mann (03:17) Yes. Tom Claburn (03:17) And they're trying to go out at two trillion now? Is that the number? Tobias Mann (03:25) Well, the number kind of depends on whether they're going to be able to sustain this. I was going to mention for the first time ever, their revenues outpaced their compute expenses two to one. This has never been true in the company's history, and it's one of the reasons that people are feeling more confident about this. The issue that really comes from all of this, and what has gotten missed somewhat in the more rosy interpretations of the S-1, is that they also are signed up to have to repay upwards of 800 billion dollars and counting of compute commitments out through the next two decades or so. Brandon (04:12) You outlined in your story just a whole host of people they owed billions of dollars to for compute. Like you said, it would be great. That $16.3 billion in [revenue] would be great if those compute costs were going to hold steady, right? But they're not. They're going to keep climbing and there are a lot of bills that are going to be due. So, profitability is relying on making more than that nearly trillion dollars in compute obligations, and that's a big if. Tom Claburn (04:43) I mean, the big question mark is in terms of what the technology does for inference costs, because I think a lot of this is betting on being able to get the same hardware that is much more efficient down the road and maybe not drop your prices proportionately and profit on the difference. But it remains to be seen whether there will be enough competition to just have the price go do with the increasing cost. And you see that a lot. I think the inference costs have dropped pretty significantly over the year, on average. I mean, it's really hard to calculate inference costs because there are so many different factors and it's really situational depending on the workload and how much caching is going on and things like that. But overall it's a lot cheaper to do inference now than it was a few months ago. Tobias Mann (05:34) Per token, yeah. Brandon (05:36) But again, I feel like if you're betting this $2 trillion IPO on the fact that we're going to keep getting better and cheaper at inference, right? I mean, I know Moore's Law is kind of a thing of the past, but at this point, what if we run up against another compute bottleneck and inference stops getting cheaper before they need it to? Obviously any IPO prospectus is one big document about risk, right? Like, "Hey, you might make a ton of money investing in this company, or we might go complete belly up and you lose everything," right? That's always a possibility. Tom Claburn (06:15) Right. And they still haven't demonstrated that the use case for AI is wide enough at volume that they claim it is. I mean, in certain sectors it's pretty obvious now there's going to be AI for a long time. Coding, everyone kind of agrees that works and we know how to manage that. And then there will be adjacent fields to that. But once you start getting into more general office work and regular business tasks that are not super-compute heavy, I don't know. It's a good question. We'll see if people are going to use it that broadly, but I just see it being overly optimistic. Tobias Mann (06:59) The big question I have right now is: Is there enough user demand to support even a $200 billion a year revenue stream? Because even going off just commitments that they can't get out of made in the first half of this year, that's $417 billion running out through about 2033 to 2036. Brandon (07:32) I think the upper end of your estimate was a total, including newer commitments, of about $807 billion. At the lower end, $782 billion at the lower end. That's not that much of a difference when you're looking at hundreds of billions of dollars. Tobias Mann (07:46) But if they can't make a profit with a two to one revenue-to-compute ratio — if they have to make twice as much in revenue in order to pay for their compute and still not break even — you extrapolate this out and they're going to have to be making $200 billion plus, assuming no additional compute contracts are made during that period over the next year, which is definitely not going to happen. They've already said they're going to keep making compute contracts. So this number just keeps getting more absurd the further out you go, unless inference magically gets dirt cheap, which we haven't seen. Brandon (08:33) Right. And it could cap. You know, I think also you made a really good point in your story, Tobias, when you mentioned that some of their biggest customers are also some of their biggest competitors. They're leasing space from hyperscalers, they're making deals with people to host their compute. But these are also companies that are operating their own AI models. And you might end up in a situation where they're like an MVNO, which, if anyone's not familiar with a mobile virtual network operator, is cell phone companies that are not T-Mobile, Verizon, or AT&T. Anyone who's not those big three in the United States is operating a virtual network that piggybacks on someone else's infrastructure. And when that infrastructure is busy, you get less priority. So we could see them run into a similar situation there, I imagine. Tom Claburn (09:26) There's an interesting trend that another piece I'm working on later today touches on. Some of the AI gateways like OpenRouter are now starting to move away from just focusing on price metering and looking towards things like fastest time to tokens and all the quality of service metrics in terms of the way that they price and deliver the models, because inference pricing has become very commoditized in terms of what they're dealing with. They're not necessarily serving all the frontier models at very high prices. They're dealing with a lot of open weight models. And if you just focus on the lower end of the market, there's not a lot of margin there. So it makes sense to go, "Well, maybe if we deliver this faster or have better reliability or service, we can move up the price and get a little profit." And I think everyone in the industry is starting to realize that the music is stopping and they have to take a seat at some point and make the business model work. So there's going to be a lot of pressure on that. And that's also showing up in things like the licensing of models. A lot of those open weight models have seen their licenses get more restrictive over time as companies realize, "Well, maybe we don't want someone competing with us with this thing that we've made." So I think there's a lot.. Brandon (10:48) That reminds me of Mistral just releasing the open weight version of Large 4, " Le Chonk ". And the licensing model basically said if you intend to use this for any down-market purposes, you've got to sign a fairly restrictive agreement with us so that you're not just using this open weight model without us benefiting from it, right? Tobias Mann (11:15) A lot of the big Chinese models, like Kimi K3, I believe were among the first to move back in this direction, basically saying, "Hey, if you're just going to deploy this internally, we don't care." If this is just for your enterprise, fine, but if you're going to be selling an API service like OpenRouter around it, you gotta cut us in. So there is definitely that. And Anthropic in their S-1 – again, every S-1 reads like a doomsday prophecy. And this S-1 of the things that they raise: open models are a threat on multiple levels, one of them being that a lot of their customers are startups sensitive to economic downturn. So those customers will likely be the first to jump ship to cheaper alternatives that are maybe not as good, but they can afford if the economy runs into any issues. Brandon (12:25) I wonder if that'll happen or not, right? Tom Claburn (12:28) Was it Elon Musk who was tweeting about the end of the neoclouds recently? With financing getting tighter, a lot of the neoclouds living on borrowed money are going to find it harder to sustain their loans and are not going to survive this. So there will be a shakeout at some point. Does it hit the big companies? I don't know. All the cloud providers look pretty happy because they get business regardless. Even if Google's AI models are not first in people's minds, they're still serving all of this stuff. Brandon (13:08) We've said that on multiple episodes, and in multiple articles we've written, right? Basically, if the AI industry does implode, Google's going to be fine, Amazon's going to be fine, Microsoft's going to be fine; these guys have other businesses. Anthropic and OpenAI, not so much. That's all they do. And in many cases they're renting compute space from these other providers. So they might take a bit of a hit there, but by and large, they're going to be okay. They've got compute, they'll turn it around, they'll find other people to use it. Which is interesting, from your article, Tobias, you kind of summarize that the entire pitch this IPO makes is that bigger is better, right? But as we were just talking about, there are a lot of reasons to say that's probably not the case. It makes me wonder if they're still living in the token-maxxing era, whereas I just wrote a story this week about AWS telling its engineers to back off, stop using so many tokens, be more judicious, use AI well, don't just use it. And Microsoft said this months ago in August – they were saying tokenmaxxing doesn't factor into how they want to do business. So you've got two very big consumers of AI basically saying, "Y'all need to slow it down and be more purposeful." So, bigger isn't necessarily... Tobias Mann (14:33) Anthropic's business is predicated on the idea that more compute means more revenue. However, the disconnect is: Can revenue scale fast enough? Is there enough user base? Is there enough token demand to support the scale they need to cash the checks they've already written? And it really looks like a house of cards. They warn about this in the S-1 – they have to – that if their revenue can't keep up with their compute commitments, they could default. And that default could turn into a cascade where if they can't pay one bill, they can't get enough compute to generate revenue necessary to pay the next bill, and it all falls apart. Brandon (15:28) If it happens to Anthropic, the other AI frontier labs are not far behind, because that's going to be a symptom of a larger problem. And that's that people are basically saying what a lot of non-AI companies or companies that do AI along with other things, like AWS, are saying: We don't need these massive frontier models for the vast majority of business purposes. They're not necessary. Tom Claburn (15:54) Right. A lot of the enterprise AI products you see now are about trying to figure out ways to reduce that cost, too.You have some sort of gateway or harness system that looks at your jobs and routes them to an appropriately cheap model so that most of the time you're not using top-tier intelligence; maybe you're using a decision model, a regular classifier, or something like Gemma to do language translation. You don't always have to use that expensive model, and that price pressure is going to hit them, too. Tobias Mann (16:37) To Tom's point, Cadence System s , which does a lot of electronic design automation and circuit board layout, just rolled out a new product line called Maestro that's built around Nvidia's Nemotron open-weights models. The idea is that they had been using proprietary APIs to power their agents that assist engineers with PCB layout and chip design, but those agents generate a ton of data that could be used to train and fine-tune open weight models. So their latest pitch is, "Hey, we know our customers like this, but it's getting expensive to continue using these proprietary models from OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google. So we're going to give you a way to take an inexpensive model, use the proprietary model to generate training data that we can use to fine-tune this open model, and then you can decide how much of the work you want done on the expensive proprietary models versus the cheap open models. You can deploy those models on-prem, in our cloud, or on your preferred cloud. Just use our agent platform and pay the subscription fee." Brandon (18:03) I can't imagine most businesses are going to fork over all this money to proprietary model providers when they don't need those resources. It really makes me wonder how much of this IPO is forecasting the bursting of the bubble. I feel sometimes like we talk about the AI bubble bursting like doomsday prophecies: "It's happening now!" But there have been more signs recently. Chinese AI stocks have been hammered recently. There have been recent earnings reports from American companies that have not looked Yeah. Tom Claburn (18:57) Google was hammered ; they lost like $500 billion in stock value based on the fact that their search was underperforming Brandon (19:07) That's that one I wasn't able to think of, that minor little blip, right? Tom Claburn (19:11) AI overviews not monetizing as well. So there's a lot, yeah. Tobias Mann (19:15) A problem they created for themselves. Brandon (19:18) Google creating its own problems? What? Tobias Mann (19:24) I would agree that Anthropic's survival depends fairly heavily on pushing the frontier forward. In order to do that, it needs a disproportionate amount of compute that it may not be able to afford on a continuing basis, especially if Microsoft, Google, and all of these cloud CSPs that provide compute for them and are among their biggest customers decide, "We don't really need cloud for this. We've reached a point where our own open-weights models or small proprietary models are good enough for drafting emails or generating code bases for our customers." So they're going to start buying fewer tokens from Anthropic or OpenAI when they eventually IPO. They're likely to go through very similar challenges because they're also getting most of their compute from companies like Oracle and Microsoft at this point. Brandon (20:38) Which was one of the questions I wanted to ask as we wrapped up: Do you think OpenAI is going to be in any better position once their IPO comes out? Because neither of them owns a lot of their compute, and OpenAI's attempts to build its own compute seem to have fizzled out a bit. Could they be in a better position or is it going to be more of the same? Tobias Mann (21:05) I don't know with OpenAI whether they're going to be able to overcome the same risks that Anthropic has. It does feel like Anthropic is sidestepping a lot of hard questions by pushing forward with their IPO now. Tobias Mann (21:24) With Anthropic going public this year, if OpenAI goes public next year, I don't think they can avoid the scrutiny, because the world is going to have woken up to the risk factors associated with these giant model houses. And I think they're going to face a much harder time with this, even before they get there. Tom Claburn (21:52) OpenAI has the distribution of ChatGPT, which is demonstrating itself to be a useful tool that people like to use. But that's not where their monetization gold mine is going to be, unless they become the Google of AI search, and Google is already trying to get to that space, too. So I don't know how they're going to make it into the enterprise business and get the margins they need to pay back all the money they've taken. Tobias Mann (22:31) OpenAI also has a different business model than Anthropic, and to a pretty hilarious degree, if you recall the advertisements during the Super Bowl about injecting advertisements into GPT.... The point being that OpenAI's revenue streams may be sufficiently different to insulate them from this. They have been trying to position themselves as an AI advertising company as another revenue stream, which Anthropic has flatly rejected. So it's possible that OpenAI's business model is sufficiently different by next year. 12 months is a long time in this industry. If Altman takes them public this time next year, the conversation might be very different. Having said that, Wall Street's eyes are going to be open to a lot of the risk factors in a way that Anthropic is sort of sidestepping right now by being the first really big model house to go public. Brandon (23:54) Which is honestly kind of surprising to see OpenAI press the brakes while Anthropic presses the gas. I'm assuming they saw an opportunity to get out the gate first and avoid answering the hard questions. Because OpenAI basically said, "Hey, we're going to pause our IPO while we assess these risks," given they've been in the doghouse regarding AI behaving badly this year, giving Anthropic that opportunity to scoot past and not have to deal with these things. Tobias Mann (24:26) I think the other tell with Anthropic is actually that two-to-one compute ratio, because that's the first time that's ever happened. And it will be very telling if in their first or second public quarter that just disappears. So the timing might be related to the fact that they can now claim their cash flows are on a positive trajectory towards being cash flow positive and moving towards profitability. OpenAI delaying their IPO, I suspect, is largely because they need to get to a similar point. Otherwise, people are going to look at this and go, "This has no possibility of ever being profitable." At least with Anthropic's S-1, halfway through 2026, it looks like they could be profitable. Whether that's true in in their first public quarter is another matter until Brandon (25:23) To close us out here, I think this statement from your article, Tobias: "The only way to justify this kind of spend and risk is if you believe the upside is enormous, like the biggest economic transformation in the history of humankind enormous." And that raises my final question for you both: Is it going to be worth it? And what's the chance that Anthropic is going to flame out spectacularly in the next year or two? Tobias Mann (25:49) Tom, I'll let you take the first crack at that one. Brandon (25:51) Ha ha ha. Tom Claburn (25:51) Yeah. I mean, I don't know how spectacular it will be. I think it's gotten to the point where it's sort of too big to fail, but I could certainly see some desperation moves where one of these big AI companies strikes a deal with Apple for distribution, because they really need the kind of money that Google was paying Apple for, or sorry, that Google is paying Apple for for distribution. And I can see something like that happening because they really need revenue. I don't really see it blowing up because it's everybody. So they're going to figure out a way to do the least harm if things go downhill. And that may mean parting out part of their businesses. Who knows? Tobias Mann (26:35) I would tend to agree with Tom. I think about what happened with the dot-com boom as an indicator. The situation is quite a bit different because the AI industry has wormed its way so deep that it's not the surface-level situation we saw with the dot-com boom. There was a ton of fiber laid during the dot-com boom that didn't get utilized until much more recently, but it did get utilized. So I think AI is probably bigger than the internet and going to go down in the history books as the next industrial revolution, in much the same way the internet felt like that. After the dot-com boom, it was big, but it wasn't as big as people prescribed the value to. It took another 10 years for it to actually become the thing everybody wanted it to become. It eventually rose to that valuation, but it took much longer than the market could sustain. And I think we're probably in for that. Brandon (27:57) So in other words, don't buy during the IPO. Don't buy high and hope to sell higher, because you might have 10 years to wait before you get back to that IPO valuation or above. Who knows? Maybe it'll go faster. No matter what happens, there's a good chance we're going to be right here to talk about it because this sure can fill a lot of podcasts and articles. Digital ink is going to be spilled on this topic for years to come. We hope you'll join us to hear all about it on the Kettle. Thanks for listening. ®

Pixel 11 Pro Fold: Sturdy rectangle in a wide wide world
7:00 AM PST · November 1, 2026
It’s strange to write this review when the world is focused on the passport-sized iPhone Duo, and China-based companies are busy releasing wide foldables with a similar design. Google, however, stuck to its guns this year and produced a Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which is pretty much similar to last year’s foldable.
The changes involve a lighter design, a brighter display, better wireless charging, and an updated camera sensor. The new olive color looks subtle but gorgeous, so that’s a bonus. However, with all the options out there, the device might not attract people who might be looking to buy their first foldable — unless they’re serious Pixel fans.
Nonetheless, I have enjoyed using the device because the Pixel 11 Pro Fold’s cameras are competent enough, even if they aren’t a match for the Pixel 11 Pro’s setup, and the screen is nice to use despite the very visible crease.
The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is 5mm thick when unfolded (vs 5.2mm of the Pixel 10 Pro Fold) and 10.1mm thick when folded (vs 10.8 mm of the Pixel 10 Pro Fold). This one is for the spec sheet because you might not feel as much difference. Despite this, the phone is not as thin as a device like the Honor V6 Magic.
The difference you might notice — if you hold both this year’s and last year’s foldables — is that the new device is 19 grams lighter. But if you are buying a new device or switching from another foldable, it’s barely noticeable.
The Pixel 10 Pro Fold was already a sturdy device. With this year’s version, the company claims to have increased durability by three times. Plus, there is a new glass-ceramic cover and a glass-fiber composite back cover to take up any impact. My Pixel 10 fell a few times from the table and from my pocket, but there wasn’t any visible dent or scratch. Well done, Google.
Image Credits: Ivan MehtaImage Credits:Ivan Mehta
One drawback of a strong hinge is that you can’t unfold the 11 Pro Fold with one hand, and that’s by design.
The outer display is ever so slightly bigger, but the more observable change is the 3,600-nit display that is an upgrade from last year’s 3,000-nit peak display. This means that you can use the phone in bright conditions better.
Google’s foldable still has a very visible crease in an age where phone makers like Oppo and Honor have managed to reduce the visibility significantly. The crease is more pronounced in bright light, given there is no reflective display on the device.
Image Credits: Ivan MehtaImage Credits:Ivan Mehta
On the back, there is the new HiLight indicator, which still lights up only for calls from your favourite contacts, and when you are talking with Gemini hands-free. There isn’t much to talk about this feature beyond that.
Reading and watching videos on a foldable is still fun, though a wide foldable might show an edge on videos. The multitasking is good, but you can only open two apps side by side. Some apps that are tuned for foldable are great to use. For instance, Gmail, being a Google app, lets you see your inbox on one side and a particular email on the other. This can help you get through emails faster. However, Slack doesn’t have this split view, and it’s frustrating because we have been through many cycles of Android foldables with apps still not suited for the expanded screen.
Given how quick Apple developer system moves, Android might feel it’s lagging in foldable experiences after the iPhone Duo is out. The camps are divided as to how apps look on Duo’s unfolded phone, but developers are rapidly updating their apps to fit the unfolded screen.
The bubbles, which let you access apps in floating windows and minimize them in a taskbar, are a good idea. That way, you can temporarily look at information in an app without having to make it a full-sized window.
Gemini updates this year were muted. The company built on its idea of Magic Cue to give timely suggestions in different apps. As I mentioned in my Pixel 11 Pro XL review, Rambler was my favorite feature to use in the new Pixel lineups. I could easily reply to emails and texts, and take notes, without involving texting on a wide keyboard.
Foldables have mostly had inferior cameras to their candybar counterparts for years now. While this year is no different, Google continuing to use the “Pro” moniker for its foldable feels like a disservice. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold cameras are good, but they aren’t Pixel 11 Pro XL good.
There are a few positives with the new version. There is an updated main sensor, still a 48-megapixel one, that lets more light in for photos with better detail. Google has also updated its models to support 30x Super Res Zoom, up from 20x Super Res Zoom.
Image Credits:Ivan Mehta Image Credits:Ivan Mehta Image Credits:Ivan Mehta Image Credits:Ivan Mehta Image Credits:Ivan Mehta Image Credits:Ivan Mehta Image Credits:Ivan Mehta Image Credits:Ivan Mehta Image Credits:Ivan Mehta Image Credits:Ivan Mehta Image Credits:Ivan Mehta Image Credits:Ivan Mehta Image Credits:Ivan Mehta Image Credits:Ivan Mehta Image Credits:Ivan Mehta Image Credits:Ivan Mehta Image Credits:Ivan Mehta Image Credits:Ivan Mehta Image Credits:Ivan Mehta Image Credits:Ivan Mehta Image Credits:Ivan Mehta
Even if Google wouldn’t include the same ultrawide and telephoto sensors as the slab Pro devices, I wish they would use the same main sensor on the Fold as the rectangle phone. The telephoto and ultrawide sensors are similar to last year’s device, so there is barely any improvement in images taken from them.
In terms of software features, there is Looks, which can change the tone of an image with different presets, and Magic Capture, which can pick the best frames from a video — useful for when you have pets or kids.
At $1,899, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is for someone who likes Pixels and wants a foldable, given it’s barely $100 less than the new iPhone Duo and the same price as the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, which are both wide-format phones. In the U.S., the taller Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra starts at $2,099.
In Europe, companies like Xiaomi and Honor are going to release their foldables, too. So Google’s foldable is going to face a lot of competition.
