summary: Fundraiser by Mark Nygate : SAVE US FROM THE MEGA EMBASSY! SUPPORT OUR LEGAL CHALLENGE Mark Nygate is organizing this fundraiser. We are 100 families taking on the CCP - and we need your help. 我們是「皇家鑄幣廠居民協會」，由約一百戶職工家庭組成。我們懇請你伸出援手。 In 2018,
content:
Fundraiser by Mark Nygate : SAVE US FROM THE MEGA EMBASSY! SUPPORT OUR LEGAL CHALLENGE
Mark Nygate is organizing this fundraiser.
We are 100 families taking on the CCP - and we need your help.
我們是「皇家鑄幣廠居民協會」，由約一百戶職工家庭組成。我們懇請你伸出援手。
In 2018, our homes-key-worker flats in Tower Hamlets were sold in a secretive deal to the People's Republic of China. We had no say. No warning. And now, we face living under the shadow of a hostile superpower.
2018年，我們居住的Tower Hamlets地段，在未經通知、無任何諮詢下，被秘密售予中國政府。我們無從置喙，如今更面對一個敵對政權的威脅。
The UK Government is expected to approve plans to build the largest embassy in Europe - right here, at Royal Mint Court, next to the Tower of London… and directly on top of our homes.
英國政府即將批准於倫敦塔旁的皇家鑄幣廠（Royal Mint Court）興建歐洲最大規模的中國大使館，預定地點正正位於我們所居之上。
This is not just a planning dispute.
我們擔憂的不僅是一項城市規劃決策，而是一場關乎國家安全、人身安全與基本權利的危機。
China has never shown any regard for our safety - and now the Government and the Metropolitan Police have abandoned us too.
自2018年起，中國政府從未就此提供明確回應，我們甚至不知道會否被驅逐、是否仍能繼續安居於此。而如今，政府與執法機關也對我們置之不理。
We are the Royal Mint Court Residents Association. People backed our previous Crowdfunder campaign that helped pay for a barrister to present our evidence including an independent security assessment showing the serious risks to us from a terror attack on the mega-embassy.
我們是「皇家鑄幣廠居民協會」。我們之前的眾籌活動獲得許多人的支持，資助我們聘請資深大律師提交證據，包括一份獨立的安全評估報告，指出超級大使館可能帶來的恐襲風險。
We are now launching an urgent legal challenge - a Judicial Review - to change the law and stop this injustice.
我們現在正展開一項緊急法律挑戰 — 即司法覆核 — 希望改變現行法律，阻止這場不公。
We need your help to protect our community from the mighty Chinese Communist Party.
我們需要你的幫助，去保護我們的社區，免受強大的中國共產黨威脅。
Whatever you can spare us, will help David stand-up to Goliath.
We are seeking to pursue a Judicial Review because we have believed all along that the planning process has been flawed. Here are some of the reasons we think are likely to be relevant:
我們決定提起司法覆核，是因為我們始終認為整個規劃程序存在問題。以下是我們認為可能相關的一些原因：
“Closed mind”: Ministers may have signalled early approval to China, before formal procedures were followed, breaking the law and abusing planning powers. In a similar vein, objections disappeared after UK ministers returned from Beijing. Residents have felt like pawns in a geopolitical game since the start.
預設立場：部長們可能在正式程序開始前就向中方表示支持，違反法律並濫用規劃權力。在部長們從北京回來之後，原有的反對聲音突然消失。居民們從一開始就覺得自己成了地緣政治博弈中的棋子。
Security concerns: Building a fortified embassy with homes on site and critical infrastructure nearby, ignoring espionage concerns and the real human risk to dissidents, is indefensible.
安全隱患：在住宅區內及重要基礎設施附近建設高度防禦的大使館，無視間諜活動與對異見人士的人身威脅，完全不能接受。
Procedural unfairness: We were shut out of the process. No consultation. No transparency. No respect for the people who live here.
程序不公：我們被完全排除在決策過程之外。無諮詢、無透明、無對居民的尊重。
Legitimate expectation: We were promised due process and protection. We got silence.
合理期望落空：我們被承諾將獲程序保障與保護，實際卻是得不到任何保障。
We still live here. 100 families. Nurses, teachers, pensioners. Our 100 homes are on land now owned by the Chinese government. That means the Chinese ambassador is our landlord - with rights to enter our homes.
我們仍然住在這裡 ，足足一百戶家庭，包括護士、教師、退休人士。我們的一百個住所現已位於中國政府擁有的土地上。這代表中國大使成為我們的業主，有權進入我們的住所。
China refuses to answer us. Since 2018, we’ve begged for assurances: will we be evicted? Will we be safe? Can we stay? Beijing’s answer: not until we get planning permission. This refusal, and the proposal to install a temporary style wooden boundary fence as a dividing line, raises fears that the Chinese Government intends to take back the entire 100 apartments at St Mary Graces Court once they secure diplomatic status for the site, leaving us homeless.
中國拒絕回應我們的訴求。自2018年起，我們不斷尋求保證：我們會被驅逐嗎？我們是否安全？我們能否繼續居住？北京的答覆是：等規劃許可下來再說。這種拒絕，以及擬議中以臨時木欄分隔的做法，讓我們擔心中國政府一旦取得外交地位，將會收回整個St Mary Graces Court的100個單位，使我們流離失所。
This embassy is a fortress. It’s not a normal diplomatic building. It will have secret communications centres, fortified walls, and surveillance technology that can monitor our entire estate, even our bedrooms. It will also stand on top of critical UK cables that MI5 warn are a security risk to the UK.
這座大使館是一個堡壘，並非普通的外交建築。它將設有秘密通訊設施、加固圍牆、監控技術，可監視整個屋苑，甚至包括我們的睡房。而它的地基下方，更有英國重要電纜 ，MI5曾警告這是對國家安全的威脅。
The UK Government knows the risk - and ignored it. Our independent security report warns that this site puts families and national security at risk. Even the UK’s Head of Counter-Terrorism originally objected - citing threats to residents and dissidents. But since ministers returned from Beijing, objections have mysteriously vanished.
英國政府明知有風險，卻選擇無視。我們的獨立安全報告指出，該地點將危害居民與國家安全。甚至連英國反恐部門首長最初也曾反對 ， 指出對居民與異見人士的威脅。但自從部長從北京回來後，這些反對聲音神秘地消失。
Ministers made no mention of the 100 families living here. We are alarmed that the letters from Home Secretary Yvette Cooper and Foreign Secretary David Lammy have ignored the fact that UK families live in 100 apartments on the land that is actually part of Royal Mint court - and is owned by the Chinese government. Our Resident’s Chairman has personally appealed to ministers, submitted the full Crilly Consultants security report, and our plight has appeared in The Times, FT, BBC, CNN, and more. What is happening to democratic accountability in this country?
部長們從未提及這裡有一百戶居民。我們對內政大臣Yvette Cooper及外交大臣David Lammy的信件感到震驚，因為他們完全忽略了皇家鑄幣廠的土地上住有英國公民、100個家庭。我們的居民協會主席曾親自致函部長、提交完整的Crilly安全報告，而我們的處境亦已被《泰晤士報》、《金融時報》、BBC、CNN等多間媒體報導。英國民主問責制度何在？
The first duty of the UK government is to protect its citizens. We understand the UK’s diplomatic obligations - but not at the expense of its own people. The refusal to acknowledge the basic risks of housing a high-security foreign embassy on top of a residential block is deeply troubling. It appears the government is prioritising relations with Beijing over the safety of its own citizens.
英國政府的首要職責是保護其國民。我們明白外交義務，但不能以犧牲本國人民為代價。將一個高安全級別的外國大使館設於住宅區上方，而拒絕承認基本風險，是極度令人不安的。
It’s not just about us. Dissidents, including Hong Kongers, Uyghurs, Tibetans, Taiwanese and Chinese exile communities are terrified. They’ve told us they no longer feel safe protesting outside the site, and on British soil. Their presence, and ours, will be met with constant surveillance and intimidation by a regime known to harass and threaten activists - even abroad.
這件事不僅關係到我們。流亡港人、維吾爾人、西藏人、台灣人及中國異見社群皆感到恐懼。他們表示不再敢在該地點或英國土地上公開抗議。他們與我們一樣，將面對來自這個以恐嚇異見者聞名的政權的持續監控與威嚇。
The people have spoken, and they support us.
On 8 February 2025, thousands of British citizens - including Hong Kongers, Uyghurs, Tibetans, Taiwanese and Chinese pro-democracy activists, and human rights campaigners - gathered outside Royal Mint Court in protest against this embassy.
2025年2月8日，數以千計的英國公民 ，包括港人、維吾爾人、西藏人、台灣人、中國民主人士與人權倡議者， 齊集皇家鑄幣廠，抗議中國大使館計劃。
They were joined by cross-party MPs, journalists, and allies. Together, they said NO to the Chinese embassy, and YES to democratic values, safety, and justice.
他們與跨黨派議員、記者及盟友並肩站立，一同說出明確立場：反對中國大使館，支持民主、安全與公義。
Further mass protests followed on 15 March, 3 May, and 14 June - showing growing national resistance to the plan.
3月15日、5月3日及6月14日亦舉行後續大型集會，反對聲浪日益壯大。
They continue to protest, and have made it clear: they won’t stop until this mega-embassy deal is over.
抗議仍在持續，並清楚表示：他們不會停止，直至該項目取消為止。
But the Government is not listening.
But we need your help - fast.
The legal fees for a Judicial Review are beyond the reach of ordinary families. But with your help, we can stand up to both Beijing and Whitehall.
司法覆核的法律費用遠超普通家庭的負擔。但在您的幫助下，我們能夠與北京和英國政府對抗。
This case is about more than one building. It’s about:
Protecting British citizens from state overreach
Defending UK democracy from foreign influence
Challenging backroom deals that put power over people
If we succeed, we won’t just protect our homes. We’ll set a precedent that no foreign government can build on British soil without respecting British citizens and British values.
如若成功，我們不僅能保護我們的家園，我們更是創下先例：任何外國政府不得在罔顧英國公民和英國價值的前提下在英國土地上建造任何建築。
Please chip in whatever you can. £10. £100. £1,000. Every penny goes to legal costs to take this to court. We are a group of teachers, nurses, shop workers and pensioners. We don’t have the Chinese Communist Party’s millions - but with your help, we do have people power.
請您捐出任何您能負擔的金額 — 不論是 £10，£100 還是 £1,000。每一分錢都將用於支付法律費用，讓我們將此案帶上法庭。我們只是一群教師、護士、店員和退休人士。雖然我們沒有中國共產黨的龐大資金 — 但在您的幫助下，我們擁有的是人民的力量。
Because if they can do this to us, they can do it to anyone.
This is a secure UK-based platform, fully registered and subject to UK law.
It is widely used to support political and legal campaigns, including by MPs, NGOs, and grassroots movements - some of which are openly critical of the Chinese government.
該平台廣泛用於支持政治和法律活動，包括國會議員、非政府組織和基層運動 — 包括曾公開批評中國政府的政治活動。
The platform offers full transparency, with public donation records and payment processing via Stripe or PayPal.
該平台提供完全透明的捐款記錄，並通過 Stripe 或 PayPal 處理支付。
There is no history of censorship or compliance with pressure from the Chinese state.
It adheres strictly to GDPR regulations, ensuring donor and campaigner data is protected.
平台嚴格遵守 GDPR 規範，確保捐款者和活動者的數據安全。
2.95% + 0.25 of each donation goes to the platform; 100% of the remaining funds will be used to cover legal costs.
每筆捐款將扣除 2.95% 加 £0.25 之平台手續費，其餘款項將全數用以支付法律相關費用。
If the legal case is dismissed, your donation will be directed to charity unless you request a refund. If you would like your donation returned, please email us. We will calculate and refund your contribution (with platform fee deducted).
如法律訴訟最終被駁回，捐款將撥捐予慈善機構，除非閣下主動申請退款。如欲索回捐款，請電郵至，我們將在扣除平台手續費後，計算並退還閣下之捐款。
We will post updates every two weeks, which you can follow directly on this page.

Fundraiser by Boston Standswithhk : US Hong Kong Safe Harbor Postcard Campaign
Boston Standswithhk is organizing this fundraiser.
***When donation, make as anonymous if you wish to hide the donator's name and make the TIPS to 0.00***
While US-China tensions continue to escalate and the November presidential elections loom near, as Hongkongers living in the United States (or any informed person in the world), we must not forget or turn a blind eye to the CCP’s continuous oppression on Hongkongers and other minority groups in China, such as Uyghurs, Tibetans, and Mongolians. With the promulgation of the new National Security Law on June 30, 2020, the government has since been arresting and charging dissidents with these vaguely-worded laws that may entail life imprisonment. In the past month alone, 12 Hong Kongers fleeing protest-related charges have been detained in China and denied meetings with lawyers since August 23, 2020; Legislative Council elections had been postponed a year in the name of “public health concerns” amidst a mass arrest of candidates; media mogul Jimmy Lai, who runs the only pro-democratic print newspaper in Hong Kong, has been arrested with the National Security Law; and the Education Bureau has begun actively censoring content they deemed politically incorrect in Liberal Studies textbooks, including concepts like “civil disobedience” and “separation of powers”, and images of Lennon Walls. Up until today, the administration has arrested more than 10,000 Hong Kongers, charged over 2,200, deployed water cannons, fired more than 16,000 tear gas canisters and over 10,000 rubber bullets against its own people. Freedom of speech, freedom of assembly and political rights as we knew it have been thoroughly eroded.
11月的美國總統大選逐漸逼近，中美關係日漸緊張，作為居住在美國的香港人或是在這個世界上任何有良知的人，面對中共對香港、維吾爾族、藏族和蒙古族的持續壓逼，我們不能容忍，更不能視而不見。自2020年6月30日頒布《國家安全法》以來，政府持續逮捕異見人​​士，並以措辭含糊的法律起訴抗爭者，香港的司法制度已經徹底淪為政府的打壓工具。及後更有12名香港抗爭者為了逃離這種不公義的審判欲流亡台灣，卻被中共非法拘捕。他們無法與律師會面，音訊全無。而香港人僅有的發聲方法——立法會選舉，卻因為「公共衛生風險」而被推遲一年；同時間，大批候選人被逮捕或是被拒絕參選。作為香港唯一異見紙媒《蘋果日報》的老闆黎智英被警方高調逮捕，《蘋果日報》總部更被大肆搜查。教育局亦積極審查通識科教科書中所謂的「政治不正確」內容，例如「公民抗命」和「三權分立」的概念，以及連儂牆相片。到今天為止，已經有超過10,000多名香港人被捕、2,200多人被起訴，警方向市民發射了超過16,000枚催淚彈和10,000多發橡皮子彈，令香港人長期生活在恐懼中。香港人的言論自由、集會自由和政治權利已被徹底侵蝕。
In light of the deteriorating situation, we plan to kickstart a new round of postcard campaign urging Congress to pass two bills related to Hong Kong as soon as possible - Hong Kong Safe Harbor Act (H.R.7415/S.4110), and Hong Kong People’s Freedom and Choice Act (H.R.7428/S.4229):
鑑於情況日益惡化，我們希望透過郵寄明信片給國會議員的方式，呼籲他們盡快通過兩項與香港有關的法案 —— 香港安全港法案 (H.R.7415 / S.4110) 和香港人民自由與選擇法(H.R.7428 / S.4229):
The Hong Kong Safe Harbor Act will designate certain Hong Kong residents who are victims of persecution or who have a well-founded fear of future persecution because of their peaceful political activities as Priority 2 refugees (excluded from refugee cap), allowing them and their spouses, children, parents to apply to the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program for protection. (Click here for more details)
《香港安全港法案》將指定某些遭受迫害，或因其參與和平的政治活動而感到恐懼的香港居民列為「優先級別2」的難民，且不受每年限額限制，亦允許他們及其配偶、子女、父母向「美國難民接納計劃」申請庇護。(詳情請瀏覽)
The Hong Kong People's Freedom and Choice Act will provide Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Hong Kongers, maintain Hong Kong’s status as autonomous for the purposes of immigration, provide special and expedited status for certain high-skilled Hong Kongers as well as expedite Permanent Resident status for Hong Kongers residing in the US. (Click here for more details)
《香港人民自由與選擇法》會為香港人提供臨時保護身份（TPS），維持香港在移民方面的自治地位，亦為部分香港專業人仕提供特殊和快速的身份，並加快辦理香港人的美國永久居民(綠卡)身份的程序。(詳情請瀏覽)
In our last postcard campaign pushing for the Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act, we delivered over 3000 postcards to Congress. We aren’t part of any formal organization and do not have operation funds. We desperately call for your contribution again to help us deliver these postcards to Congress, to remind them of Hong Kong’s urgent situation and urge them to take immediate action. Your contribution would support our printing and delivery costs. Thank you so much!
在上一次推動《香港人權與民主法》的明信片運動中，我們向國會送出了超過3000張的明信片。我們不是任何正式組織的成員，也沒有運營資金，所以我們竭誠呼籲您為我們提供資金，並幫助我們將這些明信片送交您們所屬的國會議員，提醒他們香港的緊急狀況，並呼籲他們立即採取行動。所有受到的捐款將支持我們的打印和交付成本。萬分感謝！

content:
蒋沉在台北工会活动中进行劳工投票 - 聚焦台湾
2026 年选举/蒋、沉在台北工会活动中进行劳工投票
要激活文字转语音服务，请首先同意以下隐私政策。
周六，台北市长蒋万安（左）和民进党市长候选人沉普马在台北电视辩论前合影。中央通讯社照片2026年10月31日
中新社台北11月1日电 台北市市长蒋万安周日在台北市总工会活动中表示，将改善市政府雇员的薪资、休假和工作条件，而民进党挑战者沉伯洋则概述了支持工薪家庭的建议。
正在即将举行的地方选举中寻求连任的蒋介石表示，作为市长，他已经成立了一个包括工人代表在内的劳工政策咨询委员会，并承诺与工会进行直接对话。
这位国民党候选人补充说，在他的任期内，市政雇员得到了切实的改善，包括每个假期额外休息一天，以及市政雇员的奖励上限从新台币 8,000 元（245 美元）提高到新台币 10,000 元。
台北市市长蒋万安（左）周日出席台北市总工会活动。中央通讯社照片2026年11月1日
此外，蒋介石还表示，他的政府已监督更换了134辆环保服务车辆，并投资了新台币1.78亿元，用于升级前线工人的办公室、休息室和卫生间设施。
与此同时，沉强调了帮助照顾幼儿和老年家庭成员的工人的建议，包括改善儿童保育环境以防止虐待儿童以及增加长期护理机构的床位数量。
这位民进党候选人还呼吁减少有小孩的父母的工作时间，并为城市居民提供六次免费心理咨询。
沉彪马周日在台北总工会的活动中接受采访。中央通讯社照片2026年11月1日
台湾定于11月28日举行的2026年地方选举也被称为“九合一”选举，因为该国22个市县的选民将选举市长、县长、市县议员等九种地方政府职位的官员。
高雄市长辩论聚焦第205兵工厂重建及政治捐款
周五晚间，高雄举行市长辩论，两位主要候选人——执政党民进党赖瑞隆和反对党国民党柯志恩——主要关注第205兵工厂旧址重建和政治捐款问题。
台湾地方选举最后阶段抽签拉开帷幕
台湾各地市长和地方长官候选人周二为 11 月 28 日地方选举抽签。
191名候选人注册台湾平权运动“骄傲观察”网站
该非营利组织周二表示，共有 191 名竞选地方政府职位的候选人通过注册台湾平权运动的“骄傲观察”网站来表达对性别平等的支持。

2026 ELECTIONS/Chiang, Shen court labor vote at Taipei trade union event

Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (left) and DPP mayoral candidate Puma Shen pose together before a televised debate in Taipei on Saturday. CNA photo Oct. 31, 2026
Taipei, Nov. 1 (CNA) Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) touted improvements to municipal employees' pay, leave and working conditions, while Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) challenger Puma Shen (沈伯洋) outlined proposals to support working families at a Federation of Taipei Trade Unions event Sunday.
Chiang, who is seeking re-election in the upcoming local elections, said that, as mayor, he had established a Labor Policy Advisory Committee that included worker representatives and pledged to engage in direct dialogue with labor unions.
The Kuomintang candidate added that city employees had seen tangible improvements during his tenure, including an additional day off for each holiday worked and an increase in the incentive bonus cap for municipal workers from NT$8,000 (US$245) to NT$10,000.
Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (left) at a Federation of Taipei Trade Unions event Sunday. CNA photo Nov. 1, 2026
In addition, Chiang said his administration had overseen the replacement of 134 environmental service vehicles and invested NT$178 million to upgrade office, break and restroom facilities for frontline workers.
Shen, meanwhile, highlighted proposals to help workers caring for young children and elderly family members, including enhancing childcare environments to prevent child abuse and increasing the number of beds in long-term care facilities.
The DPP candidate also called for reduced working hours for parents with young children and six free psychological counseling sessions for city residents.
Puma Shen gets interviewed at a Federation of Taipei Trade Unions event Sunday. CNA photo Nov. 1, 2026

title: How to prevent an energy quarantine of Taiwan
zh_title: 如何防止台湾能源检疫
summary: 如何防止台湾能源检疫 - 大西洋理事会北京正在为台湾能源检疫奠定基础。经济、政治、技术和军事因素可能导致能源检疫风险在 2028 年和 2029 年达到顶峰。为了阻止这种强制行动，美国及其盟国应与台湾合作，通过支持上述所有能源战略来加强其安全，重点是向台湾北部供应用于发电的柴油。中共总书记习近平多次明确表态：
content:
如何防止台湾能源检疫 - 大西洋理事会
北京正在为台湾的能源检疫奠定基础。
经济、政治、技术和军事因素可能导致能源检疫风险在 2028 年和 2029 年达到峰值。
为了阻止这种胁迫行动，美国及其盟国应与台湾合作，通过支持上述所有能源战略来加强台湾的安全，重点是向台湾北部供应用于发电的柴油。
中国共产党总书记习近平一贯明确表示台湾应该与中国大陆“统一”，并在2013年表示“两岸长期存在的政治分歧……总不能一代一代传下去”。习近平还在 2026 年 5 月与美国总统唐纳德·特朗普会面时警告称，在台湾问题上可能会发生“冲突甚至冲突”。这件事似乎不是决心的问题，而是时机的问题。出于政治、经济和技术原因，习近平可能对台湾采取行动的风险可能在 2028 年和 2029 年达到顶峰。
为了实现其长期的统一目标，北京可能会尝试通过非动能措施胁迫台湾。隔离的模糊性和灵活性可能使其成为对习近平特别有吸引力的选择。北京可以宣称，检疫——允许一些船只通过，同时拒绝其他船只，特别是油轮和液化天然气（LNG）运输船——是一种国内执法措施，而不是一种战争行为。有证据表明，习近平的军队已经在为隔离而不是入侵进行演练，因为中国海警在台湾以东海域持续存在，并试图将封锁商业交通正常化，从而挑战台北的海上控制。
切断台湾能源供应的隔离作为一种强制工具尤其有效。台湾几乎没有本土生产石油、天然气或煤炭，这使得它几乎完全依赖海运进口碳氢化合物。北京很早就明白能源安全在台湾突发事件中的重要性。目前，它不太容易受到能源中断的影响，并准备好承受根据需要切断部分能源进口的情况。
对台湾实施能源隔离对美国来说将是一件严重的事情。台湾因其地理位置、深厚的技术专长以及作为人工智能（AI）供应链关键节点的地位而对华盛顿具有重要的战略意义。中国吞并台湾将使全球经济和战略力量平衡向有利于北京的方向倾斜，美国决策者必须避免对台湾采取强制行动，否则可能升级为军事冲突。碰撞的危险怎么强调都不为过：美国和中国都是拥有强大常规军队的核武器国家；技术超级大国，尤其是人工智能领域；以及拥有一系列强制工具的庞大经济体。
应对这些风险需要大量军事投资，但联盟决策者不应忽视近期能源隔离的严重风险。为了阻止台湾的能源隔离，美国和其他民主国家应与台湾合作，通过上述所有方法以及快速部署燃料来源（特别是柴油）的战略优先事项来加强其能源安全。美国，T

How to prevent an energy quarantine of Taiwan - Atlantic Council
Beijing is laying the groundwork for an energy quarantine of Taiwan.
Economic, political, technical, and military factors could lead energy quarantine risks to peak in 2028 and 2029.
To deter this coercive action, the United States and allies should work with Taiwan to bolster its security through support for an all-of-the-above energy strategy, concentrating on supplying northern Taiwan with diesel for power generation.
Chinese Communist Party (CCP) General Secretary Xi Jinping has consistently made clear his view that Taiwan should be “reunified” with mainland China, stating in 2013 that “long-standing cross-Strait political differences … cannot be passed down from generation to generation (总不能一代一代传下去).” Xi also warned of “clashes or even conflicts” over Taiwan in his May 2026 meeting with US President Donald Trump. The matter appears to be a question not of determination but of timing. For political, economic, and technical reasons, the risk that Xi might move against Taiwan could peak in 2028 and 2029.
To achieve its longstanding unification goal, Beijing might attempt to coerce Taiwan via non-kinetic measures. The ambiguity and flexibility of a quarantine could render it an especially attractive option for Xi. Beijing could claim that a quarantine—allowing some ships to pass while turning back others, especially oil tankers and liquefied natural gas (LNG) carriers—is a domestic law-enforcement measure rather than an act of war. There is some evidence that Xi’s forces are already rehearsing for a quarantine rather than an invasion, as the Chinese coast guard is maintaining a continuous presence in waters east of Taiwan and trying to normalize interdictions of live commercial traffic, thereby challenging Taipei’s maritime control.
A quarantine to cut off Taiwan’s energy supply would be particularly effective as a coercive tool. Taiwan has virtually no indigenous production of oil, natural gas, or coal, rendering it almost totally reliant on seaborne imports for hydrocarbons. Beijing has long understood the importance of energy security in a Taiwan contingency. It is currently much less vulnerable to an energy outage and is prepared to weather a cutoff of some of its own energy imports as needed.
An energy quarantine of Taiwan would be a grave matter for the United States. Taiwan is strategically important to Washington due to its geography, deep technological expertise, and position as a critical node in artificial intelligence (AI) supply chains. China’s absorption of Taiwan would tilt the global economic and strategic balance of power in Beijing’s favor, making it imperative for US policymakers to avert coercive action against the island, which could escalate into a military conflict. It is difficult to overstate the dangers of a collision: the United States and China are nuclear-armed nations with powerful conventional militaries; technological superpowers, especially in AI; and huge economies with an array of coercive tools.
Countering these risks will require substantial military investments, but coalition policymakers should not overlook the serious risks of a near-term energy quarantine. To deter an energy quarantine of Taiwan, the United States and other democracies should work with Taiwan to reinforce its energy security with an all-of-the-above approach and the strategic prioritization of rapidly deployable fuel sources, especially diesel. The United States, Taiwan, and other actors should immediately begin preparing for a contingency by deploying a diesel-generation supply chain across Taiwan, especially in the energy-scarce northern regions surrounding the capital, Taipei. That will include diesel production at refineries, distributed storage, and ultimately generators for power supply. The humble diesel generator could be a key determinant in the future of global power.
The groundwork: Beijing is mitigating its own energy vulnerabilities
In 2003, then General Secretary Hu Jintao warned that China faced the “Malacca Dilemma,” or “马六甲困局.” Hu noted that Beijing’s reliance on seaborne oil imports from the Middle East navigating the Malacca Strait near Singapore raised acute vulnerabilities, as shipments could be interdicted by the US Navy. More than two decades later, Beijing is becoming increasingly self-sufficient in energy overall and in transportation fuels such as gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel. While Beijing will not achieve true independence in transportation fuels for several years, it is on its way to effectively mitigating the Malacca Dilemma.
Beijing has been seeking to mitigate this dilemma via a combination of reduced transport fuel demand (largely from vehicle electrification), elevated domestic crude oil production, overland crude oil pipeline imports (largely from Russia), maximizing refinery production of transportation fuels, and tapping unprecedentedly large petroleum stockpiles. Beijing’s growing oil security will enable it to increasingly decouple from international markets and allow it to act more aggressively vis-à-vis Taiwan.
Electrification has been fundamental to China’s energy self-sufficiency drive. Electricity’s share of final energy in China has grown from about 5 percent in 1990 to nearly 30 percent today, an increase of about 1 percentage point every year, and will soon surpass the percentage share of every Group of Seven (G7) economy. Mainland China’s power generation capacity has risen from 138 gigawatts in 1990 to over 4,000 gigawatts by May 2026; China has also added 24.2 million charging points (not stations) and, by 2023, had already provided $230 billion in government support to its EV industry. Finally, many Chinese cities have mandated that ride share vehicles and urban logistics vehicles must be “new energy vehicles”—in practice, usually battery EVs. These measures have enabled China to become the undeniable world leader in vehicle electrification.
Vehicle electrification rapidly mitigates Beijing’s exposure to the Malacca Dilemma by directly reducing gasoline and diesel demand, especially in politically-sensitive first tier cities. According to the International Energy Agency, electric vehicles are set to reduce Chinese oil demand by about a total of 2.7 million barrels per day (MMbpd) by 2030. In a July 2025 analysis, Rhodium Group found that China’s total electric vehicle fleet already displaced more than 1 MMbpd, with battery electric vehicles beginning to make significant headway in trucking fleets that rely primarily on diesel.
For these reasons, the International Energy Agency and others hold that Chinese gasoline and diesel demand has likely already peaked. Deployment of advanced, energy-dense batteries to medium and heavy-duty vehicles would further reduce diesel consumption, alleviating Beijing’s chief transport fuel constraint in a crisis. Adoption of advanced batteries in heavy-duty vehicles might rise sharply over the next year or two.
As it reduces its transport fuel demand via vehicle electrification, China has also stockpiled about 1.2 billion barrels of crude oil in December 2025 in total petroleum reserves, by far the world’s largest. While Beijing is drawing down oil inventories amid the oil market disruptions from the US–Iran war, storage levels remain elevated and can be expanded if the conflict winds down.
In the case of a quarantine, Beijing would rely heavily on supply flows of oil, not only on stock withdrawals.
Here it’s useful to divide Beijing’s oil supplies into different resilience tiers. Tier 1, the most secure tier, is China’s own domestic crude oil production, which ticked up from 3.8 million barrels per day (MMbpd) in 2017 to about 4.4 MMbpd in the first seven months of 2026, covering about 30 percent of domestic demand before the US–Iran war.
In addition to its own domestic production, China can also obtain additional volumes from relatively secure overland pipelines in Tier 2A. China’s secure overland crude oil shipments total about 0.8 MMbpd. This is split between the Russia-to-China leg of the East Siberia–Pacific Ocean pipeline, with deliveries of about 600,000 barrels per day (b/d), and the Atasu–Alashankou pipeline, which brings both Russian and Kazakhstani oil via Kazakhstan and delivers roughly 200,000 b/d to Xinjiang. Existing Russian and Kazakhstani overland pipelines have delivery capacity of about 1.2 MMbpd; in a crisis, China would likely be able to access these full volumes, albeit at a possible premium.
Tier 2B consists of Russian maritime crude imports. Russia typically ships about 0.75 MMbpd to China from its Kozmino port, near Vladivostok, with other export terminals typically providing about 0.25 MMbpd. The US Navy and coalitional navies would weigh carefully whether to interdict Russian ships and disable Russian exports. Targeting Russian vessels and infrastructure risks horizontal and perhaps even vertical escalation, but in a Taiwan contingency the benefits of disabling Russian energy shipments to the Chinese mainland could, under some conditions, outweigh that risk. To mitigate the risks of maritime transit, Beijing and Moscow might expand the capacity of the mainland China leg of the East Siberia–Pacific Ocean pipeline, “promoting” perhaps 0.8 MMbpd from Tier 2B into Tier 2A.
Tier 3 is the 200,000 b/d pipeline from Myanmar, which delivers oil to Yunnan. This source can be thought of as only quasi-overland, however, as it relies on maritime imports to the Made Island oil import terminal that could be interdicted relatively easily.
Tier 4 imports, meanwhile, consist of all other maritime sources.
China can reliably access about 5.6 MMbpd of crude oil supply from domestic and overland sources if all existing pipeline capacity is utilized. Adding about another 1 MMbpd from Russian maritime imports would bring the total to nearly 6.6 MMbpd. If its most secure supplies are operable in a crisis, then about 30 percent of China’s supplies would hinge on Russia, demonstrating Beijing’s interest in maintaining close ties with Moscow.
Turning to demand, China’s refinery runs for crude oil stood at about 15.2 MMbpd in January–February 2026 (assuming 7.33 barrels/ton). Amid the US–Iran war, these runs fell to about 12.5 MMbpd in June, per China’s National Bureau of Statistics. In a contingency, Beijing could again sharply reduce its demand, including in petrochemicals, which accounts for about 25 percent of Chinese oil demand and largely serves the export market. In addition, Beijing could order refineries to maximize output of transportation fuels, including diesel and jet fuel for its military.
Given that total domestic supply from production and secure import capacity equals 6.6 MMbpd, and assuming total refinery runs of 12.5 MMbpd seen in June 2026, China would face a daily deficit of about 5.9 MMbpd in a contingency today. Assuming that China has reserves of about 1.1 billion barrels of crude oil after Iran war-related drawdowns, and that it would be able to draw inventories to only 20 percent before facing constraints from geographic dispersion and tank draw, China would be able to sustain at least one hundred and fifty days of civilian and military activities before reaching physical shortage.
By 2030, however, Beijing will very likely enjoy far greater oil security. Tier 1 and 2A overland crude supplies could very easily rise to 6.8 MMbpd on higher domestic production and greater overland tie-ins with Russian and Central Asian crude oil pipelines. Crude oil demand, meanwhile, could fall to 11.5 MMbpd amid vehicle electrification, leaving a deficit of 4.7 MMbpd. Assuming 1.2 billion barrels of crude oil reserves and a maximum drawdown of inventories to 20 percent, Beijing could likely cover at least two hundred days of refinery runs in a contingency by 2030. Beijing may soon be able to withstand an oil blockade for well over half a year, and perhaps much longer if it continues to increase the size of its oil reserves, can still access Russian maritime imports, or accelerates vehicle electrification.
The United States’ implicit answer to a potential Taiwan quarantine has been to impose a counter-blockade of China’s oil imports. That strategy is increasingly outdated. Policymakers in Washington, Taipei, Tokyo, and beyond need to understand this dangerous new reality, insulate against an energy quarantine, and find other sources of coercive leverage against Beijing.
Taiwan’s exposure: Two likely scenarios for an energy quarantine
Taiwan’s indigenous energy production (including nuclear energy generation) as a percentage of all energy demand declined from 8.3 percent to 5.3 percent from 2016 to 2025.
Taiwan’s reserves of oil, coal, and LNG are required to cover ninety days, thirty days, and eleven days of consumption for each commodity, respectively, although inventories typically cover more. In March 2026, the Ministry of Economic Affairs reported oil, coal, and LNG on-hand inventories of one hundred and fifty days, forty days, and eleven days, respectively. Still, Taiwan’s actual days of consumption covered vary based on several factors, including seasonal weather patterns, its ability to export goods such as semiconductors from its energy-intensive industrial sector, and the continued operation of refineries.
Other regional democracies’ roles in a Taiwan contingency could be constrained by their energy-related vulnerabilities. Japan and South Korea also have limited storage inventories, while other US allies such as the Philippines and Australia are themselves highly reliant on energy imports. Australia’s fuel dependency is staggering: it relies on imports for 83 percent of all refined petroleum products. The coalition has serious work to do to improve its collective energy resilience, and to do so quickly.
If Beijing attempted to subjugate Taiwan via an energy quarantine, two scenarios are most likely. Beijing might straightforwardly implement a quarantine or even blockade of Taiwan, attempting to interdict any inbound energy shipments via its coast guard by claiming a legal pretext.
Alternatively, Beijing might try an indirect approach by exploiting or even stimulating a future Middle Eastern oil crisis. Surging oil prices would disproportionately damage Beijing’s regional rivals, which are relatively reliant on oil imports even as China increasingly turns into a self-sufficient electrotech state.
Timing the risk: Quarantine dangers might peak in 2028 and 2029
The dangers of an energy-weighted geopolitical crisis over Taiwan are already serious but might peak in 2028 and 2029 due to economics, politics, Taiwan’s electricity reserve margins, military readiness, and AI. Mainland China’s economy is showing significant strain even as Taiwan’s powers ahead; both Taiwan and the United States will hold key elections in 2028; Taiwan’s electricity reserve margin is on track to reach dangerously low levels in this period; US military readiness levels might be damaged by protracted deployments in other theaters; and while AI timelines are highly unpredictable, the United States might begin to experience takeoff growth, which could enable it to establish permanent technological dominance. Given these factors, and his own age, Xi might believe by 2028 that he has a limited window of opportunity to act.
Beijing has economic reasons for attempting to control Taiwan sooner rather than later. If economic trends continue, Beijing’s comparative performance legitimacy will weaken vis-à-vis Taiwan through January 2028. Taiwan’s gross domestic product (GDP) growth is projected to reach an astonishing 11 percent in 2026. While most economic growth is concentrated in the tech sector, real median incomes are rising, Taiwan’s government is flush enough to disburse cash payments, the fiscal budget is balanced, and Taiwan’s debt-to-GDP ratio is the lowest in East Asia. Taiwan’s economy is doing well, even if growth will likely decelerate.
Conversely, while Beijing retains formidable economic power, mainland China’seconomy shows significant weakness. Growth rates are undeniably slowing. Chinese debt levels are in a “league of their own,” according to Mark Williams, chief Asia economist at Capital Economics. Logan Wright, partner at Rhodium Group, warns that Beijing’s growth model is “fundamentally broken” and faces “steady decay.” The risks to mainland China’s economy may provide added urgency for Xi to pursue an energy quarantine of Taiwan and coerce it into accepting Beijing’s rule. Assuming current economic trends continue, Taiwan’s living standards will further outpace mainland China’s, significantly damaging the appeal of unification for Taiwan’s voters.
Taiwan will hold its next presidential election in January 2028. While nothing is certain, the outcome of the election is likely to lead to intense discomfort in Beijing (as the author has been warning since June 2026). In most democracies, rising living standards benefit the incumbent party. That means that the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) is likely to prevail in 2028 presidential elections, assuming Taiwan maintains robust economic growth, which is likely; the DPP is also favored to obtain a majority in the Legislative Yuan, Taiwan’s parliament. Living standards are not the only variable affecting elections, and the composition of candidates from the three main parties in Taiwan will matter greatly for the 2028 election, governing, and cross-Strait relations. Nonetheless, initial indications suggest that political economy trends in Taiwan do not appear to be moving in Beijing’s favor.
As political economy theory might predict, Taiwan’s voters may be rewarding the incumbent party for producing rising living standards. In a stunning reversal from even a few months ago, the DPP is now favored to win the Taipei mayoral race. The approval rating of President Lai Ching-te of the DPP has steadily climbed for months and is at its highest level since April 2025. Other parties could still win in 2028, especially if economic growth falters, perhaps due to an AI market correction in the United States. Nonetheless, assuming robust (and reasonably well-distributed) economic growth continues, then the DPP will likely win both the presidential and the Legislative Yuan elections in January 2028, to Beijing’s immense dissatisfaction.
The United States will also hold its own presidential election in November 2028. Political trends indicate the election will be divisive, potentially distracting Americans from cross-Strait affairs. In addition, while Beijing eyes Trump warily, CCP leaders believe Trump’s transactional approach to governing might offer opportunities vis-à-vis Taiwan in the remainder of his term.
Technical factors will amplify political and economic risks. Taipower, Taiwan’s state-run power company, projects that its nighttime reserve margin will fall to about 8 percent in 2028 and 2029, far below its targeted reserve margin of 15 percent. If current trends continue, Taiwan’s power sector could face interrupted power supplies at night even in peacetime, which would make it even more vulnerable to a potential energy quarantine.
Beijing will also be weighing US military readiness and weapons inventory levels. Where these will stand in 2028 is uncertain, especially if the US conflict in Iran escalates.
AI timelines are their own huge source of uncertainty for 2028–2029. Beijing’s perception that the United States might be on the verge of establishing permanent technological dominance via powerful AI might upend Xi’s assumptions about the desirability of strategic patience and further incentivize Xi to intervene against Taiwan, the world’s most advanced chipmaker.
Finally, there is the human element: Xi’s own sense of destiny. If Taiwan shows no medium-term interest in peacefully or semi-peacefully uniting with the mainland, then Xi might feel pressure to act. He will turn seventy-five in 2028, will have limited patience for sentiment to change through future Taiwanese elections in 2032 or even 2036, and has made clear he does not want the Taiwan issue ‘passed down from generation to generation.’
All these considerations do not guarantee that 2028–2029 will be the peak period of risks in US-China relations. Risks might persist for decades. Still, these factors suggest a convergence of serious, compounding risks that warrant preparation and mitigation.
A strategy for deterrence: Taiwan and its friends should prepare for an energy contingency
There is a need to hedge against the foreseeable and highly consequential risk of an energy quarantine of Taiwan by Beijing, perhaps as early as 2028. While Taiwan is already taking important steps to enhance its energy resilience, its government and the United States must do more to prepare for this risk—and quickly.
To address its urgent energy security challenges, Taiwan needs to take an all-of-the-above approach to electricity generation while bolstering transmission.
Nuclear energy, in particular, is one of the most important pillars of Taiwan’s energy resiliency and should be expanded. Nuclear energy can operate continuously for at least eighteen months once fueled. Additionally, reactors are unlikely to be deliberately destroyed by CCP forces in a contingency. Beijing does not want to risk radiation exposure on the island it seeks to seize. Working with the United States, Japan, and other actors, Taiwan should seek to expand nuclear energy capacity as quickly as possible and start bringing its third nuclear power plant in Maanshan back online in 2028.
In addition to nuclear energy, Taiwan should expand use of LNG, renewables, oil for generation and transportation, and even coal where appropriate. Taiwan should continue to deepen ties with the US LNG complex; expanding natural gas storage capacity will also prove useful.
Finally, and most importantly, the island should adopt a “north diesel, south renewables” approach to electricity generation in preparation for a contingency, and resource this plan effectively.
Northern Taiwan, home to the capital Taipei, is critical. While northern Taiwan has some limited generation capacity, it is a net “importer” from the southern and central parts of the island, in what officials call ”南電北送,”or “send southern power north.” In a contingency, northern Taiwan might not be able to access power generation from the southern and central regions due to sabotage of power stations, substations, transmission lines, or other infrastructure. Moreover, northern Taiwan cannot rely on local renewables generation: Taipei’s solar capacity factor is, inadequately, about the same as Seattle’s, onshore land availability to build more solar is minimal, and regional offshore wind projects, while useful, generate less power in peak summer electricity demand months and also face sabotage risks. Finally, gas-fired power plants at Datan and Tunghsiao constitute the bulk of northern Taiwan’s indigenous power generation, and northern Taiwan’s LNG inventories are finite. If south-to-north transmission lines are cut in a contingency, Taipei could run out of electricity in under one month.
Fuels, especially diesel, are therefore critical for countering an energy quarantine or blockade of Taiwan, particularly one that could occur on a short timeline before the island has time to strengthen resilience through nuclear energy expansion and other tactics. Diesel can be stored for long periods of time and can provide distributed power without transmission wires, as Ukraine is proving. Additionally, diesel units can be deployed in a matter of weeks, although deploying this systematically will require more time and resources.
For approximately $10 billion in up-front capital expenditure plus an estimated $500 million a year to maintain, test, and rotate fuel, northern Taiwan could field about 2 gigawatts of diesel generation (based on author calculations). About half of the capital expenditures would be for a dedicated diesel fuel stockpile and dispersed, hardened storage; generators would account for the rest of the initial outlay. That level of diesel generation would provide enough power to keep hospitals, cooling stations, sanitation, telecom, and emergency services running in northern Taiwan for roughly five months without any power from the south. Taiwan could very likely stand up a first tranche of this system by summer 2027, when it could conduct power generation exercises as part of the Urban Resilience drills. The full buildout could be completed across 2028 and 2029 (and accelerated as needed).
In addition, Taiwan’s southern and central regions have large existing thermal generation power plants along with good-to-excellent renewable resources that cannot be interdicted easily, as they are less reliant on vulnerable, long-distance transmission lines and infrastructure that carry power north. In addition to strengthening the resilience of thermal power plants, including by stockpiling coal and natural gas reserves, Taiwan should increase construction of onshore solar and wind resources in the southern and central regions. Distributed renewables generation is much more difficult to take offline by Chinese forces in a quarantine, blockade, siege, or invasion.
With diesel generation in the north, generation from coal, gas, and nuclear power plants in the south, distributed renewables throughout the island, and aggressive rationing, Taiwan could extend its ability to endure an energy blockade from mere weeks to months.
Taiwan need not act alone, however. The United States has a critical role to play in averting a Taiwan energy contingency. US firms should engage with counterparts in Taiwan across all parts of the energy supply chain, including diesel generators and storage, LNG infrastructure, nuclear energy know-how, and solar and energy storage systems. The chief US contribution to Taiwan’s energy infrastructure might be preventing sabotage. In a contingency, CCP intelligence services would likely seek to degrade or disable Taiwan’s south-to-north power transmission lines and other energy infrastructure with either cyber or kinetic means. To accomplish kinetic sabotage, CCP intelligence services would use the full spectrum of their assets, including their connections with criminal networks. Accordingly, the United States should rotate a far greater number of energy, counternarcotics, and countersabotage personnel through Taiwan, drawing on the Department of Energy, the Drug Enforcement Administration, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and other civilian security agencies, through the American Institute in Taiwan.
China’s vulnerabilities: Leverage that could enforce stability
In addition to precautionary defensive measures, Washington, Taipei, and other actors should find other forms of leverage over Beijing. China’s food vulnerabilities are significant, while its steel industry relies extensively on Australian iron ore imports. Analysts should carefully scrutinize these commodities, especially if China begins to build inventories.
The most effective form of leverage vis-à-vis Beijing, however, could be economic and financial. China’s economic growth model might be broken. China remains highly reliant on other countries absorbing its overcapacity, as net exports’ contribution to GDP growth stood at 32.7 percent, the highest level since 1997. Far from successfully rebalancing, China’s economic and financial model has become more reliant on exports, investments, and debt, raising the likelihood of a painful correction. If Beijing attempted to coerce Taiwan, including through an energy quarantine, China’s ability to reach export markets might be imperiled due to a combination of economic, financial, cyber, and other measures. If China loses substantial access to export markets due to an unwise attempt to coerce Taipei, the risks for its economic, financial, social, and ultimately political stability could be profound.
While the risks of an energy quarantine are significant and rising, Taipei and Washington are well positioned to mitigate these dangers. Taiwan is already making great strides in enhancing its energy resilience. It should build on these efforts by building new generation for the long term and, especially, leveraging diesel as a near-term bridge solution. Similarly, Washington should take a more active role in opposing unilateral changes to the status quo by either side. Washington should underscore its continued commitment to the “One China” policy, anchored to the Taiwan Relations Act, the three communiqués, and the Six Assurances, while warning Beijing not to undertake aggression. If Taipei and Washington can see through this moment of danger, they could settle into a period of relative stability.
Joseph Webster is a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Global Energy Center and the Indo-Pacific Security Initiative; he also edits the independent China-Russia Report. This analysis reflects his personal opinion.

zh_title: 加拿大公布20多年来首个国家安全战略
summary: 加拿大公布了 20 多年来的首个国家安全战略——突破防御 加拿大总理兼加拿大自由党领袖马克·卡尼 (Mark Carney) 于 2025 年 4 月 29 日星期二早些时候在加拿大安大略省渥太华 TD Place 举行的选举之夜活动上公布。加拿大自由党预计将连续第四次赢得选举，并授权前央行行长卡尼 (Carney) 在竞选期间承诺促进经济增长并与美国总统唐纳德·特朗普 (Donald Trump) 对抗。在贸易战中。摄影师：David Kawai/Bloomberg via Getty Images 华盛顿——加拿大发布了一份
content:
加拿大公布20多年来首个国家安全战略 - Breaking Defense
加拿大总理兼加拿大自由党领袖马克·卡尼 (Mark Carney) 于 2025 年 4 月 29 日星期二早些时候在加拿大安大略省渥太华 TD Place 举行的选举之夜活动中。加拿大自由党预计将连续第四次赢得选举，前央行行长卡尼在竞选期间承诺促进经济增长并在贸易战中对抗美国总统唐纳德·特朗普，之后他将获得授权。摄影师：David Kawai/Bloomberg via Getty Images
华盛顿——加拿大今天发布了一份以主权为重点的国家安全战略——这是渥太华二十多年来首次发布这样的文件。
“加拿大正处于历史的关键时刻，”加拿大总理马克·卡尼今天在一份声明中表示。 “世界越来越多地被有争议的边界、独裁侵略和严重的全球威胁所定义。长期以来认为我们的地理、相互联系和基于规则的国际秩序的结合可以取代加拿大保护自己的主权能力的观点不再站得住脚。”
该战略让人们明白，加拿大“掌控自己的命运”，而且是在加拿大与其北美邻国美国因紧张的贸易谈判而关系紧张之际制定的。具体来说，国家安全政策强调了几个关键优先事项，包括与美国的“合作、清晰的关系”以及“创新”的加拿大经济。
卡尼表示：“为了加强我们的主权和国家安全，我们将通过几代人的国内投资来建立长期的经济实力。” “我们将发展一个密集的贸易关系网络，以增强我们的战略能力。我们将把外交努力集中在实际合作和伙伴关系上，这将有助于我们影响全球事件的进程，为加拿大人民的利益服务。我们将重建、重新武装和再投资加拿大武装部队。”
同样，该提案强调加拿大的目标是通过“全球伙伴关系体系”促进与国际伙伴的稳定。
卡尼在致辞中表示：“我们将通过使我们在世界各地的经济和安全关系多样化，包括与中东、非洲和其他地方的新伙伴的关系，来扩大我们的选择并增强我们的韧性。”
加拿大上次发布国家安全战略是在 2004 年。

“能够告诉指挥官你不需要做某事实际上也是一个非常有力的信息。”
值得注意的是，这一消息是在加拿大周五接收首批两架 F-35 战斗机后不到一周发布的。 2025 年 3 月，卡尼就任总理后不久，由于贸易争端以及唐纳德·特朗普总统有关加拿大成为美国第 51 个州的言论，渥太华搁置了原定购买 88 架战斗机的计划。加拿大迄今为止已购买了16架F-35飞机。
据路透社报道，尽管特朗普本月重申了他希望加拿大加入美国的意图，但他今天在南卡罗来纳州的一次竞选集会上表示，渥太华“最近对待美国非常好”。

Canada unveils first national security strategy in more than 20 years - Breaking Defense
Mark Carney, Canada's prime minister and leader of Canada's Liberal Party, during an election night event at TD Place in Ottawa, Ontario, Canada, early on Tuesday, April 29, 2025. Canada's Liberal Party is projected to win a fourth consecutive election, giving a mandate to former central banker Carney after a campaign in which he pledged to boost economic growth and stand up to US President Donald Trump in a trade war. Photographer: David Kawai/Bloomberg via Getty Images
WASHINGTON — Canada has released a national security strategy today focused on sovereignty — marking the first time Ottawa has released such a document in more than 20 years.
“Canada stands at a hinge moment in history,” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement today. “The world is increasingly defined by contested borders, authoritarian aggression, and acute global threats. The long-held belief that the combination of our geography, interconnectedness, and a rules-based international order could substitute for Canadian sovereign capacity to protect ourselves is no longer tenable.”
The strategy drives home that Canada “controls its own destiny,” and comes amid tension between Canada and its North American neighbor, the US, over tense trade negotiations. Specifically, the national security policy underscores several key priorities, including a “cooperative, clear-eyed relationship” with the US, and an “innovative” Canadian economy.
“To bolster our sovereignty and national security, we will build long-term economic strength through generational domestic investments,” Carney said. “We will develop a dense web of trading relationships that bolster our strategic capabilities. We will focus our diplomatic efforts on practical cooperation and partnerships that will help us influence the course of global events to serve the interests of Canadians. We will rebuild, rearm, and reinvest in the Canadian Armed Forces.”
Likewise, the proposal emphasizes that Canada aims to foster stability with international partners though a “global system” of partnerships.
“We will broaden our options and build our resilience by diversifying our economic and security ties around the world, including with new partners in the Middle East, Africa and elsewhere,” Carney said in his message.
Canada last released a national security strategy in 2004.

"Being able to tell the commander you don't need to do something is actually a pretty powerful message, as well."
Notably, the announcement comes less than a week after Canada received its first two F-35 fighter jets on Friday. In March 2025, shortly after Carney assumed his post as prime minister, Ottawa had put a hold on original plans to purchase 88 of the fighter jets due to trade disputes and President Donald Trump’s rhetoric about Canada becoming the 51st US state. Canada so far has purchased 16 F-35 aircraft.
Although Trump has reiterated his intention for Canada to join the US as recently as this month, he said today during a campaign rally in South Carolina that Ottawa has treated the US “extremely nicely recently,” Reuters reported.

2026 年 10 月 19 日，澳大利亚国防工业部长帕特·康罗伊 (Pat Conroy) 在悉尼安杜里尔 (Anduril) 工厂的自动海底航行器 Ghost Shark 前向媒体发表讲话。（Saeed Khan / 法新社，盖蒂图片社）
新西兰基督城——澳大利亚军方官员一直对如何使用 Anduril 开发的 Ghost Shark 超大型自主水下航行器（XLAUV）守口如瓶。然而，他们最近揭开了澳大利亚皇家海军正在部署的一些有效载荷的神秘面纱。
10 月 19 日，在澳大利亚悉尼 Anduril 制造中心举行的正式揭幕仪式上，展示了三枚“幽灵鲨”有效载荷。
其中一个是水雷，另一个是一群 Altius-600 徘徊弹药，第三个是后勤补给库。
换句话说：三个有效载荷中的两个包含动能效应器，可以为幽灵鲨提供更大的咬合力。
这意味着一艘 XLAUV 可以秘密部署十几个水雷，也许是在冲突期间的海上咽喉要道。
与此同时，安杜里尔的 Altius 武器可以执行监视和打击任务。
关于补给储备，一位官员表示，“这么说吧，人们可以发挥自己的想象力，想象哪些部队会在部署时使用这些补给储备。”
国防部在一份新闻稿中表示：“这些平台的模块化设计使它们能够操作一系列不同的有效载荷，并根据所需的任务进行定制。”
幽灵鲨正在开发其他有效载荷，可能涉及轻型和重型鱼雷以及电子战。
国防工业部长帕特·康罗伊解释说，“幽灵鲨”可以从集装箱、相对较小的船只的船尾或码头部署。
“这给对手留下了问号，”他说。
由于澳大利亚必须等待数年才能获得核动力潜艇，像“幽灵鲨鱼”这样的自主水下系统可以填补六艘老化的柯林斯级柴电潜艇继续缓慢前进的能力差距。
安杜里尔澳大利亚工厂不到一年前开业，“能够在远离我们海岸执行一系列复杂任务的‘幽灵鲨鱼’现在正以越来越快的速度下线，落入澳大利亚海军手中，”康罗伊说。
堪培拉为其幽灵鲨舰队花费了 17 亿澳元（12 亿美元）。这相当于“数十艘”XLAUV，但澳大利亚并未透露具体数量。
澳大利亚皇家海军还部署了澳大利亚 C2 Robotics 公司生产的小型 Speartooth XLAUV。
海军首席副上将马特·巴克利表示：“就我们的平台本身而言，它们当然必须继续发展，而我们可以安装到像“幽灵鲨”这样的无人舰艇上的模块化有效载荷的发展……为我们创造了巨大的灵活性，并使我们能够使这些系统适应未来的任务和未来的要求。”
他补充道：“我们的目标很明确——我们需要以相关的速度提供能力，加强我们进行水下作战和海底行动的能力，为海上拒止做出贡献，

Australia’s Minister for Defence Industry, Pat Conroy, speaks to the media in front of the autonomous undersea vehicle Ghost Shark at an Anduril facility in Sydney on Oct. 19, 2026. (Saeed Khan / AFP via Getty Images)
CHRISTCHURCH, New Zealand — Australian military officials have been furtive about how they will use Anduril-developed Ghost Shark extra-large autonomous underwater vehicles – or XLAUVs. However, they recently lifted the lid on some payloads the Royal Australian Navy is fielding.
In an official unveiling at Anduril Australia’s manufacturing center in Sydney on Oct. 19, three Ghost Shark payloads were revealed.
One entailed sea mines, another was a swarm of Altius-600 loitering munitions, and the third was logistics supply caches.
In other words: Two of the three payloads comprise kinetic effectors to give the Ghost Shark greater bite.
This means a single XLAUV can clandestinely deploy a dozen sea mines, perhaps in maritime chokepoints during a conflict.
Meanwhile, Anduril’s Altius weapons can perform both surveillance and strike.
Regarding the supply caches, an official said, “Let’s just say, people can use their imagination about the sort of forces that would use these on deployment.”
The Department of Defence said in a press release: “The modular design of these platforms allows them to operate a range of different payloads, customized to the required mission.”
Other payloads are being developed for the Ghost Shark, likely involving lightweight and heavyweight torpedoes, as well as electronic warfare.
Ghost Sharks can deploy from shipping containers, off the stern of relatively small ships or from wharves, Minister for Defence Industry Pat Conroy explained.
“It places question marks in adversaries’ minds,” he said.
With Australia having to wait years for nuclear-powered submarines to arrive, autonomous underwater systems like the Ghost Shark can fill capability gaps as six aging Collins-class diesel-electric submarines continue to plod along.
Anduril Australia opened its factory less than a year ago, and “Ghost Sharks capable of a range of complex missions operating far from our shores are now rolling off the line at an increasing rate into the hands of the Australian navy,” Conroy said.
Canberra is spending A$1.7 billion (US$1.2 billion) on its fleet of Ghost Sharks. This amounts to “dozens and dozens” of XLAUVs, but Australia is not saying how many exactly.
The Royal Australian Navy is also fielding the smaller Speartooth XLAUV from Australian firm C2 Robotics.
Navy Chief Vice Adm. Matt Buckley said: “In terms of our platforms themselves, of course they must continue to evolve, and the evolution of modular payloads that we can fit to uncrewed vessels like the Ghost Shark … creates enormous flexibility for us and allows us to adapt these systems to future missions and future requirements.”
He added: “Our purpose is clear – we need to deliver capability at the speed of relevance, strengthen our ability to conduct undersea warfare and seabed operations, contribute to sea denial and help protect our critical undersea infrastructure.”
The Ghost Shark and its payloads have participated in the past few Maritime Big Play Pacific events, including one in San Diego in October.
The first Ghost Shark was handed over to the Australian Navy for testing and acceptance in early 2026.
Gordon Arthur is an Asia correspondent for Defense News. After a 20-year stint working in Hong Kong, he now resides in New Zealand. He has attended military exercises and defense exhibitions in about 20 countries around the Asia-Pacific region.

content:
Zambia: Widespread Repression in Post-Election Crackdown - allAfrica.com
Zambia: Widespread Repression in Post-Election Crackdown
A Patriotic Front supporter proudly displays his identification and voter cards, Lusaka, Zambia (file photo).
Human Rights Watch (Washington, DC)
Opposition and Critics Forcibly Disappeared, Arbitrary Detained, Beaten
Zambian police and military forcibly disappeared, arbitrarily detained, beat, and threatened opposition members, lawyers, journalists, and government critics in the days before and after general elections in August.
The post-election climate of intimidation, harassment, and repression has had a chilling effect on civic and political organizations, particularly on dissenting voices.
The authorities should immediately halt the crackdown, allow access to lawyers and medical care to detainees, release everyone arbitrarily detained, and ensure accountability for abuses.
(Johannesburg) - The Zambian police and military forcibly disappeared, arbitrarily detained, beat, and threatened opposition members and supporters as well as lawyers, journalists, and government critics in the days before and after general elections in August 2026, Human Rights Watch said today. The authorities have also yet to credibly explain or investigate the killing of an opposition leader in contested circumstances.
"Zambia's government should break this dangerous cycle of repression," said Ashwanee Budoo-Scholtz, deputy Africa director at Human Rights Watch. "The authorities should immediately halt the ongoing post-election crackdown, allow access to lawyers and provide medical care for those in detention, release everyone arbitrarily detained, and ensure accountability for abuses by security forces."
Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines
President Hakainde Hichilema was reelected in the August 13 election, which observers said was marred by irregularities such as a suspension of counting and limited fundamental freedoms. From August 24 to 28, the authorities suspended judicial services and prevented legal challenges to the presidential election results, closing and cordoning off court premises. Zambian police stated that the closures were an "intelligence-led and preventive measure," without providing details.
Human Rights Watch documented 14 cases in August that appear to have been enforced disappearances, in which the authorities refused to reveal the situation and whereabouts of a detained person. Several of these people were initially forcibly disappeared for days. Victims, family members, and lawyers said that the military held some of them.
Human Rights Watch also documented 61 cases in which detainees or their lawyers and relatives allege that they were beaten or otherwise violently abused during their arrest, in detention, or both. Eighteen have been charged with treason, with two also facing sedition charges. In many cases, the people detained were never charged with a crime while in others, the charges against them appear to be politically motivated. The government has not disclosed how many people were arrested during the crackdown or the charges against them, prompting concerns that the number of people detained is higher than presently known.
Human Rights Watch has also documented two cases in which the Zambia-based relatives of government critics living abroad say government authorities harassed and threatened them.
The post-election climate of intimidation, harassment, and repression has had a chilling effect on civic and political organizations, particularly on dissenting voices, Human Rights Watch said. On September 11, the government announced the cancellation of six government critics' passports, including that of an academic, Sishuwa Sishuwa, for "security reasons."
On August 14, security forces raided the home of the Tonse Alliance opposition leader, Brian Mundubile, in a suburb of Lusaka, the capital. Opposition members present allege that security forces killed a former government minister, Mutotwe Kafwaya, during the raid. Inspector General of the Zambia Police Service Graphel Musamba said members of a "joint intelligence-led operation" were met with "gunfire and resistance from unknown individuals" that "prompted officers to return fire," and that Kafwaya had been killed in the process. Kafwaya's fate was not known until August 19, after his wife filed a habeas corpus petition to compel authorities to disclose his whereabouts, bring him before court, and show sufficient and lawful cause for his continued detention.
Public officials made contradictory statements about the raid and who was responsible for it. On August 15, the Zambia Information and Communications Technology Authority (ZICTA) sent out a text message to all registered phones in Zambia stating: "Beware of false reports of shootings and abductions. Stay calm and peaceful." The Ministry of Information and Media dismissed reports of the raid and shooting as "disinformation intended to alarm and mislead the public."
The police also issued a media statement denying that there had been a raid and that Mundubile was in police custody. Police Inspector General Musamba later admitted that there had been a "joint security-led intelligence operation" at Mundubile's home.
Mundubile, who was later arrested and charged with treason, stated in a High Court petition that Human Rights Watch has seen that he saw a member of the military fatally shoot Kafwaya.
Given the conflicting statements by government officials about who was responsible for the raid on Mundubile's home and the circumstances surrounding Kafwaya's killing, Zambian authorities should institute an independent, impartial, and thorough investigation into the matter, Human Rights Watch said.
Detainees have implicated Zambia's military in arbitrary detention and enforced disappearance. Forty-three opposition members acting as election monitors were detained on August 14. Their lawyer said their whereabouts had been unknown for eight days and that the police had denied holding them. When a lawyer finally saw them, he told Human Rights Watch that "most of them were swollen and had terrible injuries, including broken bones. They said they had been brutalized by the military." Their lawyers filed a habeas corpus application and, on September 10, a court in Lusaka ordered their immediate release.
Under Zambian law and international human rights law, all detainees have the right to due process, including to be promptly informed of the charges against them, to have access to counsel if charged with a crime, to have their detention reviewed by a judge, and to be presumed innocent. They should also have access to adequate medical care and be able to communicate with their families.
In a September 2 call, the United Nations special rapporteur on the rights to freedom of assembly and of association said that the authorities should "release all political detainees, respect fundamental freedoms, and restore democratic accountability." The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation said in response that the call was "inaccurate, undiplomatic and falling short of the standards of objectivity, moderation and discretion expected of UN mandate holders."
The ministry said that being a member of opposition party "does not place a person beyond the reach of the law, nor does it convert a criminal suspect into a political detainee... The government is committed to ensuring that these protections are respected in every case, and Zambia's courts are open to test them."
Zambia will serve as a member of the UN Human Rights Council for the 2027-2029 term. As a council member, Zambia is expected to "uphold the highest standards in the promotion and protection of human rights."
"The Zambian government's needs to end its brazen human rights crackdown," Budoo-Scholtz said. "Leaders in Southern Africa and Zambia's development partners should encourage President Hichilema to restore the rule of law and ensure that civic and political spaces are protected."
Enforced Disappearances, Including by Military Personnel
Human Rights Watch documented 14 cases of apparent enforced disappearances of opposition members and supporters, including some in which the authorities denied holding people who were later produced after habeas corpus applications.
The authorities claimed to have arrested 11 men during the August 14 raid on Mundubile's home.
Lawyers and family members of seven of the men said that they were made to lie down and were beaten using fists, rifle butts, and sticks, kicked by men in military uniform, then blindfolded and driven away in military vehicles. Victims and witnesses identified members of Zambia's military through their uniforms and military vehicles.
During the same raid, security forces picked up several opposition members and supporters and forcibly disappeared them for days before family members or their lawyers found them. They included Bishop Trevor Mwamba, an opposition leader; Patrick Mwansa, a leading opposition campaigner; and security aides Jackson Mutyoka, Bernard Chewe, Brazil Soko, Francis Mulenga, and Richard Banda.
According to their lawyers and court documents seen by Human Rights Watch, the men were taken to a "military command center" where they were "screened and processed" then detained in "various police stations around Lusaka." Lawyers and family members said they went around police stations in Lusaka looking for the detainees, but authorities denied holding the men. However, some were found days later at the same stations where the police had denied holding them.
Mwansa's family said he had a broken finger and swollen face when they finally located him four days later in Lusaka's Central Police Station. On September 6, Mwansa was moved to a maximum security prison in Kabwe, 150 kilometers from Lusaka, and has not yet received medical treatment, a family member said.
The family of Bishop Mwamba, president of the opposition United National Independence Party, who was also picked up during the raid at Mundubile's home, said they searched for him in police stations in and around Lusaka for four days before locating him at Matero Police Station. Earlier, including on the day he was located, officers at Matero Police Station had denied holding Mwamba.
"He had spent days without food and without taking his prescription medication," the relative said. "The police had first denied [holding him] but we insisted to see him, because we had received an anonymous tip informing us that he was at Matero. When they brought him out and we asked what he was arrested for, police said they had no charge for him 'because he was brought in by the military who asked us to keep him in the cells for them."'
On August 30, when the family took food and pain killers to Benard Chewe at Kabwata Police Station, where he had been detained, officers there told them that he had been moved but claimed that they did not know where. When the family traced him two days later to Mwembeshi Correctional Facility on the outskirts of Lusaka, they were denied access.
Men in unmarked vehicles who introduced themselves as "state intelligence officers" picked up Harry Findlay, a Lusaka businessman and opposition supporter, from his residence on August 4, a family member said. Neither his lawyer nor family had access to him, and the authorities did not inform them of his whereabouts. Findlay's lawyers sent two letters to Zambian authorities, on August 7 and August 17, requesting his whereabouts and calling for his immediate release and access to doctors, lawyers, and family.
On August 20, Findlay was taken to court under a judge's order to inquire into the legality of his detention. On August 29, he was charged with treason and moved to Mukobeko Maximum Security Prison, where he remains without trial.
All the men detained in the August 14 raid were eventually charged with treason and remain in detention without having appeared in court. Human Rights Watch believes that in these cases, Zambian authorities are using treason charges, which are nonbailable, and sedition, which carries a heavy penalty, to stifle dissent and political opposition.
On August 27, police arrested Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, and subsequently also charged them with treason and seditious practices. The charge sheet, which Human Rights Watch has seen, alleges that Mundubile and Zulu went on Facebook live on August 14 stating that the opposition had won the election. The government alleges that this was meant to "raise discontent or disaffection among the people of Zambia."
On September 22, the Law Association of Zambia raised concerns about prolonged detentions without court appearances. Zambia's Human Rights Commission on September 3 said it was following 84 election-related detainees whose cases it cast as part of a "disturbing pattern of prolonged detention, delayed notification of charges, restricted access to family and legal representation and failure to bring detainees before a competent court without undue delay."
Human Rights Watch documented that 61 people had been mistreated in custody by reviewing court documents and interviewing family members.
Lawyers for the 43 opposition members acting as election monitors who were detained on August 14 said that state security agents kicked and beat them and denied them food during the first 8 days of their 21-day detention.
Lawyers representing 18 detainees accused of treason state in court documents that the detainees were abused and assaulted in custody and denied medical attention. The lawyers also said 10 of the 18--George Chisanga, Patrick Mwansa, Trevor Mwamba, Francis Mulenga, Brazil Soko, Jackson Mutyoka, Bernard Chewe, Richard Banda, Emmanuel Mulenga, and Darius Mwila--had been restricted from accessing their lawyers or family members.
In a court petition filed on September 11, Ezra Topola, Dickson Tembo, and Victor Muzyamba alleged that security personnel waterboarded them and suspended them from a metal bar and beat them. Findlay alleged that he was kept in solitary confinement in Mwembeshi Correctional Facility and denied access to his prescription medication. Mwansa alleged that he suffered serious injuries, including cuts to his face and a fracture on his hand, but was denied access to medical attention.
Family members told Human Rights Watch that when they found Mutyoka on August 17 at Lusaka's Central Police Station, three days after military detained him at Mundubile's home, he showed signs of having been physically abused. "When we saw him, his face was swollen, he was coughing blood and was limping," a relative said. "He said they had been made to lie down in the yard of Mundubile's home and beaten using rifle butts and whips by masked men in military unform. All he wanted was to see a doctor, but that request was denied and, to this day, he has not been seen by a doctor."
When Chewe's family members found him at Kabwata Police Station three days after he was taken from Mundubile's home, they said that he too showed signs of physical abuse. "He had a swollen forehead, busted lips, and complained of body pains," a relative said. "He said he had been assaulted by the military at their headquarters before they took him to the police station."
Lawyers for Chewe, Mutyoka, and Soko at Mwembeshi Correctional Facility said that Zambia Army Special Forces personnel interrogated them and that on September 10, authorities moved the three to Mukobeko Maximum Security Prison without informing family or lawyers.
On October 27, family members said medical doctors have not yet seen the three despite urgent letters written on September 9, seen by Human Rights Watch, to the commissioner of the Zambia Correctional Service and the officer-in-charge of Mwembeshi Correctional Facility.
Eight election monitors for the opposition, men aged 21 to 26, said a group of armed soldiers wearing uniforms and masks jumped over the perimeter wall into a house in Lusaka's Emmasdale township on August 15 around 8 p.m., where the monitors were meeting. They said the armed soldiers dragged them out of the house, kicked them with boots, and beat them with fists and sticks.
They were forced into a military truck and taken away but could not identify where they were held. For the next three days, security forces beat them several times a day, demanding confessions that they belonged to "Brian Mundubile's militia." All eight were released on August 18 without charge.
Human Rights Watch has also examined a petition filed on September 11 by lawyers for the 18 accused of treason that implicates the army in interrogations and abuse of detainees. In the petition, lawyers allege that special forces personnel led by Gen. Moses Shapwaya threatened and intimidated some of the detainees in prison to force them to incriminate Mundubile and Zulu.
From court records and interviews with victims, family, and lawyers, Human Rights Watch documented 71 cases in which opposition members and supporters, as well as government critics, were arrested on charges that may be politically motivated or held in prolonged detention without charge. These include the 43 election monitors and 17 musicians and comedians who were detained after performing at an opposition rally, among others.
The arrest of the 43 monitors came after the opposition leader stated that he planned to challenge the election result in court, while the government accused him of plotting an insurgency. In an electoral court challenge, the monitors would have been potential witnesses for the opposition's case. After their 21 days in detention without charge, the court ruled that their arrest was unjustified and ordered their immediate release.
Human Rights Watch interviewed a 44-year-old Lusaka mathematician who was hired to tally numbers for a potential court challenge to President Hichilema's election. He said that on August 15 at about 9:30 p.m., about eight armed men who identified themselves as intelligence and police officers broke into his house and harassed him. They demanded access to his phone and laptop, he said, and to know who was funding the court challenge.
He said they dragged him outside, put him into a vehicle, and took him to the police headquarters in Lusaka, where he was interrogated further about the election petition. The next day, he was transferred to Ridgeway Police Station, where he spent 18 days without being charged. On August 28, his lawyer filed a habeas corpus application in the Lusaka High Court, which Human Rights Watch has seen. Five days later, police charged him with a misdemeanor offense and released him the same day.
Before the election, on August 5, a group of 17 people were arrested after performing at an opposition rally in Mongu, Western province. Police detained them for over two weeks on what was initially said to be a traffic offense of travelling in a vehicle without numbered plates, a lawyer familiar with the case told Human Rights Watch.

The lawyer said that the group's arrest and prolonged detention were politically motivated because of their vocal and visible mobilization for the opposition. Police later charged and prosecuted the 17 for "riotous assembly or behavior." In a court document seen by Human Rights Watch, the state alleges that the 17 did "unlawfully assemble and begun to execute a common purpose by a breach of peace and the terror of the public." A court released them on bail on August 30, after over three weeks in detention.
Human Rights Watch interviewed seven people, including lawyers and a journalist, who said they had fled their homes because they believed they had been targeted for arrest in the days after the August 13 election. A lawyer and a journalist showed Human Rights Watch messages on their phones alerting them that they were on a "wanted list." Some left and others were in hiding within the country.
A statement by seven international lawyers' associations said some lawyers involved in preparing or lodging election-related legal challenges had fled Zambia due to threats to their safety.
A lawyer said that he went into hiding on August 15 after scores of security agents came to his home and office. The lawyer had been acting on behalf of Tonse Alliance, including working on a court petition to challenge President Hichilema's election. "There was no reason for the security agents to chase me in that manner," he said. "If the police wanted me for any reason, they should have alerted me, and I would have presented myself with my legal representatives."
Mulenga Kapwepwe, an opposition leader who worked closely with Mundubile and Zulu, said she went into hiding on August 15 after confidential sources alerted her that she was "on a wanted list." "I have had to rearrange my life," she said. "Many of my colleagues are in detention charged with treason, and I have been warned that the moment I come out of hiding, I will be targeted."
On August 17, a journalist who runs an investigative journalism website and has previously been detained for his journalism crossed the border into a neighboring country hours before security agents went to his house looking for him. "My website was following up on the raid at Mundubile's house," he said. "That is when I received messages on my phone saying: 'Stop what you are doing. We are coming after you.' I was once arrested and detained without charge for nearly two weeks. I know what these people are capable of. So, fearful for my life, I left."
While he was fleeing, the journalist said, he received a call from a family member that about five people who identified themselves as officers from Office of the President were at his house looking for him. They told his family that he was wanted for sedition.
Human Rights Watch documented two cases in which the authorities allegedly harassed and threatened the Zambia-based family members of government critics living abroad.
Police allegedly detained two siblings of a well-known diaspora critic of the government and harassed their 76-year-old father, demanding that their sibling abroad, who runs a popular social media page with hundreds of thousands of followers, take down material critical of the government.
One sibling was detained in a 3 a.m. raid on their home, in which armed police officers demanded access to their phones and laptop, a close source said, adding that one of the police officers "had a gun and said: 'This is a high security operation." The officers said the foreign-based sibling's "political commentary was 'a problem' and that they needed it to stop." The authorities allegedly demanded the removal of specific videos as a condition for their release. In one of these videos, the social media personality demanded an independent inquiry into the August 14 killing of Kafwaya.
In another case, a government critic in the United States with investments in Zambia said that three men who identified themselves as intelligence officers from the Office of the President approached family members in Zambia days after the election and threatened to "squeeze" her businesses if she continued to criticize President Hichilema's administration on social media. "They told my sister, a civil servant, that she risked losing her job if I did not tone down my criticism," the critic said.
